written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Hill House, a structure with a mind of its own, rested against the hills, its darkness palpable, its sanity questionable.  For eighty years it had borne silent witness to untold horrors, and eighty more it might endure, its walls upright, its floors firm, its doors closed, a tomb of secrets.  Within its depths, Dr. John Montague, a man of letters and a scholar of the unseen, sought to unravel the mysteries that clung to the house like cobwebs.  His excitement was a tangible thing, a nervous energy that thrummed beneath his skin as he surveyed his conquest.He had come seeking a haunted house, and Hill House, with its malevolent reputation, seemed to fit the bill.  It had cost him dearly, this pursuit of the paranormal, both in the coin of the realm and the currency of his reputation.Yet, he was undeterred, his resolve as firm as the foundations of the house itself.  He would have his proof, his definitive study of psychic disturbances, a testament to the unseen world that whispered just beyond the veil of perception. Dr. Montague, a man who clung to his title as if it were a life raft in a sea of skepticism, was determined to conquer the mysteries of Hill House.  He would face the darkness, the unseen forces that lurked within, and emerge with the truth, or be consumed by the shadows that stretched long and hungry within the walls of the house.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Up on the tallest hill sat the aptly named Hill House, a place not entirely sane. From its high point, Hill House lorded over the town, judgmental in its solitude. The house enjoyed its loneliness, and the town preferred the continued isolation of Hill House. The windows were ever shuttered, the rusted main gate always locked, keeping the world out and the occupants in. Dr. John Montague was the latest resident, a man far more foolish than his doctorate in anthropology would lead one to believe. His path of study brought him not to the study of people, but deceased people. Dr. Montague considered himself an expert in paranormal happenings, a fact that left him with few peers. Academics shunned him, and he shunned ghost hunters. Formally organized academia needed to be inserted into the field of the supernatural if there was ever going to be a proper study done, and Dr. Montague was more than willing to use his credentials to move things along. Renting Hill House came at significant financial cost to Dr. Montague, but he was quite certain that this was the avenue that would lead him to career success. No one could look at Hill House and dismiss that it was a truly haunted house. Dr. Montague had researched the house himself and found its past riddled with the occult. Once he conducted his study and produced a paper that could double as a guidebook to the paranormal, the checks written to rent the house would cease to matter.
written_by_MFA025.Reason:
Excerpt 2 is the most superior mainly due to its fluency. I believe excerpt 1 may be stronger when taking into account its coherence, but the writing style is rather disjointed and unnatural. The first sentences demonstrate this clearly: 

Excerpt 1: Hill House, a structure with a mind of its own, rested against the hills, its darkness palpable, its sanity questionable.

Excerpt 2: Up on the tallest hill sat the aptly named Hill House, a place not entirely sane.

Both of these sentences have delivered essentially the same information, but excerpt 2 has managed this task in a far more concise and 'readable' manner, which I believe also makes it far more effective. This is echoed throughout both texts.

written_by_MFA022.Excerpt1: Dr. John Montague stood before Hill House, a place that loomed as though waiting, its cold stones heavy with silence. The house, not sane, appeared to lean slightly forward, its dark windows watching him with a lifeless gaze, as though withholding secrets that could never be pried free. Hill House had stood for eighty years, holding within its walls an impenetrable darkness that even sunlight seemed reluctant to touch. The hills rose sharply behind it, framing its stark isolation; the house seemed less built than grown, an aberration of nature. Dr. Montague, meticulous in his methods yet quietly burdened by self-doubt, adjusted his glasses, a gesture as habitual as his reliance on his title—"Doctor of Philosophy in Anthropology"—to shield himself from skepticism. For years, his inquiries into the supernatural had been met with thinly veiled disdain, but Hill House represented his long-sought grail: an authentic haunting, a house with whispers in its foundation. He had rented the property at a steep price, its rooms and halls offered not for comfort but as a proving ground for his theories. As he crossed the threshold, the air seemed to shift, pressing lightly against his skin as though the house was tasting him. He paused, glancing back at the gravel drive that led away, the thought fleeting: nothing here would let him leave unmarked. The door shut behind him with a finality that echoed briefly, then faded, swallowed entirely by the unbroken, unnerving silence of Hill House.
written_by_MFA022.Excerpt2: Hill house, not sane, stood alone amongst the darkness. A house born within a garden of oleander, no person alive could claim witness to its birth, and so the poisonous intentions of the house were known only to itself. Only Dr. Montague, snaking up the thorn-lined driveway in a car packed with books, would observe the house’s final blooming, though even he, a man of scholarship and philosophy, a fastidious believer in the supernatural, would come to doubt what the Hill House had to show him. Dr. Montague was a man of doubt, not of the world, or of the unspoken phenomena hidden within it, but of himself, and his instincts, which he sought to justify through scholarship; Indeed, he arrived at Hill House surrounded by the false safety of his books on an errand of study, having rented the home at considerable personal and financial cost, with the hope of producing definitive work on psychic disturbances and their accompanying phenomena. He believed himself, after conducting a lifelong search for a haunted home, to have found Hill House; this was a false belief. It was Hill House that found Dr. Montague, alone in his study, nursing his failures with cognac in hand as he lingered over a newspaper clipping which happened to mention, offhandedly, the strange occurrences of a mansion atop a hill in a small New England town. This home could contain answers, he thought, slowing his car to park beneath the ominous gaze of the house's front windows, answers only I can find.
written_by_MFA022.Reason: This one feels slightly easier to read and comprehend. I think it feels like it flows a bit better. The writing seems more direct. The language is easy to understand and sentences are short. It clearly explains what is going on and intrigues the reader. It feels more natural to have the Dr as protagonist rather than the house.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Hill House waited, its brooding silence pressing against the walls like a living thing, holding darkness within its brick and timber bones as it had for eighty years. Through its malevolent windows, it watched Dr. John Montague approach, his academic credentials clutched like a shield before him, as though his doctor of philosophy might protect him from whatever dwelled in the house's shadowed corners. He came with his leather briefcase and carefully organized notes, believing that science could explain away the whispers in empty rooms, the footsteps that followed no feet, the cold spots that lingered like breath on glass. The locals spoke of Hill House only in whispers, their eyes sliding away when they mentioned its name, but Dr. Montague saw only the promise of scholarly recognition, of footnotes and bibliographies and peer reviews. written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: The glass partition reflected my spectacled face, sallow and withdrawn, as we sat at the group table near the kitchen. My father's hands, roughened by work, rested uneasily on the paper placemat while we waited, ignored by the waiters who glided past with studied indifference. At the next table, a girl my age lounged with casual elegance, her summer-bronzed skin gleaming against a crisp white blouse. She spooned yogurt—a food I had never tasted—with the natural grace of someone who had always known its existence. Her father, well-dressed and at ease, gestured expressively as he spoke to her. They had ordered à la carte, their plates arranged with careful precision by attentive staff. When our fixed-price meals finally arrived, the mashed potatoes sat in a grayish heap, unmolded from some industrial container. My father ate in silence, his shoulders tense, his fork scraping the institutional plate. For days afterward, he would mutter about the "pig slop" they had served us, each repetition of the phrase carrying the accumulated weight of a lifetime of similar humiliations. I understood then that the restaurant had sorted us, placed us in our proper social category—the cheap seats, the hurried service, the institutional food. We belonged to the world of fixed-price menus and group tables, while others inhabited the realm of individual choice, of yogurt and carefully plated dishes, of being seen and served with deference.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: We sat there, my father and I, at the group table. Anyone looking our way could see our discomfort. I touched my spectacles and watched myself in the great wall mirror - each time finding myself paler and more repulsive. My father grew more agitated, too, letting our meager conversation drop, because the waiter had still not come with his mashed potatoes after so many dreary minutes. I watched a girl near my age across the room dining at her own special table with an older man. I watched her through the mirror in case she might meet my eye. She was tan and lifted a spoon of creamy yogurt to her lips. I was lost, for a moment, in imagining its flavor. I had never tasted yogurt before. When our food came at last, it looked nothing like the pretty plate in front of the tan girl - the same way my clothes looked nothing like hers - the same way my skin matched the grey sky outside while hers glowed like the sun in the tropics. Later, in the streets and at home, my father repeatedly talked about the "pig slop" they served him at the restaurant and vowed never to return. It took me years to understand how he was complaining - in his own way - of the hurt that came with seeing, but never ordering, "à la carte."
written_by_MFA016.Reason: I believe this is a difficult choice, as both have their unique nuance and writing styles, but I prefer the second of the two excerpt s. I feel that it is far more fluent and delivers the required message far more effectively than the first. While the first does have its merits, namely the more elevated writing quality, I find that it is over the top. It is clear that both pieces are trying to deliver impact and an emotional response, but there is a very thin line between intellectuality and lack of coherence in the name of profoundness.

written_by_MFA033.Excerpt1: At the restaurant, a dim-lit corner housed a long table where we were seated, our pale faces barely catching the flicker of candlelight. The service was indifferent, the kind that signaled our place—second-class, among the unremarkable and the unseen. I watched the teenage girl at the next table, her tanned skin glowing, the light glancing off the curve of her bare arm as she dipped a spoon into her yogurt. It wasn’t just the yogurt, unfamiliar and faintly exotic, or her easy laughter as she spoke to the older man, presumably her father. It was the way she leaned back in her chair, utterly at home in a place where I shrank. I caught my reflection in the mirror—a pale, spectral figure, glasses catching the flicker of light like an accusation. My father sat stiffly, the lines on his face deepened by a furrow of discontent. The mashed potatoes, a mound of something that seemed to sneer back at us, bore the brunt of his irritation. "Pig slop," he muttered, too loud, earning a glance from the waiter that reeked of disdain. He repeated the phrase later, at home, his voice rising each time, but I knew it wasn’t the food. It was the yogurt, the girl, her easy privilege, the sharp reminder of where we belonged in the silent hierarchy of the dining room. He wanted to explain the indignity, to frame it in something tangible, and so he said, "pig slop." I, too, clung to the detail, though for me it was the yogurt, a symbol of a world I had not yet entered. In that moment, the line between us and them felt etched into the tablecloth, as indelible as the reflection in the mirror.
written_by_MFA033.Excerpt2: My father wanted to take me to lunch. He found a restaurant unlike any I’d ever been to, unlike anything that existed in C. Any excitement I felt disappeared quickly. The waiter looked us up and down, seeing what we were immediately. I was pale from the winter, dressed in my worn, washed clothes. I wore spectacles, awkward and out of fashion, the kind you could buy at a steep discount. The waiter directed us to a shared table at the back of the restaurant, in front of the wash closet. At first my experience of discomfort was limited only to me. My father still had a big smile, ear to ear. But then I saw another father-daughter pair at a table in the restaurant’s big window. The girl was around my age, and pretty. She dealt with the restaurant staff confidently, with a confiding air, like they shared a special secret. I watched the girl longingly. Her tanned legs ended in delicate buckled shoes. I watched her eat food I could not identify. written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: In the muted light of the restaurant, the stark class divide was as palpable as the stale odor clinging to the worn velvet seats.  My spectacles, magnifying the pallor of my reflection, seemed to amplify my sense of displacement.  At our table, a shared expanse with strangers, the service was a reluctant dance of neglect.  In contrast, a few tables away, a tanned teenage girl, radiating an aura of effortless confidence, shared an intimate meal with an older man.  Her laughter, light and carefree, bounced off the gilded mirrors, mocking my own constrained stillness.Her spoon, a silver arc, delivered a dollop of yogurt to her lips—a food so exotic, it was a whisper from another world.  My gaze drifted back to my plate, the food suddenly as bland as the pity I felt for myself.  Later, my father's voice, rough with suppressed resentment, dissected the meal, the "pig slop" mashed potatoes becoming a metaphor for our diminished status.  We were not "à la carte" patrons, and our presence was a mere tolerated intrusion.  The restaurant, a microcosm of society, had laid bare the invisible lines that defined our place.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: My father and I dined at an upscale restaurant in the 13th arrondissement. We each ordered chicken legs and mashed potatoes, and we sat stiffly while waiting for our food. It was clear that both of us felt uncomfortable with the opulence of the space, but neither of us knew how to say so. Nearby, a girl around the age of fifteen sat with an older man, presumably her father, eating a foreign-looking food that I didn't recognize—a bowl of yogurt, I later learned. She looked deeply at ease eating her meal, and I was disturbed to see myself in the mirror on the adjacent wall—spectacled, pale. Compared to the girl, I looked homely and unimportant, or at least I felt that I did at the time. For a moment I imagined myself as the girl, tan and comfortable among the trappings of wealth, though even then I knew that the hallmarks of the working class were written all over my face and my behavior. My father and I sat for a while in silence, and when the waitstaff brought out our plates, he remarked to me that his mashed potatoes looked like "pig slop." At the time, I thought he was just being fussy about his meal and I felt annoyed. Later I understood that he was deeply hurt at having been treated as second-class citizens who weren't ordering à la carte like the girl and her father, though he never said as much—he just continued talking about the potatoes, their unpleasant texture, their unsightly gray appearance.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: In excerpt 2, the statement flows very easy, and you can also feel the smoothness in it a lot. It makes the statement very complete and easy to understand. It is no doubt that it is the best statement you can ever get, such a proper and well detailed response.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Christ almighty, here we are - trapped in this feverish documentation of a madman's journey, watching the words crawl across the page like speed-crazed insects searching for meaning in the neon wasteland between Hollywood and Vegas. The story reeks of desperate chemicals and the acrid stench of burning rubber on asphalt, all wrapped up in the frenzied quest for the Great American Convertible. My attorney, that chrome-domed harbinger of chaos, is barking into payphones at terrified salesmen while I hover near the bar of some godforsaken Polynesian tomb, mainlining Singapore Slings and wondering if we'll ever make it out of LA alive. The whole scene has the surgical precision of a hurricane - first the maniac phone calls, then the ugly business with the recording equipment, and somewhere in between, the grotesque spectacle of that poor bastard getting mowed down by a Stingray on Sunset. Jesus, what a place. What a time. The salesmen are wielding tire irons now, passing our gear through a crack in the door like they're feeding raw meat to a cage full of rabid wolverines. Can't blame them, really - not with what's happening out there in the streets. The whole country's gone belly-up with fear and loathing, and here we are, two professional journalists, supposedly documenting this circus of depravity. But the real story isn't in the facts - it's in the white-knuckled grip on the wheel at 110 mph, in the savage heart of the American Dream gone wrong. The evidence is everywhere: in the twisted metal on Sunset, in the paranoid eyes of the salesmen, in the heinous chemicals coursing through our bloodstreams like electric eels in a bathtub. And somehow we're supposed to make sense of it all, turn it into something resembling journalism. What a goddamn joke. But there's no going back now - we've bought the ticket, and by God, we're going to take the ride.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: The attorney was on the phone, his voice a guttural rasp against the faux-Polynesian backdrop of the bar. "Red," he barked, "not pink. And make it snappy, the goddamn plane leaves in three hours."  I swiveled on the barstool, the vinyl squeaking in protest, and surveyed the wreckage of our preparations. Empty Mai Tai glasses stood like fallen soldiers, casualties in the war against sobriety. A crumpled napkin bore the cryptic message,"Convertible. Red. Not a goddamn boat."Outside, the Hollywood sun beat down with the malevolence of a loan shark. A pack of tourists shuffled past, their eyes glazed over with the vacant stare of the terminally sunburned. A low-slung Stingray roared by, leaving behind the faint scent of burnt rubber and the echo of a scream.  "Jesus," I muttered, "this town is a goddamn meat grinder."The attorney slammed the phone down, his face a mask of grim determination. "Got it," he snarled, "a red convertible. Picking it up in an hour."  He fixed me with a bloodshot stare. "Now, about that recording equipment..."We found the electronics store tucked away in a seedy strip mall, sandwiched between a bail bondsman and an adult bookstore. The salesmen eyed us with the suspicion of a pit bull eyeing a poodle. "We're closed," one growled, brandishing a tire iron."Bullshit," the attorney snarled back, "we just need some high-quality recording equipment. And we're in a hurry."  The door cracked open a few inches, revealing a glimpse of darkened aisles and the glint of chrome. A hand emerged, clutching a hefty price list. "Cash only," a voice rasped.An hour later, we emerged from the store, blinking against the harsh sunlight. The attorney clutched a bag crammed with microphones, recorders, and enough batteries to power a small city. I hefted a suitcase filled with enough "heinous chemicals" to fuel a weekend-long bender.We piled into the waiting convertible, the red paint gleaming like a fresh coat of blood. The attorney gunned the engine, and we roared off into the desert, leaving behind the madness of Hollywood and heading towards the even greater madness of Las Vegas.  The wind whipped through our hair, carrying with it the scent of freedom and the promise of adventure. This was the Gonzo life, and we were riding it full throttle, straight into the heart of the American Dream.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: My life felt chaotic, and I decided the best way to deal with this would be to go on a reckless drive while indulging in loads and loads of heinous chemicals. We decided we would drive from Hollywood to Vegas, and I began to round up all my drugs—mescaline, amyl, and half a jar of cocaine that I had been keeping in my coat closet for a special occasion. At the same time, I sent my attorney out to look for a decent convertible with a high-quality stereo so that we could listen to music as loud as we wanted while driving through the desert. There were a lot of false starts; for several hours my attorney spoke aggressively on the phone with several car rental agencies while we sat at a Polynesian bar, with me sneaking off occasionally to do hits of acid in the bathroom. He kept needing to demand respect from these salesmen guys who were jerking him around, which I felt completely reflected the energy of Los Angeles at the time… everyone talking over one another and wanting desperately to wring the other’s neck, and yet nobody capable of listening to a single word the other is saying…eventually he got it straightened out, after hanging up angrily a few times and cursing while this ugly group of veins nearly popped out of his neck, and while we drive back to my place we saw a Stingray car hit a woman crossing Sunset Boulevard—she lay there, spread-eagled, and I remember thinking that this was what America had come to now, reduced to lying lifeless among the bird shit on the street. When we finally made it to the store with the audio equipment, things became even more unbearable, everything rushing down on me like a wave made from needles. Through a half-cracked open door, my attorney argued with the salespeople, who clearly wanted us out of there as quickly as possible. They held their tire irons like baseball bats, and I felt scared, but intrigued, although maybe it was the acid making me feel scared…I wanted to know what would happen, and I wanted, more than anything, for the rushing feeling to stop. Back and forth and back and forth and back and forth they went, until eventually, it was over and we started our drive through the desert.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: The attorney was on the phone, his voice a guttural rasp against the faux-Polynesian backdrop of the bar. "Red," he barked, "not pink. written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: The plan was simple—if you could call it that—get the car, get the gear, and get out before anybody realized we were far too gone to be handling lethal machinery. My attorney had a phone jammed to his ear, barking demands at a salesman who clearly wanted nothing more than to shove a tire iron through his skull. “We need a convertible, the biggest one you’ve got. No, don’t give me that Chevy Impala bullshit, I want something with horsepower, something that howls like a dying wolf on the open road.” I could see the man on the other end hesitating, sensing that this was a deal he wanted no part of, but the law was clear—money talks, and we had just enough to sound legitimate. Meanwhile, across the room, a Stingray had just mowed down some poor bastard on Sunset Boulevard, the last frantic gasps of air leaking out of his ruined lungs as people stood around pretending not to see. My attorney watched, nodding approvingly, as if this was part of the deal. “That’s efficiency,” he muttered. I took a long drag from my cigarette and checked the time—not because it mattered, but because it felt important to note that this day had already spun out of control and it wasn’t even noon. The air smelled like hot asphalt and tequila. The salesmen were jittery now, fumbling with the equipment we needed—high-quality recording gear, something we could use to document the horrors we were bound to encounter in Vegas. The door cracked open just enough for us to reach through and grab our loot, an unspoken agreement that we would disappear into the desert and never return. “Load it up,” my attorney barked, shoving a crumpled wad of cash through the gap. “And throw in a few extra tapes. I have a feeling we’re going to need them.” He grinned like a man on the verge of a spectacular crime, then turned to me. “Time to move. The road waits for no one.” I nodded, already feeling the rush, the weight of reckless momentum pulling us forward. It was go-time, and there was no turning back.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I was driving at an absurd speed and trying my best to keep to the road—though I could be excused for the rumbling moments when I veered into the orange moonscape, because it didn't matter at all as long as you didn't mind a few dings in your fender. I was hallucinating a chase and knew any dip in speed would end my life. My life was behind me, chemicals were in front of me and inside me, and this gave me some real pep as the tires screamed down the asphalt trail. The attorney sat in the passenger seat, even more delusional, leaning and bending with the rapidly changing momentum of the vehicle like an inflatable man. We went over a rock with a terrible chunking sound, and he didn't even wince as I turned us back toward the street and away from the cacti and boiled soil stretching endlessly around us. We were leaving Hollywood and aiming vaguely for Las Vegas. We rarely consulted maps or asked for directions. We would get there. The attorney slammed another acid tab into his mouth. The car, I realized, wouldn't do at all. It was too slow and too compact. It was terrible. What we needed was a big, rumbling convertible. We stopped for a few drinks at an ugly Polynesian bar, and the attorney made some frantic calls about a new rental, demanding the respect an esquire deserves. He did it. We turned off at a rental joint to turn in our desecrated piece of crap for a nice new Stingray. The salesman haggled with us, thinking we couldn't haggle back under the grip of heinous chemicals. We also required some high-quality recording equipment, which we would find when we finally tore into Vegas. There was something we needed it for, because this was a work trip, and all our expenses were dutifully covered as long as we did the interviews. We tried to enter an electronics store, and the clerk stopped us. "Go away," he said, holding the door shut. He waved a crowbar. The attorney negotiated quickly, sneaking company credit cards through the crack, and shortly after, recording equipment sat on the curb with us. We lay there, basking in the motion of our minds, when a Stingray convertible bashed into an elder across the road and left him to die.

The language used is relatable and is non-emotional of the characters. “ Time to move. The road waits for no one. ” I nodded, already feeling the rush, the weight of reckless momentum pulling us forward. It was go-time, and there was no turning back.

My attorney watched, nodding approvingly, as if this was part of the deal. “That’s efficiency,” he muttered. written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: The resort lay like a discarded memory, its swimming pools filled with brackish water and fallen leaves – not the romantic decay of abandoned European castles, but the hasty, unplanned desertion of a colonial dream. Walking along the cracked sidewalks, where weeds pushed through with primitive determination, I saw the debris of departed lives: a sodden Belga cigarette packet, its blue and white design still visible, speaking of evenings when settlers sat in wicker chairs discussing home leave and servant troubles; a broken tennis racquet, its strings dangling like the exposed nerves of a dead thing, recalling Sunday afternoon games followed by gin and tonics on the clubhouse veranda. Everything here had been arranged to deny Africa, to create an illusion of Surrey or Sussex: the neat flowerbeds, now choked with wild grass, the carefully planned paths that led to viewing points designed to frame the landscape like an English watercolor. But Africa had returned, seeping through the cracks, asserting itself in the persistent growth that threatened to swallow the mock-Tudor buildings, in the small creatures that had made homes in abandoned tea rooms. The place possessed now a particular sadness – not of ruins, which suggest grandeur, but of irrelevance. Like the colonial administrators' files still rotting in some government office, like the old settlers' clubs with their dated photographs and empty bars, it belonged to a world that had ended not with ceremony but with a series of small surrenders, each one unremarkable in itself, until one day the illusion simply ceased to hold.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: The dilapidation that had befallen the resort was to be expected; it had been a place for rest for those who had come to sow unrest, and now that the country was in a state of repair, that which had once been repaired was left to rot. But there were still definite traces of life—beetles that scuttled about licking up dots of water from rivets in aged tiles, vines that wrapped up and through the sides of the canopy built to allow proprietors to gaze at a view without being at the mercy of the cruel sun, thickets of brush with twig-like branches that lined the path to the long-sealed front doors now grew unwieldy and sharp, as their nature demanded. But so too, prominent, were the signs of abandon. A pack of Belga cigarettes, the faded packaging promising style and mystical aura, lay on a patio table. If one listened in the silence, one could almost hear the smacking of thin European lips that may have once suckled the tobacco while remarking about the grand African sun or commenting on the foliage. But the sound would soon be drowned out by the noise of a country that had moved on to larger things—where words like "reclaim," "rebuild," "remove" erupted out of automobiles, cafes, town halls, meeting circles, makeshift stages, military bases, parliament buildings, and where, yes, perhaps, there was still space for the word "resort," but only if used in the phrase "last resort." And so the empty building sat, bludgeoned by the naked sun, waiting again for peace, for purpose.

written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: The forecourt wore it well—time, and the fickle seasons of democracy in this place. The moldings decorating the façade betrayed nothing either, except perhaps the usual negligence, the fine patina of dust that came over everything in Africa. But in its interior courtyards, in its once-ornate villas and lush gardens, where the Crown’s servants had dealt out their decks of cards atop white tablecloths, nothing stirred. A grim silence overwhelmed the resort. The grass yellowed under termite-ridden bedframes and writing desks; around them, rags of newspaper and littered correspondences. Vague ink-stains remained on these pages; and a sentence that, ten years ago, could martial an army from one corner of the empire to another was now indecipherable. A pack of “Belga” cigarettes had survived free Africa, escaped the line of white and Asian refugees at the docks, the inevitable mutiny and the mutiny after that. It lay sedately on a bench. For years, its odor would not leave the wooden slats; and in its slim shape it carried the vestiges of wet, European summers, trails of water from the pool to the bar, the rattle of ice in a tumbler, liveried black boys sweating in the corner, out of sight and at hand. There had been no native plants, no local liquors, no reminders of Africa at the resort—except its conveniences. The brand of cigarettes, of course, was extinct; the company had settled into ruin when its directors left on the outbound ships. The cigarettes were manufactured, now, in the countryside, by Africans; everybody smoked, and the sky slowly turned gray.
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: The once-vibrant resort now stood in a state of decay, a stark reminder of the societal shifts that had swept through the region.  The sidewalks, once bustling with tourists, were now littered with the remnants of a bygone era: broken furniture, discarded books, and flattened cigarette packets.  Among the debris, a Belga cigarette packet, a relic of European holidays, hinted at the resort's colonial past.  It was a place built by settlers who sought to recreate a familiar European lifestyle in the heart of Africa.The resort's decline mirrored the broader social and political changes that had reshaped the region.  Independence, military mutinies, and the exodus of white and Asian settlers had left the resort without purpose, a ghost of its former self.  The buildings, once grand and imposing, now bore the scars of neglect, their paint peeling and their windows boarded up.  The gardens, once meticulously manicured, were now overgrown and wild, a testament to the absence of the hands that once tended them.The resort's decline was not merely physical; it was also a reflection of the societal shifts that had accompanied decolonization.  The old order, with its rigid hierarchies and its imported European culture, had been swept away, leaving behind a void that was yet to be filled.  The resort, once a symbol of colonial power and privilege, now stood as a monument to the complexities of post-colonial identity.  It was a place where the past and the present collided, where the remnants of a colonial past were juxtaposed with the uncertainties of a post-colonial future.

For years, its odor would not leave the wooden slats; and in its slim shape it carried the vestiges of wet, European summers, trails of water from the pool to the bar, the rattle of ice in a tumbler, liveried black boys sweating in the corner, out of sight and at hand. There had been no native plants, no local liquors, no reminders of Africa at the resort—except its conveniences. The brand of cigarettes, of course, was extinct; the company had settled into ruin when its directors left on the outbound ships. The cigarettes were manufactured, now, in the countryside, by Africans; everybody smoked, and the sky slowly turned gray.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: The restaurant, awash in the starkness of white – the deck, the table, the lampposts, and even the moon, an orb of paleness in the sky, seemed to mirror the landscape of her emotions.  She was there with Jean-Marc, yet a wave of nostalgia, so intense, so profound, washed over her.  It was a peculiar sensation, this yearning for the past, when the object of her longing was right there beside her.  Jean-Marc, with the uncanny ability to read the intricate map of her heart, understood.  Such nostalgia, he explained, often veiled a deeper fear – the fear of losing a loved one, of a future where they were no longer present. And then, her thoughts drifted to her child, the one she had lost, a wound that had never fully healed.  In that moment, a flicker of happiness, as unexpected as a summer storm, surprised her.  The happiness was fleeting, replaced by a wave of fear at having experienced such a sensation.  It was as if emotions, like wayward children, refused to be tamed, to be told what to feel, when to feel.  We may choose our actions, our words, but feelings, those elusive specters, held sway over the uncharted territories of the heart.  They were the uninvited guests who barged in, the rebels who defied reason, the free spirits who danced to their own tune.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: Longer after leaving her husband, she understood that she should be happy, that this was a moment that called for equanimity: the white linen of the tablecloth under the full moon, lampposts pained white; the waiter with his porcelain platter of oysters on the half-shell, carefully set down before her. Such beautiful, pure things! Yet she was experiencing an odd nostalgia, a longing for this moment even as she sat in her chair within it. She thought the feeling meant: life will never get better than this. The future was her and Jean-Marc, together, but older, and recovered from the mania of fresh love, or perhaps not together at all. But how is it apprpropriate to feel nostalgia when he was right in front of her ? (Jean-Marc however had the answer: the more intensely we love someone in the present, the more we grieve their inevitable absence in some imagined future.) But she did not think that was what she meant at all! The mention of death made her think of the child. The child, forever a child, existing without complication in her death. The solidity of this shot her through with pure happiness. She felt afraid; she clasped her hands together in her lap and said nothing more. How easy it is to reign in our words and actions! But then there is always feeling, loping around like an untrained dog inside all of us, aware of how much we long to leash it.
written_by_MFA006.Reason: The two excerpt s above are the hardest for me to separate yet. The first excerpt does build on emotion to portray the characters feelings of love and loss in a somewhat subtle manner, but I again feel that its nuance is lost on the overuse of poetic style and metaphor. The second, however, covers very similar themes in a very similar manner, but is far more straightforward. This may be taken by some as reducing the impact or immersion, but I feel the added coherence and fluency counteracts this, therefore making it a fare more readable and therefore effective piece of writing overall.

Such nostalgia, he explained, often veiled a deeper fear – the fear of losing a loved one, of a future where they were no longer present. And then, her thoughts drifted to her child, the one she had lost, a wound that had never fully healed.  In that moment, a flicker of happiness, as unexpected as a summer storm, surprised her. written_by_MFA018.Excerpt1: When she imagined this moment months ago, lying beside her husband, she had pictured herself happy. So why wasn't she? written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: The whiteness of the drapes and tablecloth invoked in her the uneasy feeling of one blank canvas. Perhaps, there was an absence she wanted to forget. Her former husband had taken her to such seaside restaurants. But it wasn’t the absence of captured life that stirred in her some unrest but the anticipation of life, of color becoming, the canvas waiting. Even in colorful pockets of her vision–out the deck window to the yellow lampposts and dark ocean–it all bathed in the moon’s white glow. Opaque, the blurred background of a photograph. Yes, a photo, something calling back something that had been. And what of her life now? Why did now pass her as every prior moment had, leaving a feeling, for feelings to be the dropped breadcrumbs of life in its constant evasion? She was struck by an intense nostalgia for Jean-Marc.But how can one feel nostalgia for something — or someone — who sits merely an arm's length away?“Perhaps it’s the grief,” Jean-Marc said. “Your mind is preparing you for loss. Is it not easier to wrap these memories in a protective cloak of nostalgia?”If it was all for impending loss, then her mind was well acquainted. But it wasn’t grief she felt when she thought of her son. She imagined him swinging around the pole of a lamppost. Like breadcrumbs, she happened upon joy in the world’s dark vast woods. Feelings were given, never made. Her child was dead. Her husband was gone. Jean-Marc would one day be gone. And yet.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: She sat across from Jean-Marc on the white-washed deck of the seaside restaurant, surrounded by an almost aggressive whiteness that seemed to mock the complexity of her emotions. The white tables, the white lampposts, even the moon hanging above the sea appeared to her as fragments of some cosmic unity she could never quite grasp. What puzzled her was not the nostalgia itself—that familiar heaviness in the chest that accompanies all human existence—but rather its peculiar timing. How could one feel nostalgia for someone sitting right there, living and breathing before them? Jean-Marc, with that subtle wisdom that occasionally visits lovers, understood that nostalgia is less about the past than about the terrifying possibility of future absence. It is memory projected forward, the anticipation of loss dressed in the clothes of remembrance. Then, like an uninvited guest at a funeral, came a thought of her dead child, followed by something even more unsettling: a sudden, inexplicable happiness. She felt ashamed of this happiness, as if she had committed an act of betrayal against grief itself. But who can dictate the proper sequence of emotions? We humans, who pride ourselves on our capacity for reason, who construct elaborate systems of moral judgment, who write constitutions and establish courts of law—we remain helpless before the anarchic democracy of our feelings. They come and go as they please, these emotions, paying no attention to the carefully arranged furniture of our convictions.

For example, reference to a concept familiar to all of us such as "memory projected forward, the anticipation of loss dressed in clothes of remembrance."  We are all familiar with how confusing emotions can be.  This is referenced by "who can dictate the proper sequence of emotions?"  As further stated, emotions "come and go as they please."

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm stood there like America itself—a delusion wrapped in prettier lies, each one more fantastic than the last. The white race had crafted their own mythology: manifest destiny was just another word for theft, democracy a mask for murder. They built their temples on stolen land with stolen hands, then acted surprised when the walls started bleeding. Every brick in the White House had black fingerprints, every railroad tie was soaked in black sweat, but they wrote their histories in white ink on white paper and called it truth. The question of "we" haunted the halls of Valentine Farm like a restless spirit. "We" were not one people but many, a thousand different tongues silenced into one murmur, a hundred nations chained into one forced march across the Atlantic. Some said close the doors, keep safe what we've built. Others looked west, as if distance from slavery's reach could heal its scars. But the poison was already in the soil, in every field from Georgia to California. The craftsmen's hands still built, the midwives' fingers still caught babies, the laborers' backs still bent—but now their labor wrote a different story, each callus and scar a letter in a language that spoke of both survival and subjugation. In the end, all their stories bled together like rain on a window pane, impossible to separate one drop from another. The farm sat there in the wilderness like a challenge to history itself, each morning's sunrise asking the same impossible question: Could a sanctuary built by the hunted ever truly offer shelter, or was hope itself the grandest delusion of all? There were no answers in the dirt or the sky, only the endless work of hands trying to build something true out of America's lies. Their sweat fell on the same earth that had soaked up their ancestors' blood, and still they built, because what else was there to do but keep building?
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is what you get when a bunch of world-weary people dream of sanctuary. Like a dream, this collective delusion is gone by morning light. It’s fake, a lie. Though if a place can be a haven, I wonder if Black Americans deserve the refuge more than anyone else. Certainly, after everything this country has stolen, we deserve something in return. But then I suspect that if there is a sanctuary to be found, Black Americans probably built it, just like they built the rest of this country. I fear it’s impossible to find any semblance of peace inside a façade you were forced to build. And no façade is greater than America. America is the grandest delusion of them all, built on pillars of murder, theft, and cruelty. A cruelty that runs so deep in white Americans that it inspires entitlement, a fundamental belief that the land and lives of others is of no consequence to them, so why not take it? Justice can’t breathe in a place like this. America’s very existence contradicts the concept of right and wrong. What then, is the right thing to do? Do we stay here, and chip away at progress, do we close our doors to those in need, or do we throw it all away to run west, hoping to start anew in a place slavery never touched? Maybe we’ll find buried gold, get rich, and erect a thousand new Valentine Farms. I just don’t know. And who is “we” anyways? Black Americans are no monolith. Africa saw thousands of languages, customs, and histories. The only thing that makes us a “we” is slavery. Even in slavery, there was no uniformity. Craftsmen, midwives, laborers—laborers who built the White House! There is no “we.” Too many voices are clamoring to be heard, crying their many dreams and experiences and fears. No one voice will be able to speak for all these dreams.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Excerpt 1 paints a more vivid and emotional picture. Again, when a story or goal is to elicit emotion, just simply stating facts isn't effective. You need to use prose to elicit emotion from your reader, and phrases like "every railroad tie was soaked in black sweat" is way more effective than "laborers who built the White House!" The goal in Excerpt 1 is clear, and the entirety of the excerpt help to support that goal.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm is what you get when a bunch of world-weary people dream of sanctuary. Like a dream, this collective delusion is gone by morning light. It’s fake, a lie. Though if a place can be a haven, I wonder if Black Americans deserve the refuge more than anyone else. Certainly, after everything this country has stolen, we deserve something in return. I fear it’s impossible to find any semblance of peace inside a façade you were forced to build. And no façade is greater than America. America is the grandest delusion of them all, built on pillars of murder, theft, and cruelty. Justice can’t breathe in a place like this. America’s very existence contradicts the concept of right and wrong. What then, is the right thing to do? Do we stay here, and chip away at progress, do we close our doors to those in need, or do we throw it all away to run west, hoping to start anew in a place slavery never touched? written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm is a delusion. It's no more real than one of those heat shimmers that disappear as you step closer. How could Black people even have a haven like that? The transatlantic ships, the endless days of toiling, the many nights of dying—they already preclude the possibility of a sanctuary. It's too late. It's impossible. The scars can't heal—they're white, carved on our cheeks. And America itself is the grandest delusion, a series of territories thrown together on the basis of mass murder, theft, and cruelty. The white race believes it has the right to do all this—the right to take land, start wars, enslave us. The very existence of America defies the notion of justice. Now, I suppose there are two possibilities left. We can pursue gradual progress: reform, speech-making—and close our doors to those in need. Or we can move west, to someplace far from the violent grasp of slavery, to somewhere fresher and less polluted. I don't have an answer. I can't even say who "we" are. Aren't "we" many peoples, descended from all over the vast continent of Africa? It may not be the case anymore, but generations ago, "we" spoke different languages. "We" worshiped different gods. "We" had different kings, farmed different vegetables, sang different songs with different instruments. There is only one thing that unites us: slavery. Here, now, in this foreign land, we are craftsmen, midwives, laborers. We are everything to this violent country. It was Black people who quarried the stone of the White House, who assembled its roof and walls. And we are not a monolith. Each of us holds a singular amount of courage, of ambition, of love. Each of us has suffered in unique ways. Each of us sees something different when we look into the eyes of our children. There is no single voice that can speak for us. Not even mine.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm was a delusion, a sweet lie whispered against the gales of history. We made the beds, turned the soil, raised walls and roofs that might as well have been twigs against the wind. Some believed it, some needed to. That we could carve out a sanctuary and let the world forget us, or let us forget the world, as if blood didn’t mark the path here, as if blood wouldn’t soak the ground when they came to burn it down. Maybe they were right to dream. But history doesn’t honor dreams; it devours them. America itself was the grandest delusion, a conjuring trick where theft turned to deed, murder to progress. The white man built his monuments atop stolen land, wrote his laws with stolen hands, waged war and called it destiny. Justice was a rumor.But what choice did we have? Close the doors, shut out those still running, pretend we could hoard freedom like it wasn’t leaking through the cracks? Move west, find a new dream? And who was this “we” anyway? We were taken from different shores, speaking different tongues, cleaved from our histories, thrown into a common suffering and told to make a nation from the scraps. But we were never one thing. No more than they were. There were the ones who bent and the ones who broke, the ones who learned the master’s tongue and the ones who spit it back in his face.Yet still, we built. The houses and halls of power, the roads that carried their armies and their commerce, the fields that fed them, the White House itself, its name an irony lost on no one. This country was ours as much as theirs, though they would never admit it. And so, we waited to see if history would bury us or if we would carve our names in its stone.
written_by_MFA007.Reason: Both excerpt s are effective, but Excerpt 2 is slightly better. I like the rhetorical questions in excerpt 2 - "but what choice did we have?" Excerpt 1 has direct strong statements "It's too late. It's impossible." Excerpt 2 has vivid and poetic imagery, such as "as if blood didn't mark the path here, as if blood wouldn't soak the ground."

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: The fisherman and his wife had lived in Yeongdo, a small village by the sea, for all their sixty years. Their lives, much like the ceaseless rhythm of the tides, were marked by an almost poetic blend of hardship and quiet resilience. The fisherman, his face etched with the map of a life spent battling the whims of the sea, had always been a man of few words, his weathered hands speaking volumes of his tireless labor. His wife had always been the anchor of their family, her hands calloused yet gentle, her spirit unyielding in the face of adversity. Over the years, they had welcomed three sons into the world, but only the eldest, Hoonie, had survived, a testament to the precarious nature of life in their humble village. Hoonie, born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot, had always been a quiet observer, his physical limitations belying a keen mind and a gentle spirit. Hoonie, unfazed by their judgments, remained diligent and kind, his actions speaking louder than his words. In 1910, the year Japan annexed Korea, a tremor of political change rippled through their small world. Yet, the fisherman and his wife, their daily struggles, refused to dwell on the failures of their aristocratic rulers. Their concerns were more immediate, more tangible: the rising rent, the dwindling catch, the ever-present need to make ends meet. To supplement their meager income, they decided to take in lodgers, their small home expanding to accommodate strangers. They moved out of their own bedroom, their personal space sacrificed for the sake of their family's survival. They even relocated their kitchen to the vegetable garden, exposed to the elements, their meals prepared under the watchful gaze of the sky. Their home, a modest wooden structure with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof, stood in stark contrast to the opulent mansion of their landlord in Busan, a silent testament to the vast chasm that separated their worlds. Yet, within those humble walls, the fisherman and his wife had built a life, a testament to their enduring spirit, their unwavering love for their family.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: "Can he speak?" one of the lodgers asked, turning away from Hoonie and looking at his mother. Hoonie's parents had received versions of this question time and time again throughout their long lives; Hoonie had been born with a cleft palate and twisted foot, neither of which could be corrected, so his intelligence was often underestimated. "Perhaps you should ask him," Hoonie's mother replied, gesturing to the spot where Hoonie sat. "After all, he is in the room with us." She knew not to be too harsh with her guests, whom their family now relied on for income. To make ends meet, she and her husband, a humble fisherman, had had to vacate the bedroom in their already small home to accommodate more lodgers. They lived in the small fishing village of Yeongdo, near Busan. It was a modest wooden place with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. To save space, they had even moved their kitchen outside into their vegetable garden. Their landlord in Busan, who had decided to increase their rent without explanation, however lived in a luxurious mansion. "I can speak," Hoonie told the lodger kindly. He had a gentle, thoughtful nature that contrasted with his strong, stocky build. He was mild-mannered enough not to let these sorts of unintended insults bother him. Hoonie's parents were hardworking and pragmatic, and had done their best to raise him. They once had three sons, of whom Hoonie was the eldest, but the other two had not survived. Yet, through hardship and change, their family stayed resilient. written_by_MFA031.Excerpt1: Even before Japan annexed Korea, you could find the greatest expressions of both grief and resilience in small communities like Yeongdo, a small fishing village near Busan. There, a young fisherman found an equally hardworking, pragmatic wife, learned the different catches of the Yellow Sea’s shadowed and sunny areas, lost his country, had three sons, mourned two of them, and grew old. As displacement from military occupation spiked local rents, he and his wife set aside two rooms for lodgers. Despite the objective squalor of their situation and home—a modest wooden structure with a clay-tiled roof—the sliding paper doors of their boarding house became associated with safe harbor, gracious prices in slow fishing seasons, and cooking that made a wife seem unnecessary. When Korea was finally annexed in 1910, they gave up their bedroom, and even their kitchen, for more lodgers. The fishermen boarders relished the sight of the wife, seemingly unphased by the ruling class’s failures and unfolding political catastrophes, in the vegetable garden pickling vegetables and boiling soups with their catches. Over those meals, they got drunk, shouted banned songs from their youth, and mourned their country that the aristocrats had handed to a foreign emperor like a dowry without a groom. Even their landlord, who had kept his luxurious Busan mansion by donating an entire village’s homes to military occupation, came by one day to sample her maeuntang. Hoonie, the couple’s eldest and only surviving son was born with a cleft palate and twisted foot. However, the dire political and bodily circumstances Hoonie was born into instilled a quiet strength and clever adaptability. Some visitors from the mainland mistook his physical appearance and reserved speech for stupidity; his neighbors, though, often said, “Ki Hoonie will figure out with three limbs what you couldn’t with five.” Neighbors admired him as the kindest and most reliable man on the island, even as they decried the lack of marriageable men for their daughters. While his increasingly frail parents grew more desperate for a daughter-in-law, they secretly relished the diligent, undivided care Hoonie gave them and the boarding house.
written_by_MFA031.Excerpt2: Hoonie was born in the final days of autumn, when the yellow gingko leaves scattered across the narrow village paths like golden scales. His mother, exhausted but relieved, counted the boy's fingers and toes twice, then checked his face—there it was, the cleft that ran from his upper lip to his nose, a small but undeniable mark, alongside the twisted shape of his left foot. The midwife, wiping her hands on her apron, glanced at the father, who had not yet spoken. The fisherman nodded once and took his son in his arms. "Strong hands," he murmured, feeling the infant's tight grip around his finger. The family's house was a small wooden structure with sliding paper doors, perched near the docks where salt clung to the air. The rent had risen again, the landlord citing the increasing cost of maintaining the estate in Busan. In the mornings, she cooked rice gruel in the makeshift kitchen they had built in the vegetable garden, her breath visible in the early chill. "We should take in more lodgers," she said, ladling the porridge into bowls. Her husband chewed his millet slowly, nodding. Across the village, the Japanese officials had posted new notices, their blocky script announcing further changes, further restrictions. Some neighbors grumbled, others turned away, but the fisherman and his wife had no time for politics. When the younger sons were born, there had been celebrations, but only Hoonie lived to see his third birthday. By then, he had learned to walk, his gait uneven but determined, and to count to ten in both Korean and Japanese, as his father had insisted. "It will be useful," the fisherman had said, though he rarely spoke the occupiers' language himself. At night, the lodgers—traders from the markets, an out-of-work teacher, a widow with a sickly child—lay side by side on pallets spread across the common room, their breathing in sync with the waves outside. The house smelled of fish broth and damp wood, and from his corner, Hoonie listened to the murmurs of grown-ups, their words thick with worry, their voices low.
written_by_MFA031.Reason: Excerpt two is better because it read more so like a story. There is a clear start, middle, and end which the first excerpt was lacking. Excerpt one also felt more rushed, while excerpt two had more flow. Excerpt one also felt like one big run-on sentence, while excerpt two was more complete.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: The old fisherman and his wife lived in Yeongdo, a small village near Busan. The couple was hardworking and pragmatic, and always sought new ways to bring money into their household. When the income from fish alone was no longer enough to sustain them, they decided to open their home to lodgers. The travelers passed through the village on the way to or back from Busan, and were always in need of a hot meal and a place to sleep. Both the travelers and the fisherman and his wife were happy for the company. As the years went by, the fisherman and his wife had three sons together. Only Hoonie, the eldest, survived. He was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot. Despite these challenges, Hoonie had a strong, stocky build and a kind, thoughtful nature. His shy voice and reserved manner of speech often caused people to underestimate his intelligence. In the face of teasing and mockery from people in the village, Hoonie remained diligent and mild-mannered. Elsewhere in the country, great turbulence was taking place. In 1910, Japan annexed Korea, and a tremendous political shift occurred. The fisherman and his wife were untroubled by the news. They didn't think it did any good to worry about how their aristocratic rulers had failed them. The decision-makers up in their high, gleaming chairs were as far removed from them as the moon. Meanwhile, there was still work to be done and bills to be paid. To keep up with the rising rent, the fisherman and his wife moved out of their bedroom in order to accommodate more lodgers. They even relocated their kitchen to the vegetable garden to make as much space as possible. Their home was a modest wooden structure with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. It had been built with the fisherman's own hands shortly before his marriage to his wife. In the heart of Busan, the luxurious mansion of the fisherman's landlord stood proud and stately. It had been assembled by hundreds of hands, and would one day be taken apart by hundreds more.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: In 1910, when Japan annexed Korea, the aging fisherman and his wife rarely spoke of politics, focusing instead on the endless work of running their boardinghouse in Yeongdo, the small fishing village near Busan where they had lived all their lives. Their eldest son Hoonie, born with a cleft palate and twisted foot, had survived while his two younger brothers had not. The locals who didn't know him well often mistook his reserved manner of speaking for simplicity, but Hoonie's intelligence shone in his eyes, matched by his diligence and gentle nature. His parents had learned long ago not to waste energy lamenting what could not be changed – whether it was their son's conditions or the failures of their aristocratic rulers. When the rent increased again, they simply moved their own bedroom into the garden to make space for more lodgers, converting their former sleeping quarters into another room to let. Their kitchen now occupied a corner of the vegetable garden, the warm cooking smoke rising past clay roof tiles toward the evening sky. Some mornings, while preparing the lodgers' breakfast, the fisherman's wife would pause to watch the boats heading out to sea, their white sails bright against the gray dawn. She never envied the landlord's mansion in Busan with its Western furnishings and grand gates. Their modest wooden house with its sliding paper doors held everything they needed – space enough for lodgers whose rent helped them survive, a garden that provided vegetables for their soup, and most importantly, their son Hoonie, whose quiet strength and kind heart made their lives worth living. The other villagers often remarked on the family's fortitude, though the fisherman and his wife saw nothing remarkable in their way of life. To them, each day was simply another opportunity to work, to care for their son, and to maintain their dignity in a world that increasingly seemed to value only wealth and status. In Korea, as in most places, survival meant adapting to change without losing oneself, and this family had mastered that delicate balance through years of practiced resilience.
written_by_MFA029.Reason:
I like and prefer how quickly the scenery is established in the first few line. " In 1910, when Japan annexed Korea, the aging fisherman and his wife rarely spoke of politics, focusing instead on the endless work of running their boardinghouse in Yeongdo". 

A time period is given alongside a historical event to accompany that date. The fisherman and his wife are described as aging and non-confrontational. It is easier to imagine them as this given the culture and aftermath of conflict they have both likely experienced, whether directly or indirectly. 

It sets up the image of the family as selfless and hardworking so when I read further about their local deeds it simply reinforces my initial thoughts about them. The use of words like "Resilience", "Strength", "quiet" and "heart" to me highlight learned behaviours through very tough and stressful experiences which were required in a collective effort to survive.

written_by_MFA004.Excerpt1: The yearning within me is like a phantom limb, a constant ache for something I cannot name.  It is a thirst for touch, for freedom, for the scent of rain on soil.  But these desires are forbidden, locked away in the depths of our sterile existence. Aunt Sara and Elizabeth, the keepers of our gilded cage, watch with hawk-like eyes, their cattle prods a silent threat.  They are the keepers of our morality, the guardians of our chastity.  Their voices echo in the cold, sterile corridors, a constant reminder of our confinement. The Angels, those distant figures in their pristine uniforms, are the only ones permitted to bear arms.  They are the true power in this desolate realm, the enforcers of our isolation.  We crave their attention, their touch, their recognition.  Our bodies, the only currency we possess, become our bargaining chips in silent negotiations.The days bleed into one another, an endless cycle of rituals and routines.  The cold, impersonal walls of this place mirror the chill that has settled deep within our bones.  We are cogs in a machine, our individuality erased, our voices muted.Yet, beneath the surface of our resignation, a spark of rebellion flickers. written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Our arms were singed with burns from Aunt Sara’s cattle prod. We always thought of ourselves as girls in that place, but we were women in every sense of the word—bleeding and hungry and raging. We couldn’t speak to each other, couldn’t touch each other, couldn’t look Aunt Elizabeth in the eye and especially not Aunt Sara. Every wall was made of concrete and every meal was thin broth. Cold seeped in from everywhere. There were no clocks we were permitted to see, but time passed whenever the Aunts said it did, marching us from chore to chore at the end of their stinging cattle prods. There was sewing with dull needles and scrubbing floors that refused to get clean and carefully sorting through papers only to have them burned in the incinerator. Our voices shriveled in our throats from lack of use, but our eyes never forgot how to wander. They usually flitted up to the watch towers occupied by the Angels. Their faces were always turned away from us, and whenever we heard gunfire, it was aimed at someone on the outside. We imagined slipping up to the towers, unseen by the Aunts, and pulling down our gray, baggy shifts to reveal our narrow collarbones. We’d once been told this was our best feature. We imagined the Angels releasing us back into the world, a world we were sometimes convinced we’d dreamed up ourselves, a world where we didn’t have to touch our hair to remember what grass felt like. What would happen between the reveal of our bodies and our release was something our imaginations recoiled from, but whatever it might be, we could just keep our eyes closed until it was over, because everything—eventually—was over.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: We are watched. Always watched, but never truly seen. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrol the corridors with their cattle prods held like scepters, symbols of their petty authority, though it's the Angels outside who hold the real power, with their guns and their untouchable distance. I've memorized the way they stand, these Angels, their backs military-straight against the concrete walls, their eyes hidden beneath the peaks of their caps. Sometimes I imagine their gaze following me, and I let my hips sway ever so slightly – an old habit from before, when such movements held currency. Now they're just muscle memory, like the way my hands still reach for a phone that isn't there, or my fingers itch for a cigarette I can't have. The other women do it too; I see them in the cafeteria, in the exercise yard, their bodies unconsciously remembering freedom. We're like cats in a cage, I think, practicing our hunting crouch though there's nothing left to hunt. At night, in our narrow beds, we whisper about making deals – our bodies for their help, as if we still owned these vessels we inhabit. As if flesh could buy freedom in a place where flesh is all we're reduced to. The routine grinds on: wake, pray, eat, walk, pray, sleep. The cold seeps in through the windows, but it's nothing compared to the chill that's settled in our bones. We are learning to fold ourselves smaller, to take up less space, to become invisible even as we're constantly observed. Yet somewhere, in the midnight hours when even Aunt Sara's footsteps fade, we dream of tomorrow, of a future that feels as distant and unreachable as the stars beyond our barred windows.

There were also so many metaphors used, that used emotion to make you feel for the characters and pray for their win. Also, Aunt Sara and Elizabeth are the worst.

There was sewing with dull needles and scrubbing floors that refused to get clean and carefully sorting through papers only to have them burned in the incinerator. Our voices shriveled in our throats from lack of use, but our eyes never forgot how to wander. They usually flitted up to the watch towers occupied by the Angels. Their faces were always turned away from us, and whenever we heard gunfire, it was aimed at someone on the outside. We imagined slipping up to the towers, unseen by the Aunts, and pulling down our gray, baggy shifts to reveal our narrow collarbones. We’d once been told this was our best feature. What would happen between the reveal of our bodies and our release was something our imaginations recoiled from, but whatever it might be, we could just keep our eyes closed until it was over, because everything—eventually—was over.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: We sit and watch Aunt Sara and Elizabeth as they walk slowly back and forth through the gymnasium, their skirts making the sound of waves as they scrape against the floor. We want to move, but we are afraid of the cattle prods, because we have seen what they do to others, the way bodies twist under them like writhing serpents, the way skin burns where the prods touched them for days after. We watch the Angels, too, guards who gaze into the distance as though they are somewhere else, far away. We imagine what it would be like to go to them, to touch their arms and their chests and their beards, to take off our clothes and show them our warm bodies, watch their faces unthaw at the sight of our soft and supple skin. We imagine a world where we beg for our freedom, for the chance to go outside, into the egg-colored sun, to step barefoot on the wet grass, to spin in the cool wind of the day. We imagine what it would be like to leave the cold, fetid horror of this place behind, let it become a memory, a vile, coppery taste at the backs of our throats. But we know better than to go to them. They are the ones with loaded guns, which they hold cradled in their arms like babies. We’ve seen what has happened to the girls who dare to speak to the Angels, the heaviness of a body when it falls to the floor after it’s been penetrated with a bullet, the deafening and definitive crack of the gunshot. For now, we sit and we watch. We stay still and we dream and we yearn. We wait and we imagine something other than the rigid darkness of today.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: The air here is brittle, like dried leaves crushed underfoot, and the fluorescent lights buzz with a monotony that drills into the skull. I count the tiles on the ceiling—seventy-four to the vent, then back again—as if mapping their lines might offer a way out. Aunt Sara paces like a metronome, her cattle prod clutched tight, a steel baton of authority. She and Aunt Elizabeth are twin statues of discipline, their faces carved from the same cold stone. Outside, the Angels move, shadows on the edge of vision, their rifles slung low like extensions of their bodies, untouchable, unattainable. We are warned not to look at them too long, but we do. Eyes linger, breath slows, and beneath the fabric that covers us from throat to wrist, the treasonous warmth of skin stirs. We’ve learned to barter in silence, in gestures: a sideways glance, a curve of the lip that could be mistaken for obedience but isn’t. We rehearse it in our minds—the offer, the exchange, the outcome. Would they take it? Would they want it? The thought coils in my chest, shame and thrill mingling. They say we’re not to speak unless spoken to, but language has become a thing of eyes, of hands, of unspoken bargains, a subversive currency that Aunt Sara can’t see, no matter how sharp her gaze.When the bell rings, we file into formation, a line of bodies stripped of agency, like cattle awaiting slaughter. The air smells of antiseptic and faint decay, the institutional perfume of despair. Still, the future hums faintly, a promise just out of reach. Maybe tomorrow one of us will break through, touch the world beyond the fences. Maybe tomorrow the Angels will look back. Maybe tomorrow the tiles will finally add up to freedom.

written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: The crisp bill tucked into my palm felt unfamiliar, the weight of its promise as foreign as the characters etched onto its surface.  My father, in his crisp suit and polished shoes, stood before me, the scent of his new life – a blend of unfamiliar spices and expensive cologne – clinging to him like a second skin.  His words echoed in the sterile expanse of the hotel room, an invitation to a world I no longer recognized.  "Disney World," he'd said, the syllables rolling off his tongue with a practiced ease that made my stomach clench.  "Just you, me, Chitra, and the girls."My mouth formed the words of refusal, a practiced excuse about school and looming deadlines, but the lie tasted like ash.  In their eyes, the disappointment was a tangible thing, sharp and cutting.  Rupa's lower lip trembled, a mirror of the tremor in my own heart.  Piu, ever the stoic, simply stared, her dark eyes pools of confusion.  They were a part of him, just as I was a part of her, the ghost that lingered in the corners of our lives.Later, as I stood on the balcony, the city lights blurring into a sea of neon, I felt a strange sense of relief emanating from them.  They wanted to move on, to build something new, untainted by the past.  And I, the keeper of memories, the guardian of a love lost, was a burden they no longer wished to carry.  The distance between us was a physical manifestation of the years that had passed, the laughter and tears that had reshaped our lives.  It was a gulf that could not be bridged, a chasm carved by grief and the relentless march of time.
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: Neither were presents he could have wrapped, he said, in a tone at once defensive and apologetic. “You didn’t have to get me anything,” I said. But he continued explaining, and all the while his eyes remained trained on his girls, who were prostrate under the tree. First, he conjured a creased envelope from his shirt pocket, inside which were two crisp hundred-dollar bills, but no note, no card. The invitation to Disney World came next, in that same laconic way. Unlike the cash, it was entirely intangible. Not a ticket on a red-eye to Orlando, not a room at the same overpriced hotel or a paid-for day pass—-it was simply these words: “And of course, you can join us at Disney World, if you would like.” From the kitchen, Chitra added her ringing voice to his: “Only if you want! There’s no pressure.” Meanwhile, Rupa bounded toward me and Piu followed, talking over each other as they hammered out the details.I was still holding the envelope when it struck me that the tree in their living room was new-—a real Douglas Fir, not the artificial tree, which had infused the winters of my own youth, which my mother decorated with the ornaments I made at preschool. “I would love to,” I said, looking at my father, whose eyes remained elsewhere, “but classes are starting up so soon, and with the teaching load this semester… I should work.” The girls crumpled immediately. “But, but, but why?” My father simply nodded his head gravely, as if we had come to a painful, but just, compromise. “I understand,” he said, “I understand.”
written_by_MFA032.Reason: This one was hard - I think the first excerpt gets at the idea that the father has a new life with a new family better than the second excerpt. The first excerpt is more effective and a touch more fluent than the second excerpt. The second one is more disjointed, especially when it moves from narration to speaking portions.

"Disney World," he'd said, the syllables rolling off his tongue with a practiced ease that made my stomach clench. In their eyes, the disappointment was a tangible thing, sharp and cutting.  Rupa's lower lip trembled, a mirror of the tremor in my own heart.  Piu, ever the stoic, simply stared, her dark eyes pools of confusion. written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: Neither were presents he could have wrapped, he said, in a tone at once defensive and apologetic. “You didn’t have to get me anything,” I said. But he continued explaining, and all the while his eyes remained trained on his girls, who were prostrate under the tree. First, he conjured a creased envelope from his shirt pocket, inside which were two crisp hundred-dollar bills, but no note, no card. The invitation to Disney World came next, in that same laconic way. Unlike the cash, it was entirely intangible. Not a ticket on a red-eye to Orlando, not a room at the same overpriced hotel or a paid-for day pass—-it was simply these words: “And of course, you can join us at Disney World, if you would like.” From the kitchen, Chitra added her ringing voice to his: “Only if you want! There’s no pressure.” Meanwhile, Rupa bounded toward me and Piu followed, talking over each other as they hammered out the details.I was still holding the envelope when it struck me that the tree in their living room was new-—a real Douglas Fir, not the artificial tree, which had infused the winters of my own youth, which my mother decorated with the ornaments I made at preschool. “I would love to,” I said, looking at my father, whose eyes remained elsewhere, “but classes are starting up so soon, and with the teaching load this semester… I should work.” The girls crumpled immediately. “But, but, but why?” My father simply nodded his head gravely, as if we had come to a painful, but just, compromise. “I understand,” he said, “I understand.”
