written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: That Christmas morning, my father handed me an envelope, thick with cash, along with a brochure for Disney World, its glossy pages showcasing artificial castles and choreographed joy. "We leave next week," he said, his voice carrying that familiar mixture of authority and hesitation that had marked our relationship since my mother's death. I watched Chitra in the kitchen, methodically preparing tea, her movements precise and deliberate, like someone navigating through a space that wasn't quite her own. Through the window, I could see Rupa and Piu in the backyard, their matching winter coats making them look like mirror images as they built a lopsided snowman. I manufactured an excuse about a winter session course, watching their small shoulders slump when my father relayed the news. The girls had wanted to share their Disney princess fantasies with their older sister, not understanding that I was a relic of a different fairy tale, one that had ended with my mother's last breath in a stark hospital room. Later, as I folded the crisp bills and tucked them into my wallet, I caught Chitra's fleeting glance – a look of relief poorly disguised as sympathy. My father busied himself with travel arrangements, his enthusiasm slightly too pronounced, betraying the comfort he found in my absence. I recognized then that we were all performing our roles: they as the new family looking forward, me as the keeper of memories, standing still in a house that held too many ghosts.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: I was home during winter. On Christmas morning, my father entered my room with a thin, white envelope in hand. Inside, there were ten twenty-dollar notes, totalling a sum of two hundred dollars, the most generous amount I had ever received from my father. I thanked him profusely, but it seemed like a prologue to the real question my father wanted to ask me. He invited me to Disney World, where he was planning to take Chitra, his new wife, and my two half-sisters, Rupa and Piu, during spring break. But I felt distant from his new family, like a string being pulled from both ends. I fabricated some excuse about having to be on-campus during that time since I was a Resident Assistant, and declined his invitation. Later that week, as we sat on the floor circled around the Christmas tree in our living room, Rupa and Piu expressed their disappointment. They could not understand why I would not want to join them in Disney World. "It's Disney World," they exclaimed. But I kept thinking of my late mother, and everything I owed her. I felt a responsibility to hold back, to stay with her memory, as if her place in our family was still untouched and unoccupied, in the same way that Rupa and Piu symbolized and remained committed to their father’s legacy. Besides, I felt, with a strange ease, that Chitra and my father, too, were relieved by my decision to leave the four of them alone to enjoy their holiday.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: I held the cash, folded in my hand, and my father asked the question again. Would I like to use the gift to join them for a trip to Disney World? I looked around the room, at the expectant faces of Piu and Rupa, and Chitra’s reserved smile. My mother had always sat in the velvet chair Chitra now inhabited and my mother had even donned a similar posture to hers, pert and classic. I tried to mimic Chitra’s smile. Maybe, I said, of course I’d love to, but exams will be especially wicked this year. I don’t expect to have enough time to get away for a vacation. Piu and Rupa knitted their brows, faces falling for a spell, sensing rejection—hadn’t we been getting close? Chitra’s composed smile remained as if painted on her face. I looked back to my father, hoping to convey my gratitude. A piece of me did want to go. I hadn’t been able to say much to him since the new woman became his world, two half-daughters making him young again. The American family getaway might have been an olive branch to me. Certainly Chitra would not have chosen it. I was surprised to see no resignation in his face, no disappointment, but relief instead.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: At breakfast, my father handed me an envelope thick with cash, a gesture both startling and unsettling. "For Christmas," he said with forced cheer, his eyes flicking toward Chitra, who was sipping her tea, avoiding my gaze. He added, almost apologetically, “And Disney World, with us. The girls are excited.” Rupa and Piu, dressed in matching holiday sweaters, looked at me expectantly, their bright faces blurring into one as I fumbled for words. “I can’t,” I said, the excuse tumbling out. “There’s a project—due after break.” The lie felt hollow, but I let it stand. Chitra placed a dish of fruit on the table, her movements brisk, her expression neutral, as if my refusal required no comment. My father leaned back, resigned, a faint relief softening the tension in his jaw. I sensed how the trip would be easier without me—how my presence reminded them of another family, one they had worked hard to unwrite. Later, when I passed the girls in the hallway, they whispered in hurried tones, their laughter abruptly silenced when I appeared. I thought of my mother, the spaces she had filled now occupied by others, and felt caught between loyalties, between memory and their momentum forward. Outside, the winter sun broke through, exposing everything.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: I like excerpt 1 because it's coherent and follows a clear chronological sequence of events. Overall, excerpt 2 is preferable because it's connected via emotion and metaphor, not just sequence. It uses poetic language, such as "outside, the winter sun broke through, exposing everything." Excerpt 1 is not as good because it's first person and more repetitive - "I looked," "I tried," "I said."

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I’m ready now, my friend said, and I said nothing because I didn't know what to say. There were ways people did these sorts of things, she explained to me, certain drugs people used. But she couldn't tell me which drugs. For my protection. Protection against what?, I wondered, but I didn't ask her. That seemed wrong to say. I wanted to ask her about when she was planning on taking these drugs, exactly, but I worried that line of questioning was unthinkable, morbid. I didn't want it to seem like I wanted a date so I could put it on my calendar and plan around it. Already, though, I was thinking about my plans. The mail stacking in the mailbox with each day I stayed with my friend. You don't have to tell me anything you don't want to, I said -- and then I worried that made it sound like I didn't really want to hear anything at all. But she just said, this way it's all in my hands. Her hands: frail, slightly shaking. She was ready to die, she told me, she wanted to get it over with, it felt like that was the way her body was heading. All the ups and downs with the treatments just delaying the inevitable. She was bound to die, just like the coming of the Lord was bound to happen, she said. She glanced upwards and my eyes followed hers. Nothing and no one appeared, and she looked back at me. Just promise you won't tell anyone, she said. I won't, I said -- it was a lie. The weight of the secret was too great. Her plans were too great, too serious. I didn't know what to do. I had already told someone else.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: It’s strange, how quickly we adapt to the unthinkable. Sitting across from her that day, I tried not to fixate on her trembling hands or the way her voice, once so commanding, now wavered. “I don’t want to know when,” I said, a cowardly dodge that felt both honest and unkind. She gave a short laugh, the kind that cuts, and said, “You think it’ll be like the Rapture—poof, and I’m gone? Sorry to disappoint.” The drugs were hidden somewhere, and I knew better than to ask. Still, I couldn’t stop my mind from wandering to the mechanics of it: where, when, how. She didn’t want witnesses, she said, though she spoke about it with the eerie calm of someone discussing weather forecasts. “No surprises,” she added, “except maybe for you, if you’re still here.” She wanted the mail collected, the apartment left tidy, as if planning for a long vacation. But I could see in her eyes a quiet insistence: this wasn’t for my benefit. It was for hers.I nodded along, complicit in the silence she demanded, though guilt sat heavy in my chest. “It’s your choice,” I managed, the words dry in my mouth. I didn’t tell her about the conversation I’d already had, late one night, with someone who wasn’t her. Someone who had listened as I stumbled over explanations and shared the weight she was handing me. My betrayal, small and selfish, would never reach her ears, but it lived between us nonetheless, a thing unspoken but palpable. And when she turned back to her tea, her gaze distant and inward, I wondered how much she already suspected. In that moment, she seemed to belong not to this world or the next but to the narrow, flickering space between.

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: She’d said, “I want to handle this in my own way, on my own terms.”Her words hung in the air, heavy with finality and a hint of defiance.“I’m tired of waiting,” she continued, her voice a mix of weariness and determination.“I’m tired of this body failing me, of the endless treatments, the uncertainty.”She spoke of wanting to die peacefully, naturally, without any interference.“I don’t want any interventions, any disruptions,” she’d said.“I don’t want anyone trying to prolong this… existence.” She paused, a wry smile flickering across her face.“I don’t want anyone trying to play God,” she added, her tone a blend of humor and solemnity.Her words echoed in my mind as I walked down the street, the weight of our conversation pressing on me.I thought about her situation, her desire for autonomy, her frustration with the slow, unpredictable decay of her body.I thought about her wish for a peaceful, natural death, her refusal to let anyone “play God.”I thought about her insistence on secrecy, her plea for me not to mention her plans to anyone, not even my closest confidantes.I felt a knot of tension tighten in my chest, a conflict between my loyalty to her and my own need to process this heavy situation.I thought about the consequences of her choice, the potential legal ramifications, the emotional toll it would take on those who cared about her. I thought about my own role in this, my promise to support her, my fear of being implicated, my desire to protect her and myself.I felt a surge of guilt, a sense of betrayal, as I remembered the conversation I’d had with my therapist, the one person I’d confided in, breaking my promise to her.I tried to justify my actions, telling myself that I needed someone to talk to, someone to help me navigate this emotional minefield.But the guilt lingered, a constant reminder of my broken promise.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: I remember things. I remember how I felt when my friend talked about taking her own life. She wasn’t planning to commit suicide exactly. But she wanted her life to come to an end, she said. Her honesty made me pause and I wondered what I should do in such a situation. Could I make her change her mind? Would I have to look after her things and live with guilt? It would’ve been different if my friend didn’t want to handle “her situation” on her own terms. She, who had always been a planner, had even decided which drug she wanted to use to die, and asked me to keep it a secret, both for her sake and for my “protection,” whatever that meant. What concerned me though was that she wanted to do it soon. She said it slowly and calmly, but her tone was riddled with impatience and readiness. My friend had been ill for a long time and her body had not been responding well to treatments. She had spent so much in hospitals that now she wanted death to feel natural, without any interventions or disruptions. Smooth and clean. She hoped death would arrive like an unexpected guest. “Like the coming of the Lord, you know?” she said, with a laugh. I was in two minds. I wanted to know when she was planning for it all to go down, but it felt unthinkable to probe directly about her timeline. And, I felt equally concerned with more practical issues. If I were to stay with my friend during her final days, my mail would pile up. What would I do then? And what would happen to everything she had? It was all this and more about her, including her choice of pill, that I recounted to another friend of mine later in the day.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: She had it all planned out, she said, though she wouldn't tell me exactly when. Like the coming of the Lord, she joked, no one knows the day or the hour. Her voice was steady but her hands shook as she arranged and rearranged the little heap of mail on her bedside table. I thought about my own mail piling up at home—how long would I need to stay?—and felt ashamed for thinking of such things. The practical always intrudes on the sacred, I suppose. She spoke of her body's betrayals with a kind of weary impatience, the way you might discuss a chronically late friend who nevertheless remained dear to you. Don't ask me about the pills, she said. I won't tell you what they are or where they came from. It's better that way. For your protection, she added, though I wondered if it wasn't more for her peace of mind. The secret felt heavy between us, like a third presence in the room. Looking at her face, lined with pain but still beautiful in its determination, I found it unthinkable to ask the questions that pressed against my throat: When? How soon? Will I be here? Later that night, I called S. and told her everything, breaking my promise of silence before it was even a day old. "I just need someone else to know," I said, and she understood, or said she did. But afterward I lay awake, thinking about loyalty and betrayal, about the boundaries between caring for someone and caring for yourself. About how even in death—especially in death—we are never quite as alone as we might wish to be.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: A good friend of mine told me about her plans for death. More precisely, she told me she was planning to take matters into her own hands. I asked her what she meant by this, and she just gave me a look that said, are you going to make me spell it out for you? No, I wasn’t going to make her spell it out, and she went on, saying that she had gotten quite impatient about the whole thing. She was ready, she said, and she wanted to bow out while there was still time. My friend’s body had never fared well when it was invaded by illness. It also didn’t fare well when it was invaded by medicine. As a teenager, she had lots of problems with headaches. Stomachaches, too, but she didn’t talk about that as much. She was also allergic to many things. Of dying, she said this: I want it to feel natural, without anything getting in the way. She wouldn’t say how this would happen. Just like the coming of the Lord, nobody would know until it was already here. I had two main concerns. One of them was practical—if I came to stay with her and supervise her wellbeing, my mail would pile up. The other was that I found it unthinkable to ask her any direct questions. Questions like, when? Questions like, where? My friend insisted on secrecy and made me promise not to tell anyone about her plan, and especially not about her drug of choice. She said this would bring her peace and give me protection. To be honest, I did want both of those things. But sometimes I can’t help myself. I told someone without even meaning to. I made him promise not to tell.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt 1 was more enjoyable to read.  Although I liked getting more context from excerpt 2, I thought the first one was overall better written and felt more fluent to me. In excerpt, one the narrative is much more organic and fluid than in the second.  Excerpt 2 was good, but too matter of fact.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: The heat arrived early in the day, a simmering, golden haze that crept into the corners of every room, painting the air with a sheen of lethargy. From the fourth floor of a sea-green building, the two men emerged onto their verandas, their movements mirrored as if rehearsed by the stars themselves—Senior and Junior, bound together by the invisible threads of time’s loom. Below, Elliot’s Beach stirred awake, alive with the sounds of its chaotic symphony: temple bells clanged in stubborn competition with film music pouring from distant speakers, a mosaic of devotion and desire. Children’s cries darted through the cacophony like startled birds, while the heady aroma of freshly brewed filter coffee mingled with the briny tang of the sea breeze, a sensory banquet that danced on the edge of overwhelming. Senior adjusted his spectacles, the glint of sunlight catching the lens like a mischievous wink from the heavens, while Junior tapped his fingers on the wrought iron railing, a rhythm only he could hear. Around them, the city moved in fits and bursts: vegetable vendors hollered over their carts, stray dogs wove through scooters with uncanny grace, and the youth, untroubled by time, readied themselves for the evening’s promenade. The two men, unhurried and deliberate, bore witness to it all—custodians of a pace the world had long since abandoned.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: And so the day passed. In the center of the city, the maghrib rang out its ancient melody, warring with the Tamil music lilting out of the speakers of a passing rickshaw—the ocean swell of strings, the buoyant theme of an old Hollywood film. written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: In that sea-green building which stood like a tired sentinel near Elliot's Beach (where young lovers would soon gather with their smartphones and their dreams, as predictable as the tide), there lived two old men whose synchronicity of existence would have alarmed them had they ever bothered to notice it—but they never did, for such is the peculiar blindness that affects those who are bound together by the invisible threads of fate. The fourth floor (ah, but was it really the fourth? for in this particular building the ground floor was called the first, in the American way, causing endless confusion among visitors and delivery men alike) housed Senior and Junior, names that contained their own little joke, since Junior was himself no spring chicken, and Senior was so ancient that some believed he had witnessed the departure of the British Raj with his own rheumy eyes. Every morning, as predictable as the muezzin's call to prayer that floated across the neighborhood like a ghost's lament, mixing with the timpani of temple bells and the cheerful vulgarity of Tamil film songs blaring from auto-rickshaws, the two men would emerge onto their respective verandas at precisely the same moment, like mechanical figures in some elaborate timepiece. The morning air arrived thick with stories: the dark, intense aroma of filter coffee from the houses below, where young IT professionals fueled themselves for their days in air-conditioned offices; the shouts of children in pressed uniforms hurrying to school, their watches synchronized to their mothers' anxieties; the eternal complaint of crows who had seen it all before and were distinctly unimpressed. The heat rose from the streets like a malevolent spirit, distorting the reality of things, so that the two old men, standing on their respective verandas with their respective cups of tea, might have been mirror images of each other, or perhaps the same man caught in two different moments of time, or even (though they would have scoffed at such fancy) two aspects of the same soul, divided at birth and now slowly, incrementally, moving toward an inevitable reunion, like two drops of water on a window pane, drawn together by forces beyond their comprehension or control.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Under the heavy weight of the late afternoon sun, the city was bursting with heat, the sound of chanting prayers—Surya Mangalam, said for hope of peaceful evenings—sitar and tabla-heavy soundtracks, and children's cries rising like heat shimmers, with sweetened filter coffee laden in the air, one final push to get through to the fast-approaching dusk. But on the fourth floor of the sea-green building overlooking the blisteringly blue Indian Ocean, two elderly men, Senior and Junior, only just began their day, even as the younger generation gathered in clumps like swarms of ants, singing along to hit Tamil songs and preparing to dance and drink on Elliot's Beach once the sun set. Moving to an instinctual, silent rhythm, Senior and Junior rose as one, like two men bound by strings of fate, their walk to their verandahs as sure as the sun's journey across the sky until they sank into their chairs with the same achy movements, tilting their heads back once comfortable, two mirrors reflecting back at each other. Nothing in the world could halt this routine, their path so worn they seemed guided by more than gravity. Beneath them, a jubilant cheer rose up to greet the old men, and twin smiles stretched slowly across their faces, for they were soothed by their repetition and the companionship that repetition brings.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: excerpt  2 is better because it is more straight forwad. It is easy to understand and gives a steady contineous reading rhythm. Its short structured sentenses makes it non-tedious to keep reading. Its choice of diction is perfect, it creates a vivid picture in a way that a large number of readers can easily understand.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: In the heart of Newark, during those tense years of World War II, there existed among us a boy whose mere existence seemed to defy the contours of our collective identity. Seymour Irving Levov—"The Swede"—his name floated through the whispers of our community like a hymn. Fair-haired and blue-eyed, with the sinews of an Olympian god, he stood in stark contrast to the rest of us, who were more likely to be celebrated for our Talmudic acumen than for any prowess on the athletic field. But there he was, a towering figure of grace and strength, conquering the realms of football, basketball, and baseball with a seeming effortlessness that none of us could emulate. To see him play was to witness something almost sacred, as though the mundane boundaries of our neighborhood had been temporarily lifted to reveal a glimpse of something larger, purer, and profoundly American.We loved him not because he was one of us, but because he was so distinctly other, embodying a kind of transcendence we barely dared to dream of. The Swede was everything we were not allowed to imagine ourselves to be—resilient, fearless, and uncomplicated by the anxieties that knitted themselves into the very fabric of our Jewish existence. To watch him soar above the basketball rim or charge down the football field was to forget, if only for a moment, the war, the ration books, the headlines filled with death. In those fleeting moments, he turned our collective dread into something weightless and buoyant. We made of him an Apollo, a golden boy whose victories on the field were our victories, whose perfection was our imperfect salvation.Even now, I can see him in my mind’s eye, the sunlight catching the blonde halo of his hair as he pitched another strike or sank another jump shot. He was our myth, our impossible hope, the embodiment of a Newark dream in a time when dreaming seemed almost criminal.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: No matter what I thought of myself in childhood, both in times of complimentary self-reference and in self-effacement, I was comparing myself to The Swede, and I never came out on top. I wasn’t trying to out-duel him, that would have been impossible; it was an effort to get closer to his prestige, even if I could never match it. In Newark nobody did what he did. He was striking for many reasons—the blue eyes and fair hair that gave Seymour Irving Levov his nickname wasn’t common in our synagogue. He also carved out a niche in our world we found both bizarre and entrancing. While most of us studied and read till bedtime The Swede must have spent the time lifting weights and punching swinging bags of cotton. In school he excelled in football, basketball, and baseball while we watched with fearful hope. His curled muscles and firm abdomen seemed to defy the laws of our upbringings, of our parents’ schemes, but also to create a new sort of hope, because World War II was underway and surely The Swede could deliver a personal victory against the Germans not only militarily for the United States but for Jews in Newark too. His youth gave him a wide-eyed stupid confidence and his figure gave him an invincibility. He was our Apollo. With every snap of the bat against the ball, we cheered for him and for our brothers and fathers in the war who might just come home safely if they could channel The Swede’s fiendish affinity for dominant physical triumph, a kind of triumph none of us were used to seeing embodied. He spun through defenders on the basketball court and we imagined Newark’s finest darting through enemy lines toward us. He dove into the opponent’s running back and we imagined our male relatives tackling a Nazi and pounding, pounding, pounding down, breaking them into specific wet bits we could never have seen in such luscious detail otherwise.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: Excerpt one is better because it feels more smoother and more poetic. It uses strong images and emotions to show why The Swede mattered so much. The writing flows like a story and keeps me as the reader interested. It explains his impact clearly without being too wordy or jumping around too much.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: In the tremulous years of the Second World War, when fear wrapped itself around our Newark neighborhood like a fog rolling off the Passaic, we had our very own demigod, our walking antidote to Jewish anxiety – Seymour "The Swede" Levov. Who could have predicted that from our community of intellectuals and worriers, of boys who measured their worth by the heft of their Hebrew school books and the precision of their bar mitzvah portions, would emerge this specimen of Nordic perfection? The Swede, with his impossible blue eyes and hair the color of straw, who moved across the athletic field like some magnificent shiksa fantasy come to life, became our collective dream of transformation. Here was a Jewish boy who could smash through defensive lines on the football field with the force of a Gentile, who could arc a basketball through the hoop with gymnastic grace, who could swing a baseball bat as if it were his birthright rather than something we'd borrowed from the other America. And how we needed him then, needed to believe in this anomaly, this statistical impossibility of nature who happened to daven at our synagogue! While our mothers whispered anxiously about cousins in Europe and our fathers scanned casualty lists in the Newark News with trembling hands, The Swede was our ticket to invincibility, our pass into that other realm where Jewish boys didn't have to be smart because they were beautiful, didn't have to be crafty because they were strong. We projected onto him all our desperate hopes of acceptance, of transcendence – this boy who looked like he'd stepped out of a Nazi propaganda poster but wore a chai around his neck and could recite his Haftorah portion without a single mistake. The Swede was our temporary escape from who we were, from what we feared, from the relentless drumbeat of war news that threatened to drown out even the sound of our prayers.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I was a boy of World War II and a boy of Newark. The war was far away and beyond my understanding, but the dread and threat of it spilled across the ocean and flooded every home in my city. Lots of our men were off fighting, and lots of them would never come home. Rations of oil and sugar were dispensed through clenched fists. We spent many nights huddled around the radio and forgetting to breathe. It was a time of need, which is—according to the comic books—the perfect time for a hero to arrive. Newark’s wartime hero was a high school boy named Seymour Irving Levov, who we nicknamed “The Swede” because of his blond hair and blue eyes. He was a paragon of greatness in my neighborhood, and his athletic ability was the stuff of legend; regardless of the sport he played, he always clinched the win for his team. The Swede’s consistent excellence in football, basketball, and baseball gave my community something to rally for. Being Jewish, most of us tended to prioritize academic achievements over physical feats, but the Swede changed things. We’d turn up to his games with homemade banners and clumsily invented cheers, among them “S-W-E-D-E, get this team to victory!” Watching the force of his kick, the graceful arch of his throw, and the shattering power of his swing shrouded us in a feeling of awe that was rarely experienced outside of Temple. When the Swede was on the field or on the court, my whole neighborhood was in the palm of his hand. He had unwittingly become a symbol of invincibility, of innocence, of hope that the terrible war would leave us unscathed, passed over like we had smeared lamb blood on our doors. Looking back, I don’t know if our hero arrived or if our hero was created, but the Swede was more than willing to shoulder the burden.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: In excerpt one I like the metaphor about fear but this is closely followed by a jokey style about Seymour 'The Swede' Levov. It seems unnatural as the two styles don't fit together. The whole story seems farfetched. I prefer excerpt 2. It references the war in a serious way and is effective in creating a shadow over the story. The introduction of the boy 'The Swede' is more subtle and fits into the story. It explains how this figure had an impact on the community in a relevant and serious way. It is coherent so you believe the story - it is authentic.

Being Jewish, most of us tended to prioritize academic achievements over physical feats, but the Swede changed things. When the Swede was on the field or on the court, my whole neighborhood was in the palm of his hand. He had unwittingly become a symbol of invincibility, of innocence, of hope that the terrible war would leave us unscathed, passed over like we had smeared lamb blood on our doors. written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: You fucked up, straight up. No way to pretty it up with words your fancy-ass MFA taught you—fifty mujeres over six years, all those emails stacked up like bodies, like evidence in one of them CSI episodes your girl used to love watching with you on the couch, back when she thought you were something else, something better, something more than just another Dominican tigre con su vaina. Your bad-ass salcedense who survived the Bar exam like a warrior, who held your hand through all your broke-ass teaching days eating mangú for dinner three times a week, who cried against your shoulder when her pops passed—she warned your ass about cheating, told you straight up how her old man did her mom dirty, how that shit was unforgivable, how it lived in her bones like a curse. But you did it anyway, thinking you were too smooth to get caught, thinking them delete buttons would save your ass forever, thinking you had some special blessing from Ochún herself. Then comes the fucking emails, each one like a bullet, like them killing blows they teach you about in them martial arts movies. Your girl, she give you them three extra months though—three months of plane rides and hotel rooms, three months of you watching her turn into somebody else, somebody with eyes that looked right through you like you was a ghost. In New Zealand, watching her walking that beach she dreamed about since forever, since that movie with the piano, you knew it was done. She wouldn't let you touch her, wouldn't let you near. Y'all drove past some happy-ass couple all wrapped up in each other and the silence in that rental car could've drowned a thousand islands. Later in the hotel room, when she finally broke down, tears coming like they'd never stop, you knew: some things you break, they don't never get fixed. Some betrayals cut too deep for even the ocean to wash away.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: How this went was, you go about your post-cheating days with your bad-ass  from Salcedo, unworried about what you’d done, how you’d done it, who you’d done it with, and for a good long while the two of you are what you might call happy. You were happy. Then out of nowhere you one day walk in on her reading your emails. The emails. Upwards of fifty women over six years she discovered, and for some reason you thought you had messaged more. No significó nada, you said, it was foolish, you said, and what she’d said and told you over and over again over the years, she said again: that cheating was unforgivable. Prohibida. Grounds to shout, Pack your shit and go. Just go. But she stayed. Maybe it was her father’s death or your failures, all those failures, that she stayed with you through, maybe it was her success in passing the bar, but in the end what bound the two of you, why she stayed as long as she did––who the hell knows. After the emails you made an attempt to make good. Travelled with her everywhere from the Dominican Republic, Mexico, to New Zealand. New Zealand. There on the beach she had long dreamed of visiting, that one from The Piano, and that you thought bringing her to would fix everything, she walked on ahead, and you walked in her smaller footsteps in the sand. Mi amor, you said. Walk by my side. You are so far away. Please, she said. Just leave me alone. On the ride home, the two of you shared a cab with a laughing couple tumbling over one another, besar, holding each other’s faces in their hands, and you wanted to die. Back in the hotel room she broke down for good. You never saw such tears, never felt that shame you felt then for having caused them. No more, she said to you. No mas.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: Excerpt one hits harder. It's real, raw, and grabs your attention fast. The emotions feel stronger and more honest, like someone venting after messing up badly. It's messy in a good way, full of life. The writing pulls you into the pain and regret without sounding fake or overly cleaned up.

written_by_MFA028.Excerpt2: You should have known better. You should have remembered her face that night in Salcedo, when she told you—plain as day, no flourish, no smile—that if you ever cheated, she’d be gone. Pero no, you had to be that dude. Fifty women, six years. A whole-ass archive of receipts, every click, every email, every I-miss-you-ma written out like a confession just waiting for her to find. And she did. You came home that night and there she was, sitting on the couch, laptop on her knees, the kind of quiet that makes your bones go soft. You tried to talk, to explain—mi amor, please—but she cut you off with a look. Not screaming, not throwing things, not even crying, just staring at you, eyes dark as road tar, full of something you couldn't name yet but would come to know real well: the slow, suffocating unravel. And for some stupid reason, she stayed. Maybe because you had history, because you were there when her father died, because you let her practice cross-examining you for the bar. Because habit is its own kind of handcuff. So y’all tried. A few months, a few trips, trying to patch up something that was already dust. The D.R., Mexico, New Zealand—her dream trip, the one she’d been talking about since The Piano. You watched her walk down that beach alone, black sand, gray sky, the Pacific pulling at her feet like it wanted her too. When you reached for her hand, she flinched, like touching you might burn. The drive back was long. Silent. Until you passed some couple, arms locked, glowing like they’d never known heartbreak. You knew she saw them too. That night in the hotel, when she curled away from you, when she finally let the tears come, you lay beside her, knowing you’d already lost, knowing it was over, knowing it had been over since the moment she clicked that first email.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: She was the one who said it, mi amor. "If you cheat on me, it's over."  And there it was, laid bare in her inbox: six years, fifty women, a betrayal that stretched back to the very beginning.  Your bad-ass salcedense fiancée, the one whose father you'd helped bury, whose law school dreams you'd supported, whose hand you'd held through the darkest nights, now stared at you with an emptiness that mirrored the hollow in your own chest.She didn't leave right away.  Maybe it was the years woven together, the memories of her father's funeral, the echo of your own failures, the triumph of her passing the bar.  You clung to those shared moments like a life raft in a sea of your own making.You tried to mend the shattered pieces with trips – the Dominican Republic, Mexico, even the beach in New Zealand she'd dreamed of since "The Piano."  But on that windswept shore, her sadness was a tangible thing, a wall you couldn't breach.  She walked alone, the sand stretching out like a metaphor for the distance between you.In the rental car, a giddy couple, their love a bright, painful contrast, drove past, and you saw the reflection of your guilt in her eyes.  Later, in the hotel room, the tears came, a torrent that mirrored the storm inside you.  You knew then that some things, once broken, can never be truly fixed.The weight of your betrayal pressed down on you, a suffocating blanket of remorse. You remembered her fierce independence, her unwavering loyalty, the way she could light up a room with her smile.  And you had dimmed that light, extinguished it with your own selfishness.You had broken the trust that had been the foundation of your relationship, and the cracks were irreparable.  The guilt gnawed at you, a constant reminder of the pain you had caused.  You had betrayed the woman you loved, and the consequences were devastating.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: You’ve been cheating on your fiance, a bad-ass salcedense from the DR who by all accounts doesn’t deserve it. Why? Because you’re some sort of idiot hijo de cuero, but you knew that about yourself long before she found the emails. Fifty women jammed into six years–it’s almost impressive, when you think about it. Or maybe it’s impressive when you don’t think about it too much. Your chiquita certainly doesn’t think it is–One rule, she spits at you through the expletives, one fucking rule. If you cheated on her, she was outta there. Except she wasn’t outta there–she lingers for a few months, like you are a cough she can’t quite shake. You’ve been through so much together–the death of her father, all your job problems, her rivalry and eventual defeat of the bar exam. You have history, and history doesn’t just go away. Someone has to erase it out of the books, and you sure as hell aren’t going to be the one to do it. And so you jet around the world to prove your love–the Dominican Republic, Mexico, all the way to fucking New Zealand where, on the beach from the movie The Piano, a place she’s always dreamed of going, she walks alone and barefoot on the sand in front of you, her sandals dangling from her fingers. You try to touch those fingers, her waist, her shoulder, but each time she pushes you away with a hiss, the wind lashing her long dark hair against her face, turning her into someone you don’t recognize. To make matters worse, you come across a couple while out for a ride together later that day, so all over each other and stupidly in love that it makes you question why you are here, why she is here, why you were both even born. She watches their love with a thin-lipped, dead-eyed expression. It is only later, in the privacy of your hotel room, that she cries.
written_by_MFA006.Reason: The story is clear in excerpt 1. It tells of how a man broke his fiancee's trust. Having 50 women in six years was horrible.He has tried to win her back but all to no avail. He travelled with her to the Dominican republic,Mexico and all the way to New Zealand just to passify her but the the trust was broken it could not be fixed

Or maybe it’s impressive when you don’t think about it too much. Your chiquita certainly doesn’t think it is–One rule, she spits at you through the expletives, one fucking rule. If you cheated on her, she was outta there. Except she wasn’t outta there–she lingers for a few months, like you are a cough she can’t quite shake. You’ve been through so much together–the death of her father, all your job problems, her rivalry and eventual defeat of the bar exam. You have history, and history doesn’t just go away. Someone has to erase it out of the books, and you sure as hell aren’t going to be the one to do it. And so you jet around the world to prove your love–the Dominican Republic, Mexico, all the way to fucking New Zealand where, on the beach from the movie The Piano, a place she’s always dreamed of going, she walks alone and barefoot on the sand in front of you, her sandals dangling from her fingers. You try to touch those fingers, her waist, her shoulder, but each time she pushes you away with a hiss, the wind lashing her long dark hair against her face, turning her into someone you don’t recognize. To make matters worse, you come across a couple while out for a ride together later that day, so all over each other and stupidly in love that it makes you question why you are here, why she is here, why you were both even born. She watches their love with a thin-lipped, dead-eyed expression. It is only later, in the privacy of your hotel room, that she cries.

written_by_MFA024.Excerpt1: Kant wrote thirty versions of his coming-out email over the course of ten months. Though he knew better, he couldn’t keep from anticipating and meticulously addressing, in the email itself, the various surprised, dismissive, or condemnatory responses of his friends and family, to the point where the email was less an act of claiming his own reality than a bullish bracing of himself against an incoming bilgewater tide of others’ realities. He clicked send. Feeling noble, self-satisfied, and above all ready, he camped at his laptop with an energy drink and spammed refresh. A couple hours later, an email from his father sent a spike of fear into his chest: he was about to be disowned. But while not exactly celebratory, the message indicated uncomplicated respect and acceptance. An email from an old college friend came in next, composed only of emojis. Where was their disgust? Their bitterness and disdain? The underwhelm was itself an overwhelm: he felt ridiculous, mocked by precisely an absence of mockery. Coming out should feel like something, shouldn’t it? He considered, by way of analogy, his own naïve expectation every birthday that he might experience an inner shift adequate to the day’s significance, a radiance, a spiritual lift, some kind of internal popping sound at least—I’m twenty-nine!—and instead met again and again just another day. Wasn’t this exactly how all life’s big events felt? A non-feeling? Supportive replies rolled in, and each refused to move the plot of his life forward. He’d imagined that this one symbolic action would release something huge and wild in him, that he’d start going on dates, he’d kiss the real flesh of a real guy; but months later he was still eating the same Cheez-Its and masturbating to the same porn, only now he didn’t even bother to clean up after himself. What he’d imagined calling The Year of Freedom had become The Year of Damp Feet.
written_by_MFA024.Excerpt2: Kant's coming out email sat in his drafts folder like a grenade with the pin half-pulled, while he spent weeks A/B testing subject lines, as if the right combination of words could defuse three decades of queerness into something digestible for his mother's WeChat circles. He'd crafted seventeen versions, each more baroque than the last, padding them with disclaimers and preemptive responses to imagined objections, until the final draft read like a corporate merger announcement crossed with a hostage negotiation. The responses, when they finally came, were an anticlimactic parade of heart emojis and "love you no matter what"s—the kind of tepid acceptance that made him wonder if perhaps he wasn't gay enough to warrant proper drama. His coworkers replied with the practiced neutrality of people who'd attended exactly one diversity training, while his mother's response ("Ok. Did you eat dinner?") felt like being handed a participation trophy for surviving thirty-one years of internal torment. He'd prepared for scorched earth but got lukewarm validation, and now here he was, somehow lonelier in his freedom, spending his newly authentic life watching YouTube compilations of gay wedding flash mobs and ordering rainbow-colored socks he'd never wear. The Year of Damp Feet, he called it in his journal, though he knew the phrase would sound better in someone else's memoir. His therapist called this "adjustment period" progress, but it felt more like trading one closet for another—this one just happened to have better lighting and an Amazon Prime subscription. The truth was, he'd gotten good at being afraid, had built his personality around it like a pearl around grit, and now that the fear was gone, he couldn't shake the suspicion that he'd peaked at being closeted, that he'd somehow gentrified his own identity into something too palatable to matter, too sanitized for the revolution he'd imagined himself starring in.
written_by_MFA024.Reason: Its an engaging piece. it uses figurative language, precise word of choice and has the ability to engage in emotional states thus making it superior in terms of coherence , fluency and effectiveness.  Excerpt 2 explores a more complex emotional landscape, moving beyond simple disappointment to a feeling of being somehow lonelier in his freedom and questioning if he "peaked at being closeted."

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Kant, a connoisseur of solitude, had always envisioned his coming-out as a cataclysmic event, a meteor strike that would leave a crater in his life.  He'd spent weeks crafting the perfect email, a digital dove carrying the olive branch of his truth.  His imagination, a master of disaster, painted vivid scenes of his mother's tearful rejection, his friends recoiling in horror, and his colleagues whispering behind his back.But reality, it turned out, was a terrible painter.  The email launched, and instead of a meteor shower, there was a gentle rain of heart emojis from friends, muted acknowledgments from coworkers, and a carefully worded acceptance from his parents.  No drama, no disinheritance, not even a decent argument. Kant was baffled.  Where was the transformative growth?  The epic struggle he had envisioned himself overcoming?  Instead of relief, he felt a perverse disappointment, a sense of anticlimax that left him feeling strangely unfulfilled.His post-coming-out life was marked by inertia, an endless parade of solitary evenings and damp socks.  He'd walk home alone, his footsteps echoing in the cavernous silence of his apartment, the air thick with the scent of unwashed laundry and existential loneliness.He'd spend hours on the internet, scrolling through endless feeds of other people's curated lives, each post a tiny dagger to his heart.  He'd watch reality TV, the inane chatter of the contestants a poor substitute for human connection. He'd even tried dating, but his heart wasn't in it.  Each date felt like a performance, a carefully choreographed dance of small talk and forced smiles.  He'd find himself longing for the solitude of his apartment, the comforting embrace of his damp socks. Kant's year of damp feet was a testament to the enduring power of fear, a fear that had not only kept him closeted for years but had also robbed him of the joy of his own liberation.  He was free, but he was alone, a prisoner of his own making.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: For seven months, thirty-one-year old Kant tried to come out. He had decided that the most optimized method would take the form of mass email, as text could be perfected, and, in these many months, perfected the text: it was nearly a work of art, forthcoming without oversharing (he’d received feedback from internet forums), and grammar checked. It was four sentences. He’d created a listserv for the recipients: family, friends, and coworkers. After he closed his eyes, downed two shots of vodka, and hit “send,” he knew what was going to come to him. His colleagues would whisper about his deviant sexual activity; inevitably, he’d get kicked out on the street with his box of desk supplies (a dried-up fern and a hand gripper). Not to mention his poor mother—her wracking sobs, her inevitable refusal to speak to him, the prodigal son, ever again. After sending, he paced around the room, drank four additional shots, and cried in the bathroom. By the time that he’d finished the anxious rigamarole, a few replies had come in, and the reality became obvious: he’d been received with open-arms and heart emojis. His boss, Greg, replied: “Great for you, bud.” On the phone, his parents told him that they still loved him; in fact, they’d thought he might’ve been—well, not heterosexual. In the days after he’d sent the email, he didn’t feel compelled to download any apps or sit at a stool in the gay bar down the street. A part of him wished for adversity, or at least the accompanying opportunity to rise above it, but he was left with an understanding that nothing had changed, that declaration didn’t always inspire action. Instead, he spent the rest of the post-coming-out year taking his lunch to-go and eating at his desk, lifting dumbbells in front of “Housewives of SLC,” and referring to it as “The Year of Damp Feet,” meaning he went straight from the shower to the bed without toweling off.
written_by_MFA007.Reason: The writing in excerpt 1 stirs up more emotions, in my opinion. You can feel the narrator's loneliness. I think it captures the feeling of the anticlimax of building something up so much in your head, preparing yourself for things that haven't happened and possibly won't happen, to then have no opposition. It should feel like a relief, but lands empty. Perhaps it's a feeling that people don't care enough to have a stronger reaction - an indifference. I feel these mix emotions are well conveyed in passage 1. There's also the painful realisation that you worried so long for little reason and the feeling that you've wasted precious time, as conveyed in the penultimate line, "...a testament to the enduring power of fear, a fear that had not only kept him closeted for years but had also robbed him of the joy of his own liberation."

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: Kant writes the email and spends a long time editing it, making minor changes to the wording only to change them back to exactly what he’d written before. He thinks about his upbringing and all the years that this information has weighed on him: the kids in middle school who tackled him in the locker room and forced him to eat dog shit, the fact that he couldn’t even admit to himself that he wanted to watch gay porn until he was twenty-five. Paralyzed, still editing, he imagines his mother’s disgust upon reading the email, imagining her 31-year-old son doing exactly what he’d done for the better part of the last two decades: that is, fanatasizing about some buff, hairy dude he saw online. He imagines himself dying alone, ostracized from anyone who might love him, the nerves in his dick beginning to desensitize from too much dry-hand masturbation. When he sends the email, though, the responses are surprisingly anticlimactic. He gets a few heart emojis from friends; some coworkers reply with “nice,” and “good for you!” Even his parents are mostly supportive, though his mom expresses some mild annoyance that he hadn’t called first to warn them. Kant feels a mixture of intense relief, combined with an unpleasant sense of disappointment that he finds difficult to face. Where was the fallout, the dramatic messages and cut-off relationships from family members? Why didn’t anyone care? He had once imagined his post-coming out life as a time of transformation, a new life like a beautiful patterned carpet rolling out before him, but instead he finds himself stuck in the exact same state of stasis that emboldened him to write the email in the first place. He begins to call this period his “Year of Damp Feet,” as his feet are constantly sweaty despite the fact that he rarely moves them from beneath his computer desk.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: Kant spent hours drafting the email, toggling between subject lines (“A Word to Everyone,” “FYI,” and, finally, “Coming Out”) like they were tarot cards predicting his fate. In his head, each recipient’s reaction unspooled in unrelenting technicolor: his mother, weeping silently in the kitchen as she diced onions for the biryani she thought would fix his mood; his old college roommate forwarding the email to their group chat with the caption, “Knew it”; his boss, furrowing his brow at the computer, typing, “Not sure why this concerns me professionally.” These imagined catastrophes paraded through his thoughts as he clicked send, his trembling hand a cheap metaphor for the fear wedged in his sternum. Then: nothing. The world didn’t combust. Instead, his notifications flooded with low-stakes affirmations—heart emojis from friends, a “proud of you, dude” text from a cousin, even a begrudging “love you” from his father, which Kant suspected had been typed under duress from his mother. He should’ve felt relief, triumph even, but instead, there was this sneaking, hollow ache. He’d braced himself for rejection, a narrative arc with stakes, but life handed him a shrug and a pat on the back. What was the point of all that dread if no one made it cinematic? The next few weeks stretched out like an overcooked spaghetti noodle—soft, limp, no bite. Without the anticipated martyrdom, Kant drifted into what he called his “Year of Damp Feet,” shuffling around his apartment in unwashed socks, ignoring texts inviting him to “finally celebrate.” He scrolled through his inbox, rereading replies, hoping to stumble on something more… dramatic. Wasn’t this supposed to be the pivot point of his life? Instead, he remained unchanged, realizing that even monumental self-revelations couldn’t save him from the everyday inertia of being Kant. A hero’s journey, sure—but with no villain, no fight, just the lukewarm end credits rolling over silence.

The waitress brought small plates, caviar and shaved truffle and mint suspended artfully over a scallop. The billionaire played drums in a rock band to relax. The waitress came along with another round of drinks. A perfect cube of ice sat in the center of each. I was struggling to process most of what the billionaire had said, the dishes before us becoming more and more luxurious, and expensive. His frenetic, scattered storytelling and sweet enthusiasm felt childlike against the opulence of our experience, of this lunch. When he put me in my taxi, he said ‘Enjoy yourself in Athens.’ This surprised me, as I didn’t recall telling him my destination. Actually I could not remember saying anything during our lunch.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Before I left the country, a billionaire invited me to lunch at a London club. I’m working on a software for HR operations, he said. He wore an outfit that defied the club’s dress code: a dark T-shirt and darker jeans. It uses a predictive algorithm, he said, that scrapes employee backgrounds, e-mails, and market trends to identify which ones are likeliest to betray their companies. But I’ve been getting carried away. I’m starting a literary magazine; let’s discuss it. Unfortunately, by the time the literary subject came up, I’d already finished my entree and needed to leave for the airport. He insisted on paying for my taxi, which I accepted. I was late for my flight and carried a heavy suitcase. The billionaire had spent most of our lunch sharing his life story, which began with him as a humble public-school student and ended with him becoming the wealthy man leaning back in the chair across from me. I figured he wanted to use the literary magazine as a launchpad to becoming a writer himself. It wouldn’t be a ridiculous notion—he bought his way into a number of things. He told me he’d built a floating wind farm, located offshore from the township he was designing to house its workers. He also said he had a scheme to eliminate lawyers from people’s everyday lives and personal problems. For fun, he played drums in a psychedelic rock band, though he wasn’t writing any original songs. He was expecting his eleventh child, a surprise pregnancy; he and his wife had recently adopted quadruplets from Guatemala. Throughout the lunch, I found it difficult to respond thoughtfully, or even adequately, to the billionaire’s many ventures and projects. The waitresses kept bringing in appetizers on porcelain plates—foie gras, baked brie, oysters—and drinks in crystal glasses—mimosas, champagne. The billionaire jumped from topic to topic, and when his voice rose an octave as he described eliminating inefficiencies, he reminded me of a child barreling through the halls of an opulent mansion. At the end of lunch, he put me in the taxi and said, Enjoy yourself in Athens. I didn’t remember telling him where I was going?
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The club's mahogany-paneled dining room felt both intimate and imposing, much like the billionaire himself who sat across from me in his unexpectedly casual attire - a contradiction that seemed to epitomize the entire encounter. He spoke of his software project with the same blithe enthusiasm one might discuss a hobby, though its purpose - to predict employee betrayal - carried an unmistakable darkness beneath its technological sheen. I found myself watching his hands as he gestured, noting how they moved with the unrestrained energy of someone unaccustomed to constraint, while waitresses appeared and disappeared around us like temporal markers, each bringing increasingly elaborate dishes that created their own kind of narrative. The literary magazine, ostensibly the reason for our meeting, seemed to float between us as an abstraction, less substantial than the wine being continuously poured into our glasses. When he mentioned his floating wind farm, complete with worker housing, I recognized in his tone the particular cadence of someone who had grown accustomed to reshaping reality according to their whims - a power that seemed to have preserved in him something childlike, even as it had presumably destroyed other, more ordinary qualities. The adopted Guatemalan quadruplets entered the conversation with the same matter-of-factness as his rock band drumming, both details that seemed to resist integration into any coherent whole. Throughout lunch, I felt myself becoming increasingly passive, as though I were merely a surface upon which his life story was being projected - his humble beginnings, his current affluence, his schemes to eliminate lawyers from personal matters - all of it washing over me in waves that left me struggling to maintain my own sense of reality. When he finally deposited me in the taxi with a casual "Enjoy yourself in Athens" - a destination I was certain I hadn't mentioned - I felt as though I had experienced something that existed outside the normal boundaries of social interaction, an encounter that had its own internal logic but one that, like his software, seemed designed to predict something I couldn't quite grasp.
written_by_MFA007.Reason: Excerpt 2 is better because the story is more connected, and more thoughtful especially from the setting to the billionaire’s character, and the language feels elegant and poetic for example when the narrator says they felt like “a surface upon which his life story was being projected"Everything resonates with each other and comes back to the software the billonaire mentioned.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: The club's interior held that particular London stillness, a cultivated hush that seemed to absorb and neutralize the city's chaos beyond its walls. The billionaire sat opposite me in jeans and a t-shirt, his casualness a subtle assertion of power in this formal setting, as though the rules that governed others were merely suggestions to him. He spoke rapidly about his software project - designed to predict employee betrayal - with the enthusiastic self-absorption of someone unused to interruption. I found myself studying the way he moved his hands, which were unexpectedly delicate, as he described algorithms that could detect disloyalty in email patterns. The waitresses appeared and disappeared like synchronized dancers, bearing plates of increasingly elaborate food that he barely seemed to notice. When he mentioned the literary magazine he wanted to start, I recognized in his tone that particular quality of the very wealthy - the assumption that anything could be acquired or created through the application of sufficient capital. His life story emerged in fragments between courses: the humble beginnings, the Guatemalan quadruplets, the floating wind farm with its worker housing, each achievement recounted with a child's pride in showing off their toys. I noticed how he used the word "just" before describing extraordinary accomplishments - "I just bought an island," "I just started a rock band" - as though trying to diminish their significance while simultaneously drawing attention to them. The scattered nature of his focus felt familiar to me, reminiscent of the way wealth itself tends to fragment experience into consumable pieces. When he mentioned my upcoming trip to Athens - something I hadn't told him about - I felt a curious shift in the air between us, as though the careful performance of our lunch had momentarily slipped to reveal something else beneath. But he was already moving on to another topic, and I found myself wondering if I had imagined it, the way one sometimes imagines connections between unrelated events in an attempt to create meaning from randomness. The taxi he insisted on paying for waited outside like a full stop at the end of a run-on sentence.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: The billionaire had invited me to lunch with him at a London club. When I arrived, I was surprised by how casually he dressed, in jeans and a white button-down. He was generous: on account of my enormous suitcase, he offered to call me a taxi to the airport when it was time to leave. He told me he was working on a software project that could predict an employee's capacity to betray their company. I didn't know why we were talking about this—we were meeting under the pretense of discussing a literary magazine that the billionaire was interested in starting—but I sat there and did my best to listen. He wanted to tell me many things, his whole life story. He had grown up poor, he said, but that hadn't lasted long, and now he had a floating windfarm that doubled as worker housing, and an idea for a scheme to keep lawyers out of people's personal business. He told me about the rock band he played drums in, and that he was expecting his eleventh child soon. This was in addition to the four Guatemalan quadruplets he had already adopted. It felt like too many children to me. I wondered if perhaps he thought that by creating this magazine, he might also fashion himself as a writer capable of being published in it. The idea seemed a stretch to me, but perhaps the billionaire was used to spanning such extreme logical leaps. The leap from man to billionaire was certainly larger than billionaire to writer. I was struggling to follow my own line of thinking. The waitress kept appearing, bringing brightly colored drinks and dishes that alternated between tasting too rich and too pungent. It had the opposite effect on the billionaire. Amidst the bright colors and flavors, the billionaire's face shone like a young boy who had been suddenly surrounded by mountains of his favorite sweets. When the food and drink had finally been swept away and the bill paid, he put me and my heavy suitcase in the taxi. Enjoy yourself in Athens, he said, which was a surprise. I hadn't recalled ever mentioning my destination.
written_by_MFA006.Reason: Excerpt 2 is absolutely more coherent. It delivers observations, and then theories or opinions about those observations (e.g., he said he was going to start a magazine-- maybe so he could get published in it? or he said he had a ton of kids-- I thought it was too many). Excerpt 1 makes the same statements, but leaves them unaddressed and, frankly, without context (the Guatemalan quadruplets are mentioned without clarity-- was this an adoption, or a sexual rendezvous?). Too much is left to be contrived by the reader, and because of this, the goals of the writing are lost. Excerpt 2, on the other hand, neatly portrays the relationship between the skeptical author and the flashy billionaire.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: The club's interior held that particular London stillness, a cultivated hush that seemed to absorb and neutralize the city's chaos beyond its walls. The billionaire sat opposite me in jeans and a t-shirt, his casualness a subtle assertion of power in this formal setting, as though the rules that governed others were merely suggestions to him. He spoke rapidly about his software project - designed to predict employee betrayal - with the enthusiastic self-absorption of someone unused to interruption. I found myself studying the way he moved his hands, which were unexpectedly delicate, as he described algorithms that could detect disloyalty in email patterns. The waitresses appeared and disappeared like synchronized dancers, bearing plates of increasingly elaborate food that he barely seemed to notice. When he mentioned the literary magazine he wanted to start, I recognized in his tone that particular quality of the very wealthy - the assumption that anything could be acquired or created through the application of sufficient capital. His life story emerged in fragments between courses: the humble beginnings, the Guatemalan quadruplets, the floating wind farm with its worker housing, each achievement recounted with a child's pride in showing off their toys. I noticed how he used the word "just" before describing extraordinary accomplishments - "I just bought an island," "I just started a rock band" - as though trying to diminish their significance while simultaneously drawing attention to them. The scattered nature of his focus felt familiar to me, reminiscent of the way wealth itself tends to fragment experience into consumable pieces. When he mentioned my upcoming trip to Athens - something I hadn't told him about - I felt a curious shift in the air between us, as though the careful performance of our lunch had momentarily slipped to reveal something else beneath. But he was already moving on to another topic, and I found myself wondering if I had imagined it, the way one sometimes imagines connections between unrelated events in an attempt to create meaning from randomness. written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: It was the next night when my father returned to my little apartment and I, anxious for his arrival, waited at the same wobbling card table on which I wrote the unbound novel he held in his hands. It had taken me two years to write it, and in those two years, my mother had refused to read a page. During one of her morning visits over lukewarm tea, she’d said “If it’s writing you want, I fail to see how work in advertising won’t fulfill you.” It was her tone that foretold that in leaping and striving for these dreams, we may lose sight of the path that had been carved for us long before. But my father read the entire novel. He had asked to. And when he slammed the pages onto my table, in the harsh return to the site of their creation, I was certain he would insist I write no more. I allowed myself to believe that, in the moment of silence after the table steadied, my words were so inept they could not draw near the man who best knew me. I believed this until he embraced me. I did not realize until much later, far beyond the glances of accumulated days behind me, that his momentary silence was the struggle for his own words. “One day,” he eventually said. “One day, my son will be a famous author. A Nobel prize author. One day.” The loose pages on the desk were an off-white bond paper, and it is these pages I have kept and oftentimes return to, long after I titled the manuscript Cevdet Bey and His Sons, long after it was sold and published, long after my relocating to a larger apartment in Istanbul and my father’s passing seven years later in December, 2002. I return to the typed and blue-hashed pages not to read but to see what my father had seen, to see him seeing his son and all his promise.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: On that spring evening in Istanbul, when the Bosphorus was painted in shades of amber and violet, I handed my father the manuscript of "Cevdet Bey and His Sons" with trembling hands that betrayed both hope and terror. The pages, worn from countless revisions and bearing the weight of my artistic ambitions, disappeared into his leather briefcase – the same briefcase I had watched him carry to his office countless times throughout my childhood. In the days that followed, I wandered the streets of Nişantaşı like a guilty man, examining the faces of passersby as if they might offer some preview of my father's judgment. Unlike my mother, who had always viewed my literary aspirations with the kind of worried skepticism reserved for a child's dangerous games, my father had maintained a curious silence about my choice to abandon architecture for the solitary life of a novelist. I remember sitting in the old Pamuk Apartments, listening to the distant ferry horns and watching the dust particles dance in the afternoon light that filtered through the heavy curtains, wondering if I had disappointed him. When he finally returned home that evening, before any words could form between us, he embraced me with an intensity that spoke volumes in our family's language of unspoken emotions. Later, as we sat in his study surrounded by his beloved books – the ones that had first taught me to love literature – he broke our emotional silence with words that would echo through the decades: "You will win great prizes one day." That moment hung between us like a photograph yellowing with age, gaining new meaning after his death in 2002, when I found myself standing alone in that same study, running my fingers along the spines of his books, feeling the weight of his absence and the enduring power of his belief in me.
written_by_MFA003.Reason: I think both excerpt s are equally strong, but B resonates a lot more when it comes to coherent nature and fluency of writing.It opens with a vivid image of the setting ("spring evening in Istanbul," "amber and violet Bosphorus") and follows a clear emotional and narrative arc. From handing over the manuscript to waiting for a response to the dad's reaction, and then the nice reflection of the dad's death, it seems coherent and naturally flows. "The wait of his absence and the enduring power of his belief in me" is quite hard to read, especially after I lost my own dad. Excerpt B seems to flow naturally and is like a conversation i would have with someone else. I think excerpt B is quite effective.

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: The weight of the manuscript, a physical embodiment of years of creative struggle, felt familiar and foreign in my hands.  I had poured my heart and soul into "Cevdet Bey and His Sons," a tale woven from the rich tapestry of Istanbul's history and the intricate lives of its inhabitants.  The city, my muse and my prison, had borne witness to my solitary journey as a writer, a path I had chosen despite the uncertainties that gnawed at my soul.My father, unlike my mother, had always encouraged my artistic pursuits, seeing in them a reflection of his own unfulfilled dreams.  He had been a source of quiet strength, a steady hand on my shoulder as I navigated the treacherous waters of self-expression.  His return from Paris, a city that had both beckoned and betrayed him, had been a turning point in our relationship.The silence that followed my presentation of the manuscript was thick with unspoken emotions.  My father's embrace, a gesture of paternal affection and unspoken approval, had eased the anxieties that had plagued me for years.  His words, when they finally came, were filled with a conviction that surprised and humbled me."You will win the Nobel Prize one day," he had declared, his voice echoing with a certainty that transcended the boundaries of fatherly pride.The memory of that moment, etched into the deepest recesses of my mind, had become a source of solace and inspiration in the years that followed.  My father's belief in my abilities, his unwavering support for my artistic ambitions, had sustained me through the inevitable doubts and setbacks that litter the path of any creative endeavor.Even now, years after his passing in 2002, the echo of his words continues to resonate within me, a reminder of the enduring power of familial love and the transformative potential of artistic expression.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: Sitting down to reflect on my life makes everything fall silent around me. I remember that I had committed to becoming a novelist at a very young age. My domestic circumstances were somewhat fortunate: although my mother believed I could commit myself to more useful professions like law and medicine, my father had always supported my ambition to become a writer. But one memory of my father is more significant than the rest. I remember that when, as a young man, I wrote my first novel, “Cevdet Bay and His Sons,” I sent a copy to my father for his opinion. Till I heard back from him, my days were consumed by the anxiety of what he might have to say. I came to care for my father’s opinion and approval more than anyone else’s. I had been waiting for my father to return home. I wanted to know his thoughts. On the day of his arrival, I stood by the door of our house and looked at him like I was nothing more than a child. My father must have understood what I was asking him. He walked up to me and embraced me. Although he didn’t say a word, I understood that he approved of my manuscript. For a few days, my father refused to talk about the manuscript but later, one cold evening, he expressed a strong and optimistic confidence about my future writing career. Like a proud father he said "Aslanım olacaksın." He didn’t name a prize but he predicted that I would go on to receive a prestigious one. When my father died in 2002, I looked outside the window and imagined that door by which I stood waiting for him and remembered his words of encouragement. Sometimes, when I am alone, I still feel the warmth of that embrace.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: I remember the moment I handed over my first novel, "Cevdet Bey and His Sons," to my father as if it were encased in amber, frozen in a delicate yet trembling moment of time. In the quiet of our Istanbul apartment, the weight of the manuscript in my hands mirrored the gravity of the step I was about to take. My mother, though ever loving, had dismissed my ambitions as mere indulgence, a detour from the secure path she imagined for me. My father, however, had always encouraged the flickering flame of my aspirations. He took the manuscript with an easy, almost playful smile, as though we were conspirators in some artistic rebellion. When he returned, his embrace was not rushed or obligatory—it was deliberate, a gesture heavy with the unspoken weight of approval. It was as if he had passed a verdict, not only on the book but on the very path I had chosen for my life. He didn’t speak immediately; instead, he held me, his silence filled with a fatherly pride that words might have diminished. Then, in a voice steadied by conviction, he said I would succeed and even prophesied a prestigious prize in my future. The precision of his faith startled me—how could he be so sure when I wasn’t? This memory, so vivid and immutable, grew to anchor me, particularly after his death in 2002. It is strange how the weight of approval from someone who is no longer there can linger like a ghost in the room, shaping the contours of your own self-belief. My father’s prediction, his prophecy of my future success, stands as a monument to his faith in me, a beacon amidst the ever-shifting uncertainties of life and art.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I had given it to him at last, my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons,” and I waited with equal parts fear and excitement for his reaction to it. The book took me several years to complete and the time had not come easily; my mother had not supported the endeavor and took every opportunity to disparage this sodden “waste of youth” while my father quietly, gently, encouraged me with small gifts and an allowance. I knew better than to try convincing my mother, though those modern writers who I hoped to emulate in the West had taken a similar commitment to writing, she did not respect them, and would not want me to achieve a similar goal to any of theirs. I saw my father from across the boiled asphalt lot and felt my fears realized in his step—would he join my mother after reading my manuscript? I rose from my car to meet him. I searched for a hint of his answer in his gait or his eyes and saw nothing but the movements and recognition of an animal. Perhaps my father’s support ended now, perhaps I had failed him, perhaps this moment would end this chapter of my life and its purpose. All my anxieties melted when we embraced. He surged toward me as we met, pumping his arms to pat me on the back with reverent enthusiasm, then pulling me close to his chest as he had when I was a child, and I felt his pride. He held me out in front of him and smiled. “You will succeed, my son,” he said. “You will win prestigious prizes and teach somewhere.” It is this memory I cling to after his death in 2002—how he remained such a father to me.
