written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I often long to be a better feminist. I know what a good feminist, a correct feminist, looks like. A woman who shouts down men who try to dominate her, a woman who refuses to ever be under the thumb of a man and shows up at all the right marches and always has her pink pussy hat at the ready for whatever protests comes next. I see those women, and I respect them, and often, I want to be them. But the fact of the matter is sometimes when men try to dominate me I let them, so they can mow my lawn without much of a fuss. When my father rattles off five misogynistic things in a row on our phone call I am silent, because I am too tired to fight back. And sometimes it is too cold outside to protest, pink pussy hat or no pink pussy hat. I want to be a good feminist, one that believes that women can do anything by themselves and we don't need any man. But sometimes I long to be cared for, sometimes I think I really do need a man. I long to be soft and weepy, and wear long flowing dresses and lipstick. This is the type of women the patriarchy praises, and feminists despise - and sometimes that is the type of woman I want to be. I want to be a good feminist, but often I am a bad feminist. I like dancing to rap songs with lyrics that are categorically misogynistic. I like wearing pink and scrolling through Pinterest pictures of those 'perfect' women that I know are there to make all us regular women feel terrible about ourselves. I like wearing those long maxi dresses that make me look like I could be on a farm, tending chickens and popping out babies dutifully for my husband. Not only do I like wearing those dresses, but I even have opinions on those dresses -- there are certain prints I love and other prints I find gauche, and when I see women wearing the latter I judge them. Another thing a good feminist would never do. And yet - I believe in the equality of the sexes. I am against male domination. I love women, and I want women to thrive. I just refuse to step up onto the pedestal of 'good feminist'. If I did, I'd fall. I'm a bad feminist.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I am a contradiction in motion, a living, breathing paradox who spends far too much time thinking about the ways I fail to measure up to some imagined feminist ideal. There are days when I scroll through Instagram, double-tapping photos of women in impossibly high heels and perfectly curated outfits, while simultaneously drafting tweets about the toxicity of beauty standards. I tell myself I'm participating in critical discourse, but really, I'm just another woman trying to make sense of the impossible space between who I am and who I think I should be. Sometimes I find myself in department stores, running my fingers over silk blouses that cost more than my weekly grocery budget, imagining the kind of woman who wears them—successful, put-together, somehow both feminine and feminist enough. Then I remember how I once wrote a scathing essay about consumerism and capitalism's commodification of feminist empowerment, and I feel like a fraud. But here's the thing: I am tired of apologizing for these contradictions. I am tired of feeling like I need to justify why I can write about dismantling patriarchal beauty standards while also spending forty-five minutes watching makeup tutorials on YouTube. The truth is, I want to be taken seriously as a feminist scholar and intellectual while also wearing sparkly nail polish and watching reality TV shows that probably set feminism back twenty years. I want to rage against the machine while sometimes, just sometimes, finding comfort in the very structures I critique. My feminism lives in this messy middle ground, where theory meets reality, where academic discourse crashes headlong into human desire. I keep thinking about how we're all just trying to navigate this complicated terrain of identity and authenticity, how we're all just fumbling in the dark, reaching for something that feels true. Maybe that's why I find myself drawn to these contradictions—they're the most honest part of who I am. They're the space where my humanity refuses to be neat and tidy, refuses to fit into the boxes we've created for what it means to be a "good" feminist or a "real" woman. So yes, I will continue to critique the patriarchy while also watching "The Bachelor." I will write about intersectional feminism while also obsessing over my skincare routine. I will hold space for all of these seemingly incompatible truths because that's what it means to be human in this complicated, messy world we're trying to change.

I think it does a good job with achieving its goals.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: At one time I imagined that being a desirable woman made you an object and being an undesirable woman made you a person. In the years since I’ve learned that being an undesirable woman actually makes you less than a person, makes you something subhuman. If you are a woman but not a beautiful woman, are instead a fat woman scorned by men and more largely scorned by a society that understands women as objects subjected to male desire, then you are not allowed to be human. And this is me. Not quite a human because of the body I live in. This realm is where my own bad feminism is seen again and again, in my understanding that there is no right way to be a woman, no way to be a woman and live an uncomplicated human existence, put in conflict with a desire to be a woman who is allowed to be. When I think about weight loss, about changing myself so that I might live in an uncontroversial body, I see in this transformation some proof of concept: if I can be normal, if I can be accepted in my body, then my life will be made significantly simpler. The thin woman is a woman who is allowed to be a woman. These fantasies border phantasmagoria, bad feminist rhetoric equating internal change with external corroboration. What does it mean, then, if I long for independence and long also to be cared for, to surrender to care. If I want to present myself as a professional and want also to be vulnerable, to handle my vulnerability as a weapon. This, too, tied with physicality—to want to look like woman, wear pink and enjoy fashion, and simultaneously live as a professional who critiques beauty standards asking women to starve themselves into shadows and silhouettes. I might listen to rap with inherently anti-feminist lyrics, I might wear pink skirts and loathe maxi dresses made for thin bodies and thin bodies alone, and I might hate myself for all this—I may find myself mortified by these choices, by the bad feminist implications therein. But none of this posturing, none of these feelings, exempt me from the womanhood I was born into. There is no good feminist, I could argue. There is no way out. If you want to be human, you cannot also be a woman.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: Feminism is a complicated thing. It’s a word I wear like an oversized coat, too heavy in some places, too tight in others, but always mine. I say I’m a feminist, but then I catch myself singing along to a rap song where the chorus is basically a hate crime against women. I’ll roll my eyes at beauty standards while simultaneously scrolling through Instagram, obsessing over how that one influencer makes every maxi dress look so effortless. And pink? Don’t even get me started. I own a pink coffee mug that says “Boss Babe” in gold script, which makes me cringe every time I see it, but I still use it every single morning. It’s an emblem of my contradictions, a piece of evidence in the case I’m building against myself.I often wonder if these contradictions make me a bad feminist, a hypocrite. But then I think, isn’t that what being human is? Aren’t we all just patchworks of our contradictions, held together by loose stitches of guilt and self-awareness? I laugh at myself, at my ridiculousness, at how I try to intellectualize everything, including my love of trashy reality TV, which I’ve somehow convinced myself is a feminist act because it’s “women owning their narratives.” That’s bullshit, but it’s my bullshit.I try, in my way, to reconcile these things. I write about them, hoping that if I untangle these thoughts long enough, they’ll make sense, that I’ll make sense. But clarity doesn’t always come, and honestly, I’m not sure I want it to. There’s something freeing about admitting you’re a mess, that you don’t have it all figured out. It’s like stepping off the pedestal before someone else can shove you off.The truth is, I want what I want. I want to be a feminist and a mess. I want to call out misogyny while dancing to songs that degrade women. I want to rage against the patriarchy and wear lipstick that costs more than a week’s worth of groceries. I want to be seen, to be loved, even when I can’t love all the parts of myself. And maybe, just maybe, being a bad feminist is better than not trying to be one at all.

written_by_MFA002.Excerpt1: To be a feminist — perhaps, to be a woman at all — is to teeter on the edge of a chasm between principle and performance. This week I rode the subway for the first time in months. In a moment of hyperperception, I swept my awareness over the scene: dusty bottles at the edge of the track, a lone rat scurrying into the bowels of the public transit system, three men hulking at one side of a gum-stained bench, blasting Drake on a tinny speaker. I found myself acutely aware not only of my perception of the scene, but of the men’s perception of my perception of the scene, and my perception of the men’s perception of my perception. Was I to admonish these men for listening to an artist well-known for wrapping misogyny in a catchy tune and feeding it to vulnerable audiences of young, troubled men? Did they expect this of me —were they waiting for my reprimand, already preparing their rebuttal? Should I be bracing myself for a flurry of calm downs and lighten ups? I did none of these things. Instead I found myself nodding slightly to the beat. Because, to tell the truth — it was a catchy tune. Perhaps this makes me a bad feminist. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for wearing pink flowy maxi dresses that highlight my femininity, a choice in line with the beauty standards and fashion requirements long used to subjugate women — to make women seem weaker, more delicate, more frivolous. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for ceding, at times, to this perception of the feminine as frail and foolish when it conveniences me: allowing a gallant male stranger to change my tire on the side of the road or letting my professional persona slip in a rare moment of vulnerability. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for thinking any of this at all — by discounting my true nature, I am participating in the classic erasure of women’s personal desires in favor of the welfare of others. Perhaps I am a bad feminist. But I am also a tired feminist. Where does it end? Am I to be trapped forever in this infinite moral calculation of every action and every thought? Candidly, I don’t mind being a bad feminist, if it means I can be like the subway rat — revolting and dirty, maybe, but free to scurry at my whim.
written_by_MFA002.Excerpt2: I'm a mess of contradictions, a walking paradox in pink. I love fashion, the way a dress can make me feel powerful, yet I scoff at the societal pressures that dictate what a woman should wear. I blast rap music with lyrics that would make a sailor blush, then cringe at the misogyny I'm internalizing. I devour feminist literature, yet I can't seem to shake the feeling that I'm not "feminist enough."My internal monologue is a constant tug-of-war between my desires and my ideals. I crave independence, the freedom to be my own woman, but I also yearn for the comfort of being cared for, of surrendering to vulnerability. I strive for professionalism, to be taken seriously in a world that often dismisses women, but I also want to embrace my femininity, to express myself without fear of judgment.I'm a kaleidoscope of conflicting emotions, a whirlwind of passion and doubt. I'm fiercely independent, yet I long for connection. I'm confident and self-assured, yet I'm plagued by insecurities. I'm a feminist, but I'm also a woman who loves all things pink and sparkly.I oscillate between wanting to burn the system down and simply wanting to find my place within it. I rail against the patriarchy, yet I find myself drawn to men who embody traditional masculinity. I champion body positivity, yet I struggle with my own body image.I'm a walking contradiction, a living embodiment of the complexities of womanhood. I'm not sure what it all means, this jumble of contradictions that makes up who I am. But I'm learning to embrace it, to accept that I can be both a feminist and a woman who loves fashion, both independent and vulnerable, both confident and insecure.I'm a work in progress, a constant evolution of self-discovery. I'm not perfect, but I'm perfectly me. And in a world that demands conformity, that's my own small act of rebellion.I'm not sure what the future holds, but I'm excited to find out. I'm excited to continue to grow and learn and evolve as a woman, a feminist, and a human being. I'm excited to continue to challenge myself, to push the boundaries of what it means to be a woman in today's world.I'm excited to continue to find my voice, to speak my truth, even when it's messy and complicated. I'm excited to continue to embrace my contradictions, to celebrate the beautiful mess that I am.

written_by_MFA027.Excerpt1: The night air, maybe tinged with the scent of some flowering tree I can’t identify, swirls through the gaps in the fencing.  The thrill elicited by this view—the tiny illuminated windows, the way human-scale elements are visibly enmeshed with the inhuman scale of the skyline—is something I associate with urban spaces.  The Hudson River, the Palisades on the other side, even the movement of the clouds, fail to trigger the same response.I breathe deeply, trying to identify the chemical compounds in the air.  I’m high up enough to see the bridges spanning into Brooklyn and Queens.  I imagine the collective exhalation of eight million people, the collective inhalation, the movement of hands over innumerable screens, the scrolling, the tapping, the repetitive stress injuries.  I picture the vast network of pipes, mains, and cables extending below the streets, the nighttime deliveries to bodegas, the movement of trains underground.I see the skyline as the material manifestation of a second person plural, a collective to which all art, even the most intimate, is addressed.  A yet-to-exist “we” glimpsed in the bundled debt, the traces of antidepressants in the water supply, the elaborate traffic system, the weather patterns. written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: I inhale the night, which has the faint taste of blossoms hanging on it. I always found it thrilling to watch the city this way, how the illuminated windows on apartment buildings and offices cling together as parts of an expansive and profoundly intricate skyline. The beauty others find in a mountain, a valley, a crested hill, I find in looking at urban mosaics like these, like Manhattan, this grand forest of buildings and bridges and smoke and air. I find that nature feels too much like a singular entity, a crystalline cohesion, whereas urban landscapes feel like a second person plural, something that does not exist now, but exists only in the future, a future where everything, art and intimacy and joy and expansion, has room to breathe and move. It’s almost unbearable, the sublimity of the bundled debt, the anti-depressants that stream through urine and into the water supply, the light pollution, traffic in the sky and on the ground, all connecting to create something artful and strange and united. This is what I think of when I gaze at the skyline, how I will become an artist, one who transforms and reshapes bad modes of collectivity into the possibility for good, into a broad future where all entities can exist in the same body. I think of Noor—how can I not?— and my connection to her, her connection to us all, her large and shapeless body, which the fiction of the world organizes itself so perfectly around. I am alone. I am alienated. And I am the alienator—I have no false pretenses about this. How ironic it feels, sometimes, to know that I am alone, and yet not even identical with myself. Is it foolish that I find some hope in that? That I think of Noor and I feel her and I smell the blossoms of the city night and I understand that the past and present are formless, shapeless, and can be reorganized, reimagined into something bigger? I sit here and I look at the skylight. It’s midnight, and I am on a bench that’s cold and, I think, slightly damp, though it’s hard to tell. My eyes are blurry with exhaustion, my hair flattened by that blue bandanna from Goodwill, and I am eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango from a Ziplock bag. My eyes begin to burn, a mild lacrimal event, as I think of all this possibility. My fingertips are slightly slippery, sugared from the fruit I’m eating.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: The Manhattan skyline at night is, for me, an argument against the concept of singularity, not merely because it’s the result of innumerable hands and minds, bundled debts, and traces of antidepressants in the water but because the multiplicity of its forms evokes a sublimity alien to natural landscapes. Standing there, breathing in air tinged with blossoms or exhaust fumes, my gaze skips between the architectural vastness and the tiny illuminated windows, each a human-scale element folded into a collective fabric that feels, somehow, alive. The skyline is not a skyline; it is a second person plural, an as-yet-unrealized "we" that all art addresses, even the most intimate. This thought emerges less like revelation than residue, clinging stubbornly to my attempts to organize experience into some semblance of narrative. The more I reflect on the idea of this "we," the more it unravels into the sublime traffic of urban life—the shifting weather patterns mirrored in high-rise glass, the ebb and flow of bundled debts that keep the city afloat, and the anonymous networks of pipes, trains, and storm drains humming just below the surface.It is in this interwoven complexity that I find my vocation as an artist, not to produce artifacts but to transform what I’ve termed “bad forms of collectivity” into fleeting glimpses of unity—never full, never final, but enough to sustain a flicker of hope for a communal body. In this endeavor, Noor—or, perhaps, the fiction of Noor—becomes a locus, a gravitational pull around which my fragmented thoughts and projects reorganize themselves. Noor is not Noor; they are the shorthand for an idea, an abstraction that reminds me how little of myself is mine, how often I am alien to my own being. And yet, in that discomfort, that acknowledgment of not being fully identical with oneself, there lies the faint shimmer of possibility—a utopian flicker in which past and present collapse into a unified whole, not resolved but reinterpreted.I am, however, just a body on a bench at midnight, my bandanna flattening my hair, my hands sticky with the juice of unsulfured mango as I project myself into futures too many to count. A mild lacrimal event—a phrase borrowed, revised—wets my cheek. The tears are neither despair nor ecstasy but a texture of the moment, the salt of an urban meditation that hovers between the profound and the ridiculous. I do not attempt to resolve it, knowing the real art is in letting the tension linger, illuminating the skyline from within.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. Yet it didn’t matter: the world was a sprawling racket of collaboration, full of bad forms of collectivity which, as an artist, I could transform into something more, a brighter “you.” Of course, at that moment, as I meditated on the skyline, Noor insinuated herself into my thoughts. It was only natural, considering how the fiction of the world swarmed around her. As I sat on the bench, I almost felt as if I was sitting upon Noor, upon “you.” My consciousness waned into another—and was this such a crime? One could not be identical with oneself—but could one be better? After reaffixing my bandana to my head, and consuming an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, I found myself suffering a mild lacrimal event. Would the world make a skyline within you? Would we ever be a part of the human tangle?
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: Standing before Manhattan's impossible geometry at midnight, I felt arrested not by anything in the natural world—I had long since ceased to find redemption in sunsets or mountain ranges—but by the peculiar dialogue between scales, how the tiny illuminated windows punctuated the massive edifices, creating a syntax of light I could almost read. The skyline manifested what I'd come to think of as the second person plural, the collective "you" to which all art, even the most intimate, must ultimately be addressed. I thought about the bundled debt floating above us, the antidepressants cycling through the water system, the neural network of traffic patterns, all these bad forms of collectivity that somehow contained within them the kernel of their transformation. When Noor appeared in my mind, as she inevitably did, the fiction of the world reorganized itself around her presence—not Noor as an individual exactly, but Noor as a figure for my own dissolving sense of self, my growing awareness that I wasn't identical with myself, which was both terrifying and, paradoxically, hopeful. The city seemed to pulse with the possibility of a communal body yet to emerge, one that would transform these alienated moments into components of a shared experience, a new kind of "we" that would retroactively justify my conviction that art could still matter, could still gesture toward utopia. The warm spring air carried traces of cherry blossoms from somewhere distant, maybe Brooklyn, and I found myself contemplating how each illuminated window represented a story, a fragment of the collective consciousness I was simultaneously part of and alienated from. I sat there on the bench, my hair flattened against my skull by a bandanna, working through an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, its sweetness almost medicinal on my tongue, as a mild lacrimal event began. I watched the clouds pass between me and the fluorescent towers, feeling time curl around the edges of the evening, imagining a future moment in which this present would be reinterpreted, in which my tears would signify something other than what they did now, although I couldn't specify what. The city's vastness seemed to collapse and expand simultaneously, each moment pregnant with the possibility of transformation, each solitary figure on each bench somehow connected through the invisible threads of urban consciousness that bound us all together in our collective solitude.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Samad leaned back, fingers tightening around the stem of his glass, watching the amber liquid swirl, gathering his thoughts like a man recalling a half-forgotten dream. "You know, Irie, I did not come here to stay," he began, with the kind of dramatic pause he enjoyed, as if delivering some great revelation. "No. It was meant to be temporary, a short stint, a little adventure before going home, but then—ah, then!—this country does something to you, something insidious. You come thinking you are a visitor, and before you know it, you have children who speak back to you in accents you don’t recognize, who call you old-fashioned, who think the way you eat, the way you pray, the way you exist is some sort of historical relic." He sighed, gesturing vaguely at the street outside. "One son, a lawyer. A proper pukka Englishman, with his nice suits and his nice house and his nice friends who politely pretend not to see the color of his skin. The other?" A mirthless laugh. "A warrior. A martyr. At least that’s what he believes. This place—it stretches you, splits you down the middle. And you, you keep asking yourself: where do I belong? Here? There? Nowhere?" He shook his head. "They tolerate us, Irie. Tolerate. Like a mild skin condition." Irie frowned. "Oh, that’s not true, surely." Samad just smiled, a tired, knowing thing.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: "If I could tell my own father about this!" cried Samad. "One son, with his marmite on toast and his football games. The other, a downright fundamentalist! More Bengali than I ever was. What would he have done, my father, if he could see me now? He would have said, It serves you right, Samad. That is what you get for going somewhere you are only tolerated." Samad paused and took a long sip of his tea. "Oh, Irie," he continued. "If I’d known that England was the way that it is. A place where we are merely tolerated. A place where belonging and not belonging both feel like a trap. Was it not pure foolishness, then, to come here? Not sometimes, but every single day, I know it was a mistake. We should have stayed put. What didn’t we stay put?” Irie shook her head. “That is not true, surely, Samad,” she said. “It’s England. It’s what we have always wanted. We dreamed of this place all our lives." "We dreamed of a version of this place, certainly," said Samad. "Truthfully, I don’t know what I believe anymore. I thought I knew what it meant to be born somewhere. But now? What does it matter where you are born? How can you belong anywhere if you feel... adrift. Every day. Completely adrift."

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: "There is a speck of ash at the bottom of this cup of tea." He was not sure why he was telling this to the waiter, because he couldn't tell if it was real ash or maybe just little crumbs from the tea itself."Oh dear, I'm sorry sir. I'll get that swapped out for you right away.""He didn't even think to argue. Part of me wants him to tell me to go back to whatever 'istan' I'm from. That's what they used to tell me when I first arrived. Before my voice began to sound like theirs, before I knew what a three-piece coat was, before I knew how to take the trolley.And now, he insists on talking to me as if I'm just one of them. 'Sir,' he calls me, 'sir.' Like part of me has rotted to be like the forever rotten core of them and they smell it too. But isn't that what I always wanted? Isn't that why I came to this country? To join the ranks of those torn, of those divided? I swear these warring sides of myself must have migrated to my reproductive organs, for just look at my children," said Samad bitterly."I think of the children. Varush, he just sticks out that stiff upper lip all day and god, that accent—sometimes I just want to unhook his jaw and stuff it full of chai, and tell him to go back where we came from. But then Malik, the other boy, always complaining that everything is offensive and everyone is oppressing us. These children, I swear, sometimes I just want to walk away from them.""Oh, that's not true, surely," Irie says."Please do not underestimate the ability of a father to forsake his children! If I was a man before I made the devil's pact and came here, I am something less now.". The waiter is taking long. Samad drinks the tea and the ash all in one gulp. "I want to feel all of its worlds inside me. But really, they just vanish, like they never existed at all", he says.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: Samad sat there, his fingers drumming against the pub table, each tap a tiny rebellion against the polished oak surface that had witnessed centuries of English contemplation. "You see," he began, his voice carrying that particular tone of a man who has rehearsed his grievances in the mirror, "this country, this England, it's like one of those fancy department stores where they let you browse but never expect you to buy anything." He paused, taking a theatrical sip of his whiskey—a drink he'd adopted precisely because it made him feel like a fraud. "My son—the one who wears those ridiculous pinstripe suits—he thinks he's fooled them all. Barrister this, Westminster that. But they see through it, oh yes, they do. And the other one?" He laughed, but it was the kind of laugh that carries more warning than humor. "He's gone and done exactly what they feared we all would. Turned himself into their worst nightmare, hasn't he? A proper fundamentalist. Both of them are just different sides of the same bloody English pound." Irie, who had been watching this performance with the patient attention of someone who had seen it many times before, interjected softly, "Oh, that's not true, surely." But Samad was already racing ahead, carried by the momentum of his discontent. "When I came here, I thought—just a few years, make some money, go home a success. Instead?" He spread his arms wide, encompassing the pub, the street outside, the whole of London, "Instead, I've become this strange creature who belongs nowhere. Not here, where they 'tolerate' us—" he spat the word like a pip from a bitter fruit—"and not there, where I'm now too English to fit in. Tell me, what is a birthplace anyway? A cosmic accident? A life sentence? Or just another pretty lie we tell ourselves while we're busy being lost?" He turned back to his whiskey, his reflection in the mirror behind the bar showing a man caught between what he was and what he had become, between where he was from and where he had landed—a man trapped in the hyphen of British-Bengali identity.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: Samad sat there, his fingers drumming against the pub table, each tap a tiny rebellion against the polished oak surface that had witnessed centuries of English contemplation. "You see," he began, his voice carrying that particular tone of a man who has rehearsed his grievances in the mirror, "this country, this England, it's like one of those fancy department stores where they let you browse but never expect you to buy anything." He paused, taking a theatrical sip of his whiskey—a drink he'd adopted precisely because it made him feel like a fraud. "My son—the one who wears those ridiculous pinstripe suits—he thinks he's fooled them all. Barrister this, Westminster that. But they see through it, oh yes, they do. And the other one?" He laughed, but it was the kind of laugh that carries more warning than humor. "He's gone and done exactly what they feared we all would. Turned himself into their worst nightmare, hasn't he? A proper fundamentalist. Both of them are just different sides of the same bloody English pound." Irie, who had been watching this performance with the patient attention of someone who had seen it many times before, interjected softly, "Oh, that's not true, surely." But Samad was already racing ahead, carried by the momentum of his discontent. "When I came here, I thought—just a few years, make some money, go home a success. Instead?" He spread his arms wide, encompassing the pub, the street outside, the whole of London, "Instead, I've become this strange creature who belongs nowhere. Not here, where they 'tolerate' us—" he spat the word like a pip from a bitter fruit—"and not there, where I'm now too English to fit in. Tell me, what is a birthplace anyway? A cosmic accident? A life sentence? Or just another pretty lie we tell ourselves while we're busy being lost?" He turned back to his whiskey, his reflection in the mirror behind the bar showing a man caught between what he was and what he had become, between where he was from and where he had landed—a man trapped in the hyphen of British-Bengali identity.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: "There is a speck of ash at the bottom of this cup of tea." He was not sure why he was telling this to the waiter, because he couldn't tell if it was real ash or maybe just little crumbs from the tea itself."Oh dear, I'm sorry sir. I'll get that swapped out for you right away.""He didn't even think to argue. Part of me wants him to tell me to go back to whatever 'istan' I'm from. That's what they used to tell me when I first arrived. Before my voice began to sound like theirs, before I knew what a three-piece coat was, before I knew how to take the trolley.And now, he insists on talking to me as if I'm just one of them. 'Sir,' he calls me, 'sir.' Like part of me has rotted to be like the forever rotten core of them and they smell it too. But isn't that what I always wanted? Isn't that why I came to this country? To join the ranks of those torn, of those divided? I swear these warring sides of myself must have migrated to my reproductive organs, for just look at my children," said Samad bitterly."I think of the children. Varush, he just sticks out that stiff upper lip all day and god, that accent—sometimes I just want to unhook his jaw and stuff it full of chai, and tell him to go back where we came from. But then Malik, the other boy, always complaining that everything is offensive and everyone is oppressing us. These children, I swear, sometimes I just want to walk away from them.""Oh, that's not true, surely," Irie says."Please do not underestimate the ability of a father to forsake his children! If I was a man before I made the devil's pact and came here, I am something less now.". The waiter is taking long. Samad drinks the tea and the ash all in one gulp. "I want to feel all of its worlds inside me. But really, they just vanish, like they never existed at all", he says.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: "Bloody hell! One son a pukka Englishman lawyer, the other a fundamentalist terrorist. And me, I'm stuck here in this bloody country, this England, this devil's pact of a place! They said it was temporary, they said it was a stepping stone, but they lied! Thirty-odd years and I'm still here, still tolerated, still an immigrant, still not one of them! My sons, they've got it figured out, they fit in, one way or another. But me, I'm neither here nor there, a bloody ghost, a man without a country! This England, it sucks you in, chews you up, and spits you out! There's no place for us here, no place for anyone who doesn't fit their mold!"Oh, that's not true, surely," Irie offered, her voice a gentle counterpoint to Samad's bitter outpouring."True? Of course, it's bloody true! Look at me, look at my life, what does it mean? What am I? A joke, a parody, a failed experiment! They talk about birthplaces, about roots, about belonging, but what do they know? What do they know about being torn from your home, about being a stranger in a strange land, about never truly belonging anywhere? This England, it's not my home, it will never be my home, and now, after all this time, I can't even go back to where I came from. I'm adrift, I'm lost, I'm a man without a place, without a home, without a bloody identity!"
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: "It's all a joke, a cosmic joke and God is laughing somewhere, but me? I ask to raise two good Muslim sons in this country and walk away feeling as though I've made a devil's pact," Samad cried. "One son has fully converted, a pukka Englishman. He tells his mother he wants to wear those ridiculous wigs and practice law. My other son, a fundamental terrorist! I just don't understand it, you raise your children the best you can, but they still grow into strangers."Irie said tentatively, "Oh, that's not true, surely."The disembodied loneliness of the past 20 years collapsed in on Samad as he thought about the state of his family, the state of himself."It's this place. I know it. You come here for all the right and righteous reasons. You don't mean to stay, not forever, but this place, it traps you. It's cold and wet here, and no one knows how to love, but you stay because things are working. By the time you realize you've made a mistake, you've been stained," Samad said. He looked at Irie, desperate to get the words out. "You can never fully be here, be English, because you're from someplace else, but you can never go back there, either! I know I can't. I'm tainted from my time here. I can never go home. I'm from nowhere now, and I'm going nowhere."

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: The Black Panther Party, a whirlwind of raised fists and righteous fury, had been my crucible. I'd joined partly to prove a point, to silence the whispers that trailed me like a shadow. "Not Black enough," they hissed, both Black and white voices mingling in a chorus of disapproval. My crime? Muttering "Egads" during a heated basketball game, perhaps. Or maybe it was my novels, those unruly beasts that dared to explore the retelling of Aeschylus, drawing accusations of elitism and worse, cultural betrayal. One particularly scathing review declared, "His Aeschylus is a betrayal of his Black heritage, a misguided attempt to elevate himself above his roots." The New York literary party, a swirling vortex of ambition and pretense, was no different. A literary agent, her eyes scanning the room for the next big thing, dismissed my work with a wave of her hand. "Forget Aeschylus," she scoffed, "write true, gritty real stories of Black life. That's what sells." I wanted to retort, "My life, my experience, isn't that Black enough for you?" But the words caught in my throat, choked by the weight of expectation. The agent, sensing my hesitation, moved on, her attention snagged by a performance artist reciting a monologue about the Black experience. The irony was thick enough to cut with a knife.  Later, nursing a drink and a bruised ego, I found myself staring out at the city lights, their glittering expanse a stark contrast to the darkness within. Race, that insidious construct, was a ghost I couldn't shake. I didn't believe in it, rarely dwelled on it, except when guilt gnawed at my conscience. Yet, I couldn't deny its power, its ability to shape lives, to inflict violence, to perpetuate discrimination. The world saw me as Black, and that perception carried a weight I couldn't ignore. As the night wore on, the party's revelry faded into a distant hum. I was left with my thoughts, my identity a tangled knot of contradictions. Was I Black enough? Was my experience valid? The questions swirled, unanswered, unresolved. But in the quiet solitude of that late hour, I found a strange solace. My journey, my struggle, was uniquely my own. And that, I realized, was enough.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: There came a point in my life when I seemed to have to "prove" my Blackness, despite my inherent identity as a Black man. As a result, I joined the Black Panther Party in college. I needed some validation that I was, indeed, who I appeared to be, not only on the outside but on the inside as well. Both Blacks and whites alike told me that I was "not Black enough" for them (they saw the way I played basketball, muttering "Egads" under my breath with every foul or missed layup—Egads). Later, nursing a drink and a bruised ego, I found myself staring out at the city lights, their glittering expanse a stark contrast to the darkness within. Race, that insidious construct, was a ghost I couldn't shake. I didn't believe in it, rarely dwelled on it, except when guilt gnawed at my conscience. Yet, I couldn't deny its power, its ability to shape lives, to inflict violence, to perpetuate discrimination. The world saw me as Black, and that perception carried a weight I couldn't ignore. As the night wore on, the party's revelry faded into a distant hum. I was left with my thoughts, my identity a tangled knot of contradictions. Was I Black enough? Was my experience valid? The questions swirled, unanswered, unresolved. But in the quiet solitude of that late hour, I found a strange solace. My journey, my struggle, was uniquely my own. And that, I realized, was enough.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: As a college freshman, I joined the Black Panther Party. I didn't quite fit in; I didn't wear my beret tilted just right, didn't raise my fist with enough fury, didn't speak with the necessary cadence that marked the truly radical. I muttered "Egads" during basketball games, to the collective horror of my teammates, who were often split between exasperation and bemusement. White classmates with their predictable condescension said I was "articulate," while Black peers muttered under their breaths, "Not Black enough." A professor once called me “fascinatingly displaced,” as though I were a museum artifact. This dislocation seeped into my writing. My first novel was a retelling of Aeschylus—a reviewer described it as “a charming but ill-advised venture into the Greeks, woefully devoid of authentic Black experience.” I reread the critique three times, marveling at how one could misinterpret authenticity as a monolith.Years later, I stood in a dim Manhattan loft at a literary party where the wine was as dry as the wit was acidic. A literary agent in a glinting blazer cornered me by the hors d’oeuvres, leaned in conspiratorially, and said, “Listen, you’ve got talent, but all this Greek tragedy nonsense—leave it behind. Write something real. Something gritty, raw, Black life in the streets. That’s what sells.” He patted my shoulder, as though certifying my potential to commodify my identity, then floated off to fawn over a performance artist wearing a gown made of egg cartons.I sipped my wine, the bitterness cutting through my amusement. The transactional nature of the room was suffocating, the smiles wide but hollow, the handshakes quick but calculating. Authenticity, here, was a currency as fleeting as the trends that shaped it. I thought of race—the way it sat heavy on me when others decided it should, the way I refused to believe in it except when guilt or societal violence forced it into my consciousness. Guilt for what? For not being Black enough? For being too Black? It was endless. I walked to the window, feeling the cold glass against my palm, and let the city’s hum drown out the noise of the room. “Authenticity,” I whispered, watching my breath fog the glass, “is just another mask they want me to wear.”
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: I remember those college days. The grass peeking over cement, the columns of the buildings thick, stuffed, presumably, with knowledge. Though, admittedly, I had a hard time juggling it all, having joined the Panthers on campus, less for their social cause, and more to reject the budding questions about my Blackness. Needless to say, it didn't work. Everywhere I went, strangers, white and Black, would tell me I wasn't Black enough. The white friends wanted to know why I didn't keep a gun, like a real Black Panther, and the Panthers wanted to know why I was so busy doing the white man's homework. Once, an entire basketball court stopped the game to laugh for five minutes when they heard me mutter egads after missing a shot. I can take these teases in everyday life, but when it comes to my literature, that's when the blade cuts deepest. The most recent was a slack-mouthed reviewer who wondered why my last novel, a retelling of Aeschylus, did not portray adequately, as they put it, "the Black man's experience." This was no unusual comment. At a literary party, I was once told to abandon my passion for classic retellings in favor of "true, gritty real stories of Black life." There were millions to be made here, an agent had said. When I refused their suggestion, telling them that all of my stories are stories of Black life, because I, a Black life, made them, they moseyed over to a performance artist, with whom they spent the rest of the evening talking about sword-swallowing. I looked at the paintings on the walls of the luxury Harlem apartment, all of Black strife, contorted faces, hands in yearning, bodies that seldom looked like bodies. Pictures of poverty worth millions. I couldn't say that I believed in race at all - I saw it merely as a construct. And yet, its grasp over me and those around me felt crushing, inevitable, real. I knew if I burned the apartment to the ground, as I felt the growing desire to do, the newspaper would not say "Established Author Sets Party Ablaze in Fit of Misplaced Justice." No, it would simply say, "Black Man Commits Arson." That would be how I would be remembered.
written_by_MFA030.Reason: I enjoyed reading excerpt 1 more. The writing style is more captivating and immediate, I think because of the use of quotations from different characters. The use of rhetorical questions is effective. Excerpt 2 feels less stylish, less accomplished, though it was still enjoyable to read. Both are fluent and coherent but excerpt 1 is especially effective.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: As a college freshman, I joined the Black Panther Party. I didn't quite fit in; I didn't wear my beret tilted just right, didn't raise my fist with enough fury, didn't speak with the necessary cadence that marked the truly radical. I muttered "Egads" during basketball games, to the collective horror of my teammates, who were often split between exasperation and bemusement. White classmates with their predictable condescension said I was "articulate," while Black peers muttered under their breaths, "Not Black enough." A professor once called me “fascinatingly displaced,” as though I were a museum artifact. This dislocation seeped into my writing. My first novel was a retelling of Aeschylus—a reviewer described it as “a charming but ill-advised venture into the Greeks, woefully devoid of authentic Black experience.” I reread the critique three times, marveling at how one could misinterpret authenticity as a monolith.Years later, I stood in a dim Manhattan loft at a literary party where the wine was as dry as the wit was acidic. A literary agent in a glinting blazer cornered me by the hors d’oeuvres, leaned in conspiratorially, and said, “Listen, you’ve got talent, but all this Greek tragedy nonsense—leave it behind. Write something real. Something gritty, raw, Black life in the streets. That’s what sells.” He patted my shoulder, as though certifying my potential to commodify my identity, then floated off to fawn over a performance artist wearing a gown made of egg cartons.I sipped my wine, the bitterness cutting through my amusement. The transactional nature of the room was suffocating, the smiles wide but hollow, the handshakes quick but calculating. Authenticity, here, was a currency as fleeting as the trends that shaped it. I thought of race—the way it sat heavy on me when others decided it should, the way I refused to believe in it except when guilt or societal violence forced it into my consciousness. Guilt for what? For not being Black enough? For being too Black? It was endless. I walked to the window, feeling the cold glass against my palm, and let the city’s hum drown out the noise of the room. “Authenticity,” I whispered, watching my breath fog the glass, “is just another mask they want me to wear.”

written_by_MFA002.Excerpt1: My awkward undergraduate years are better left undiscussed, but lately I have found myself turning them over in my head in search of an insight that has eluded me since – what drove me to join my university’s chapter of the Black Panther Party? Ostensibly I supported the movement and its ideologies, but in retrospect – and in all honesty – my desire to resist the oppression of my people was, perhaps, not the most pertinent factor in my decision. Really I joined the Party as a means of proving myself – more specifically, proving my Blackness. And to whom was this posturing directed? Certainly at the white and Black basketball players alike who laughed me off the court when I mumbled “Egads” upon a fumbled shot. Certainly at Todd Henderson, the literary critic who called my retelling of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound “disconcertingly cerebral” for an author like me. And candidly, perhaps at myself. I needed to convince myself that I was Black enough. And maybe I still do, decades later. The other day I attended a literary party in the city and somehow found myself sucked into a conversation with an agent of an acquaintance. “Don’t bother with the Achilles,” the agent told me. (Privately I considered correcting his pronunciation of Aeschylus, then decided it wasn’t worth the effort.) “It’s not what they want. They’re looking for true, gritty, real stories of Black life. They want authenticity.” This puzzled me. I asked him to define authentic. What makes me, a Black man writing material guided by my lived experience, not authentically Black? To this, the agent laughed, clapped me on the shoulder, and moved on to debate the prevalence of body shaming in social media with a bemused performance artist perusing the hors d’oeuvres. Today, as I write, I consider my opinion on it all – Blackness, whiteness, authenticity. I don’t really believe in race. I regard race as a construct of convenience, a societal demarcation on which I rarely dwell. And yet, I recognize the self-indulgent folly in the popular adage, I don’t see color. I am not blind to the concrete consequences of racial divides: oppression, discrimination, violence, subjugation. But there’s something artificial and contrived about the Blackness that I feel I must actively demonstrate.
written_by_MFA002.Excerpt2: I joined the Black Panthers in college, not out of revolutionary fervor but from a peculiar need to authenticate my Blackness, as if membership cards and raised fists could offset my tendency to mutter "Egads" during pickup basketball games. The Panthers, to their credit, were more amused than offended by my professorial affectations, though one member did suggest I try saying "damn" instead. My novels drew similar bewilderment – a reviewer once wrote, "While technically accomplished, his adaptation of Aeschylus' Oresteia to a housing project seems more interested in postmodern discourse than authentic Black experience." As if authenticity came with a manual, complete with approved vocabularies and prescribed narratives. At a Manhattan literary soirée, between sips of overpriced wine and precisely cubed cheese, a literary agent cornered me with the air of someone about to dispense life-changing wisdom. "Look," she said, adjusting her horn-rimmed glasses with manicured precision, "nobody wants to read about Black people discussing Aristotelian ethics. Write something real, something gritty. Give me projects and pimps, give me struggle." She might as well have asked me to perform a soft-shoe routine. The irony of being told my Black experience wasn't Black enough by someone whose closest connection to the culture was probably watching "The Wire" wasn't lost on me. I watched her glide away to fawn over a performance artist who'd painted himself in crude oil to protest environmental racism – now there was some authentic Blackness she could sell. Standing alone by the cheese plate, I contemplated how race was like quantum mechanics: a construct I didn't believe in but couldn't ignore, something that only seemed to materialize when observed or when guilt compelled me to notice it. Yet its consequences were undeniably real, manifesting in broken bodies and broken dreams, in rejection letters suggesting my characters weren't "relatable enough" to my own people. The violence of these expectations was subtle but persistent, like water wearing away stone, and I found myself wondering if authenticity was just another mask we wore to please the observers of our particles, another performance in the endless theater of racial identity where even our silences were scripted and our rebellions came with stage directions. I smiled at my reflection in the wine glass, watching it distort and fragment like truth itself.
written_by_MFA002.Reason: Excerpt 2 sounds more like it is a college essay. There is something too formulaic and constructed about the way it is telling its story. The first excerpt feels like a conversation being had, or something far more personable than the second one does. It just flows more naturally despite being a shorter excerpt.

Today, as I write, I consider my opinion on it all – Blackness, whiteness, authenticity. I don’t really believe in race. I regard race as a construct of convenience, a societal demarcation on which I rarely dwell. And yet, I recognize the self-indulgent folly in the popular adage, I don’t see color. I am not blind to the concrete consequences of racial divides: oppression, discrimination, violence, subjugation. But there’s something artificial and contrived about the Blackness that I feel I must actively demonstrate.
written_by_MFA002.Excerpt2: I joined the Black Panthers in college, not out of revolutionary fervor but from a peculiar need to authenticate my Blackness, as if membership cards and raised fists could offset my tendency to mutter "Egads" during pickup basketball games. The Panthers, to their credit, were more amused than offended by my professorial affectations, though one member did suggest I try saying "damn" instead. My novels drew similar bewilderment – a reviewer once wrote, "While technically accomplished, his adaptation of Aeschylus' Oresteia to a housing project seems more interested in postmodern discourse than authentic Black experience." As if authenticity came with a manual, complete with approved vocabularies and prescribed narratives. At a Manhattan literary soirée, between sips of overpriced wine and precisely cubed cheese, a literary agent cornered me with the air of someone about to dispense life-changing wisdom. "Look," she said, adjusting her horn-rimmed glasses with manicured precision, "nobody wants to read about Black people discussing Aristotelian ethics. Write something real, something gritty. Give me projects and pimps, give me struggle." She might as well have asked me to perform a soft-shoe routine. The irony of being told my Black experience wasn't Black enough by someone whose closest connection to the culture was probably watching "The Wire" wasn't lost on me. I watched her glide away to fawn over a performance artist who'd painted himself in crude oil to protest environmental racism – now there was some authentic Blackness she could sell. Standing alone by the cheese plate, I contemplated how race was like quantum mechanics: a construct I didn't believe in but couldn't ignore, something that only seemed to materialize when observed or when guilt compelled me to notice it. Yet its consequences were undeniably real, manifesting in broken bodies and broken dreams, in rejection letters suggesting my characters weren't "relatable enough" to my own people. The violence of these expectations was subtle but persistent, like water wearing away stone, and I found myself wondering if authenticity was just another mask we wore to please the observers of our particles, another performance in the endless theater of racial identity where even our silences were scripted and our rebellions came with stage directions. I smiled at my reflection in the wine glass, watching it distort and fragment like truth itself.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: “Thing is,” Jack said, “I’m fucking sick of it. Tired of goin nowhere but up the mountain with you. Givin me just Brokeback Mountain is bout as good as givin me nothin, and you know it. I want more–I want it all–and I don’t reckon you’ll ever give it to me. I’m like your dog, chokin on your short leash. All I want is to…it doesn’t matter, do it? Imma dog frothin at the end of your fuckin leash. Goddammit.” He paused for a moment, his breath coming out in short, steaming pants that warmed the tent. “Goddammit. I wish I knew how to quit you.”Jack’s words acted like a rusted arrow upon Ennis–tired, worn out, but not without their raw edge, dangerously sharp. They pierced through him, brought him down to his knees. He lay there on the ground, clutching himself, pale, his wide-eyed gaze fixed on the mountain. “Jesus–” Jack stooped down as if to help him. Was he sick? Jack wondered. Was he finally able to see? Jack’s hands hovered around the other man’s body, but Ennis looked so far away, as if dreaming, and impossible to touch. Ennis got up without his help, recomposing his face into that flat, familiar expression. He rose up from his knees, a man rewound–the dramatic act reversed, so that again he became just a man with a lockbox of feelings. Just Ennis, slumped against the valley. That same far off expression on his face, his hand, gently trembling, grasping at nothing. And that same pain was there too, a shared pain–hot, palpable, unresolved and unrelenting–like clouds of steam rising between them.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: “Brokeback Mountain’s the only place I’ve ever felt happy. ” Jack’s voice, a raw rasp of longing and frustration, sliced through the quiet Wyoming air.“Four measly weeks a year, that’s all we get. Four weeks, Ennis, while the rest of the year you keep me on a goddamn short leash. Like I’m some kinda stray dog you picked up along the road. ” “I wish I knew how to quit you.”The words hung heavy, a confession and a curse.   Jack’s eyes, the blue of a high-desert sky, were clouded with torment.   “But I can’t.   I’m no good at quittin’. Never have been. Not you, not anything. ”Ennis, his face a mask of pain, crumpled to his knees.   Jack’s words, sharp as barbed wire, had pierced his defenses, drawing blood from his soul.The silence that followed was deafening, broken only by the wind whistling through the pines.“Ennis? ” Jack’s voice was thick with alarm. “What’s wrong? You sick? ”“Jesus,” Ennis choked out, his breath coming in ragged gasps.Jack watched, helpless, as Ennis wrestled with the emotional storm. He’d seen Ennis break horses, wrestle calves, but he’d never seen him like this.Raw, exposed, a man stripped bare by the force of his own feelings.Ennis slowly regained his composure, the storm within subsiding into a dull ache. He stood up, his legs shaky, his eyes fixed on the distant horizon, a vast expanse of sagebrush and sky. The confrontation had changed nothing. Their pain, unspoken yet palpable, hung between them like clouds of steam rising from damp earth on a cold morning.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: “You the storm that stranded me here,” said Jack. “Ain’t no other way to put it. I been thinkin on it, bustin my brain to try and fit the bits together, but it’s bullshit. You know it is, Ennis, don’t pretend like you don’t. I’ve called you, sent you letters first class, and you actin like the offseason applies to us. Brokeback’s just a little vacation, a couple ranch-hands in heat. Maybe you like it like that. You sure got me on a short leash. That’s all I am to you, Ennis: a bitch for the summer. I’d swallow glass if it meant I could spend the rest a my life on Brokeback, but you won’t even pick up the goddam phone.” Jack looked at the ridgeline. “I wish I knew how to quit you.” Ennis got down on one knee, and for a second Jack thought he was tying his shoe. Sobs wracked his ribs. “Jesus!” yelled Jack. Ennis kept crying. He looked down at the earth, the denim of his knee stirring up dust. To Jack he looked like a wounded horse, its hooves at rest. He feared for Ennis, this man for whom he had stored up so much love and hate. A cold distant man making a scene on the roadside—it didn’t make much in the way of sense. Jack had more to say but his jaw stayed shut. Ennis sobbed. After awhile he went still. Ennis pulled himself to his feet and pushed the dust off his jeans. Jack looked at him and Ennis looked back, but there was nothing there. Just the clouds of steam rising.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: Jack leaned against the post, his chest heaving, words spilling out in a torrent, raw as the gouged earth beneath his boots. “I can’t do this anymore, Ennis. It ain’t just the damn mountain. You hold me like I’m some stray dog on a leash, pullin’ me close when you want and kickin’ me away when you don’t. Ain’t a life, this. Not for me.” His voice cracked, ricocheted into the dry air. “Wish I knew how to quit you, but it’s like tryin’ to wrench a fishhook outta your own throat.” He tipped his hat back, his eyes watery but fierce, daring the other man to respond. Ennis stood frozen, fists tight, the sinews of his neck stretched taut like old barbed wire. When the words hit their mark, it was like a shot fired too close—he crumpled, knees buckling, gasping for air as though Jack’s truths had knocked it clean out of him. “Jesus,” Jack muttered, rushing forward, unsure if he should steady Ennis or step away. The distance between them felt insurmountable, a chasm carved out of years of furtive touches and unspoken words. For a moment, there was only the rasp of their breath, mingling with the faint hum of crickets and the whisper of dry grass. Ennis lifted his head, the shadows on his face deep, his expression unreadable. He staggered to his feet, brushing off Jack’s hand, and the weight of their shared silence pressed in. Nothing was mended, no path forward uncovered. Just the same cycle of longing and restraint, heartbreak hanging in the air like steam from a kettle left too long on the flame, inevitable and unyielding, rising but never dispersing.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: Jack stood there, fists balled in his jacket pockets, words tearing out of him like barbed wire through flesh. "Twenty years we been at this, En. Twenty goddamn years of sneakin up here like outlaws, like we done somethin wrong. You got me on this short leash, always yankin me back when I get too close to somethin real. Christ, I'm sick of it. Sick of these few days we grab like scraps under the table. You think I wanted this half-life? Living off memories of Brokeback till they're wore thin as old leather?" His voice cracked, raw as windburn. "I wish I knew how to quit you." The words hung between them like smoke in still air. Ennis swayed, color draining from his face like water from a broken cup, then his knees buckled and he went down hard on the packed dirt. "Jesus," Jack shouted, lunging forward, thinking heart attack, stroke, something busted loose inside that couldn't be fixed. But Ennis's shoulders were heaving, great gasping sobs tearing out of him, the kind that leave a man hollow. Jack stood frozen, watching his friend shake apart, knowing any touch might shatter what was left. When the storm passed, Ennis climbed to his feet, brushed dirt from his jeans like nothing had happened. They stood in the heavy silence, steam rising between them from their breath in the mountain air, neither looking at the other. Nothing changed. Nothing could change. The moment passed like so many before it, settling into the collection of hurts they carried, weight added to weight until the burden seemed natural as breathing.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: “I just cain't wrap my head 'round it, Ennis. Just give it to me straight up: you want me around or don't ya? Cause this here between us ain’t anything in full, and because it ain’t anything in full it ain’t hardly anything at all. All we see of each other is here, alone with ourselves. I only got you here. Out there, you ain’t anybody I ever known. All we got here are moments on Brokeback Mountain, and moments ain’t a life, ain’t close to living. How much more of ourselves are you willing to let die? Don’t you know how much less of me I feel of myself? You keep all that I am on the shortest leash, Ennis. You are the one keeping us from the fullness of what our lives could be. Maybe you can keep on like this, but I can’t. I’m at the end of that rope. God, Ennis. I want to quit you. I wish I knew how to quit you.” Nearing the tailend of these words Ennis’s knees buckled, his body softened, as if having taken birdshot to his backside, though to Jack any outer wound could not be found. Jack went silent then, and kept it, unsure what to do with Ennis screaming, “Jesus, Jesus…” And though Ennis calmed, and the air on the mountain steadied, nothing had changed. Still they would go on as they had before, no one in the world knowing what they had between them, except them. The pain on that mountain would go on with them, too, would follow them into the days and weeks ahead, so weighty, like clouds of steam rising between the two.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: The shadow of the sash falls down the curtain, a pallid crescent in the gloom of the room.  I can hear the ticking of the watch, a steady pulse in the quiet.  It was Grandfather’s watch, and now it is Father’s, and someday it will be mine.  The watch ticks on, a metronome marking the inexorable passage of time.  Father said, “You cannot conquer time.  You can only try to forget it.”  But how can one forget time when it is always there, ticking away, a constant reminder of our mortality?  The watch hands move, a slow, relentless dance towards the end.  “Time is a relentless and hungry force,” Father said.  “It devours all things – youth, beauty, even memory.”  The watch ticks on, a tiny machine marking the moments of our lives.  Each tick brings us closer to the end, to the final silence.  “Victories in life are fleeting,” Father said.  “They are but illusions in the face of time’s infinite and hungry maw.”  The watch ticks on, a constant reminder of our mortality.  It is a sound that haunts me, a sound that echoes the futility of our existence.  “Jesus walking on Galilee,” Father said, “and Saint Francis, speaking to his Little Sister Death.  Both of them knew that time could not be conquered, that it could only be endured.”  The watch ticks on, a steady beat in the silence of the room.  It is a sound that I cannot escape, a sound that reminds me of my own mortality.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: A moment came when I stirred from my private twilight and noticed two things. First, the stain of shadow upon the curtains. Then, the ticking of the watch. It was a fine instrument that had been passed down from my grandfather to my father to me. Both of these men were long dead, and it seemed that in my inheriting the watch, I had inherited their fate: the impending loss of a war with time. It was a fate my father had tried in vain to prepare me for.“Time,” he once said to me, “is inexorable. It can be fought, but never conquered. Our victories are as futile as our struggles.” Time was and is and had and always would win. All I could do was lay in bed and listen to the steady, measured thump of its advance, like the footsteps of an army unafraid of being spotted by its enemy. The ticking seemed to stop coming from the watch. Now, it was coming from everywhere. Time bled from the walls and windows and floors, and with the flood came memory. I thought of my father describing Jesus walking along long and lonely light rays. I thought of his stories about St. Francis’s “Little Sister Death” who left no flower un-plucked. The waters of time rose and roiled around me. I wondered if I would be able to float, and as swiftly as the question came upon me, so did its answer. Time would rise; I would sink.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: The shadow moved like time itself across the curtain, not marking but mocking, and I could hear it, the watch, grandfather's watch (not mine because how can time belong to any man when time owns all men), ticking away beneath my pillow where Father had placed it saying Time is the mausoleum of all hope and desire, boy, and you'll learn that too, and I lay there hearing it not with my ears anymore but with my blood, my bones, each tick-tick-tick like Christ's own footsteps walking not on water but on those long golden light-rays that stretched across eternity, across all the Compson failures and pride, across Sister Death herself who waited patient and humble like that shadow on my curtain, and I knew then what Father meant about time being dead until the clock stops because I could feel it dying with each breath, each tick, could feel it running through my fingers like the river I would find later, running away from all the Quentins that ever were or would be, and still that shadow moved, and still that ticking came, and I thought about how Father said a man is the sum of his misfortunes, and how that sum was ticking away beneath my pillow, beneath my head, beneath my thoughts that weren't really thoughts anymore but just the sound of time itself, marking nothing, changing nothing, just being, like that shadow, like that watch, like all the Quentins that ever were.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt 1 is easier to read because it is like a story in a book. The second excerpt is a bit confusing and ideas seem to ramble on. Excerpt 1 flows smoother and effectively conveys ideas from one to the next. Excerpt 1 is better because it is descriptive and coherent.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: The shadow of the sash curved across the dim curtains, and the watch on the nightstand ticked steadily, a quiet insistence that time itself bore witness to all that was and all that ever would be. I could feel it in my chest, that weight, a pressing reminder of my grandfather's words—words handed down through my father like a relic, tarnished by the grime of despair, polished by futility. Time does not pause, does not forgive. Its victories are hollow, its passing immutable, carving grooves into the soul like water wears down stone, relentless and unyielding.The ticking grew louder, or perhaps it was my thoughts that gave it resonance, filling the room, saturating the air. And in that sound, that metronome of inevitability, I found the tether of memory and the dread of its permanence. Was it my father’s voice I heard or my own thoughts as they spiraled? His words wrapped around my consciousness like the fraying tendrils of a dream that refuses to die. Jesus walked once, on light-rays long and lonely, and Francis whispered to Death as though she were kin, a sister who waited not cruelly but certainly.I lay there, the watch’s rhythm tethering me to the present even as my spirit floated, weightless, into the past and future. Time, unbroken and unseen, bore its teeth, gnawing at the fragile membrane between what is and what is not, what could be and what will never be. I closed my eyes, and still, the ticking remained.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: And before long lying in bed in this room my senses narrowed in totality. There was no escaping the shadow on the sash of the curtains flooding out in further shadows darkening the windowsill and washing the floorboards in lengthening patches of darker darknesses though still I attempted to move away from them even as they drifted over my legs in bed. They almost had me then. But I would not let them. No I would never let them. Not once. Because once is always. And the ticking hiccups of my grandfather’s watch that my father gave me in my pocket I could not either escape. Its rhythm beating hiccups against my leg made me think only of my father and every word he ever gave me to hold on to. The inescapability of clocks never outweighed by the conquered, momentary kingdoms of victories, he said, never outdone by wordly doings done in the face of all that we are faced with. These are but illusions and facades in the battlegrounds of time, he once said. But consider Jesus walking forty days forty nights and the long and lonely light-rays and consider even still Saint Francis’s Little Sister Death, consider the weight of Jesus and light and death, he said. Consider them. Thinking of my father in this way and his words in bed amid the shadows and the ticking he gave me so long ago only deepened my fear of the inevitable. The ineffable. The possible, terrible pointlessness of it all.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: Excerpt one is better than excerpt 2 because it was able to give a distinct and interesting story between reality and imagination, making us live in this imagination as reality. It was more engaging and smooth. Excerpt 2 was engaging but not as smooth in writing as the excerpt 1.

They almost had me then. But I would not let them. No I would never let them. Not once. Because once is always. And the ticking hiccups of my grandfather’s watch that my father gave me in my pocket I could not either escape. Its rhythm beating hiccups against my leg made me think only of my father and every word he ever gave me to hold on to. The inescapability of clocks never outweighed by the conquered, momentary kingdoms of victories, he said, never outdone by wordly doings done in the face of all that we are faced with. These are but illusions and facades in the battlegrounds of time, he once said. But consider Jesus walking forty days forty nights and the long and lonely light-rays and consider even still Saint Francis’s Little Sister Death, consider the weight of Jesus and light and death, he said. Consider them. Thinking of my father in this way and his words in bed amid the shadows and the ticking he gave me so long ago only deepened my fear of the inevitable. The ineffable. The possible, terrible pointlessness of it all.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: The shadow of the sash curved across the dim curtains, and the watch on the nightstand ticked steadily, a quiet insistence that time itself bore witness to all that was and all that ever would be. I could feel it in my chest, that weight, a pressing reminder of my grandfather's words—words handed down through my father like a relic, tarnished by the grime of despair, polished by futility. Time does not pause, does not forgive. Its victories are hollow, its passing immutable, carving grooves into the soul like water wears down stone, relentless and unyielding.The ticking grew louder, or perhaps it was my thoughts that gave it resonance, filling the room, saturating the air. And in that sound, that metronome of inevitability, I found the tether of memory and the dread of its permanence. Was it my father’s voice I heard or my own thoughts as they spiraled? His words wrapped around my consciousness like the fraying tendrils of a dream that refuses to die. Jesus walked once, on light-rays long and lonely, and Francis whispered to Death as though she were kin, a sister who waited not cruelly but certainly.I lay there, the watch’s rhythm tethering me to the present even as my spirit floated, weightless, into the past and future. Time, unbroken and unseen, bore its teeth, gnawing at the fragile membrane between what is and what is not, what could be and what will never be. I closed my eyes, and still, the ticking remained.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: Though I understand the meaning behind ‘You Can’t Go Home’, the title of that great novel by Thomas Wolfe, I myself cannot agree with his sentiment. I have found myself returning home many times over the years. There may no longer be a geographical place that bears more than a passing resemblance to the home of my girlhood, yet “home” itself is something inescapable and internal, a place of shadows, dreams, fears and dragons that is formed in childhood and carried deep inside for the rest of one’s life. I have returned again and again to that place, an imaginative landscape mapped and defined not by geography nor by cultural differences but by our youthful perceptions, during a time when the adults in our lives—parents, neighbors, siblings—are but shadowy figures whose actions are an enigma to us even as they shape our very selves. Many of us will grow old without truly growing up. We may fulfill the roles demanded of us as we age, whether by paying a bill, finding a parking space, or any of those actions that comprise an adult life. We may wander to other continents and may never return to the physical houses of our pasts, if these houses even remain standing for us to visit. But we are always one moment away from retreating to this inner world. It is here where we immerse ourselves in the comforts that defined our sense of home as children, whether those comforts were real or half imagined and exaggerated by our childlike innocence. I have returned home in spirit countless times, to this inner world that is a refuge and sanctuary, a place of ultimate belonging. It is this home which keeps me whole, a place I will never fully leave.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: I disagree with Thomas Wolfe. Home, it seems, is something you can never leave. It is a shadow, a dream, a fear, a dragon that follows you, forever tucked away in the deepest corner of your heart. It is the space you were first allowed to be yourself, the place where you learned to see the world through your own eyes, a child's eyes, where everything seemed as it should be.The adults in this region of your world, your parents, neighbors, siblings, were mysterious figures, moving in and out of your awareness like fleeting shadows. Their voices echoed in the hallways of your mind, their laughter and tears shaping the contours of your memories. You never questioned their presence, their belonging. They were as much a part of your world as the sun and the moon, the trees and the stars.And then, one day, you grew up. Or so they said. But did you really? Did you ever truly shed the skin of your childhood, the innocence of your youth? Or did you simply grow old, fulfilling the roles and responsibilities that society thrust upon you, finding parking spaces, paying bills, all the while carrying that child within, seeking the safety and comfort of home?Home is not a place, not really. It is a feeling, a sense of belonging, of being truly known and accepted. It is the refuge you seek when the world becomes too much, the place where you can always return, no matter how far you may have strayed. It is the echo of your childhood, the whisper of your dreams, the shadow of your fears, the dragon of your heart. It is the place where you are always welcome, the place where you are always loved.
