written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: Home, that perennial thing. The place we’ve heard a million aphorisms about—telling us how much it matters, that it’s always there for us, and trying to answer the biggest question: where to find it. Thomas Wolfe’s novel, You Can’t Go Home Again, seems to offer a concerning counter to this, but this is actually a trick of the light, for one can never truly leave home to begin with. Home is in the sinew, in the flesh, home, in all of its shadows, dreams, fears, and dragons, is a place deep in the bosom, straight in the center, right up the spine and down through the feet. And what is truly at the core of home is not the wood beams, the forest hills, the patio furniture, metal gates and paved roads—it’s the youthful perception, those rose-tinted glasses, a time of understanding before the world laid its full hands on us. It is childhood, not just the memory or the idea of it, but the physical self that was once to a child, learning the way of the world, ignorant to the ways of man, the race, the place, the pace. It is a version of the self that navigates only through imagination, through interaction with those mysterious figures of the land, the adults, the mailman, the clerk, the aunt, the neighbor, the siblings. And it is this version of the self, the child, that we try to run to when we get older when the bills pile, when you can’t find a place to park, when the kids won’t listen, when we crave that time again, that little pocket in our chest we can tuck into to know that there was life before these little bothers. When we nestle in there, we find the key to ultimate return, to a place of comfort, to belonging to your own world— to coming home.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: When Thomas Wolfe declared you can't go home again, he hadn't reckoned with the stubborn geography of the heart, that relentless compass that forever points to our beginning place. Home isn't merely the creaking floorboards beneath our feet or the worn doorknobs our palms remember—it's the shadow-dance of memory that lives in our bones, as natural as breathing and just as necessary. I've watched children, those clear-eyed prophets of truth, who know nothing of north or south, east or west, but understand perfectly the latitude of belonging. In their world, grown folks move like planets in a universe they haven't yet learned to question, their orbits unbroken by doubt. Mama's laugh rings true as church bells, and daddy's footsteps mark time like drums in the evening, while neighbors drift through the streets like familiar ghosts, their stories settling into the soil of young minds like seeds waiting to bloom. Lord, how we fool ourselves thinking we've grown up just because we've learned to navigate parking meters and mortgage payments! The truth is, most of us are still those wide-eyed children wearing adult clothes, playing at being grown, while deep inside we're running home through twilight streets that exist now only in memory. We carry our dragons and dreams tucked away in secret pockets, and when the world proves too sharp, too cold, we retreat to that internal sanctuary where everything makes sense according to the logic of childhood. Home isn't a place you leave behind—it's the story that writes itself in your blood, the mirror that shows you your truest face, the song that keeps singing long after the music has stopped. It's the place where our first tears fell and our earliest laughter echoed, where we learned the shape of love and fear, and where we return, again and again, in the quiet moments when our hearts need healing.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: I imagined him taller than he should have been, his head near the ceiling of an unfamiliar apartment he couldn’t love as he wrote his novel You Can’t Go Home Again looming over his refrigerator. Home, to Thomas Wolfe, was a quiet town in a temperate valley of the Blue Ridge Mountains. From such vantage points, the world becomes diminutive, entirely comprehensible. Only when you venture into those views do you see the world’s vastness beyond its landscapes, how you can’t see home through eyes that have left, that have taken in new views, new worlds, a new you. But can home be truly gone without you? Is home not a dark chamber you carry within, with its shadows, dreams, fears, and dragons? I remembered my childhood home for the woods that circled the property, where things belonged because they resided there. A childhood home is the childhood. It is the wilderness unknowing children frolic through. It is the security of a warm blanket before they learn it can be ripped away. The adults in their lives seem impossibly, staggeringly old, years beyond the years children know. Like enigmatic peaks of mountain ranges, parents, older siblings, and neighbors loom from a distance. They cast only shadows on the sunny region of play that is the childhood home. But the sun falls and the shadows grow long. With time, the children grow taller than they should, than they feel they should. They leave the wilderness. Through the vague groping around in the night to their parkings spaces and their dinner tables strewn with bills, they long for childhood, for return. But as sure as that longing pulls from within them, there is that dark chamber waiting for light. It has always been there. You have never left home.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: Home, I have found, is not simply a place but a feeling that nestles deep in the folds of one’s soul. It is the shadowed hallway of memory, the faint scent of grandmother’s soap, the creak of a floorboard that seemed alive under hurried feet. Thomas Wolfe’s declaration that one “can’t go home again” lingers in the air like a challenge, for he must not have known that home is not a place you return to; it is a space you carry, ever-present, with its jagged edges and tender sanctuaries. It is where your fears grow fangs and your dreams sprout wings, where dragons curl in the corners of your mind, guarding treasures of old laughter and quiet heartbreak.In the eyes of a child, home stretches as far as the world itself—an empire shaped by the curve of a dirt road or the towering majesty of a neighbor’s oak tree. Adults are gods of that kingdom, figures who wield their power with mystery, speaking in codes that seem unknowable. Yet, even as we grow, we seldom outgrow the pull of home. We may wear the masks of adulthood—secure parking spots, pay bills on time, and rehearse the lines of responsibility—but inside, we are still children. We navigate the world like sailors tracing their fingers over a map, searching for familiar shores that no longer exist except in the sanctity of our own minds.Home is a refuge, a sanctuary of belonging, but not because of its walls or windows. It is the gathering of whispers, the embrace of something so profoundly personal it could never be truly shared. And so, as I carry its essence within me, I know that the journey is not about leaving or returning—it is about understanding that home was never outside of me to begin with.
written_by_MFA003.Reason: excerpt  1 is easier to comprehend as its more clear statements that flow well together and effectively portray what the author is trying to convey about the childhood descriptions and emotions as excerpt 2 is usually words that is more poetic and for me does not flow well with the article.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: I’d spoken with Reva last week, but it was a short conversation filled mostly with platitudes. She’d seemed distracted and said she was at the gym. written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: I stood in the dim light of my living room, the boxed TV/VCR perched on the coffee table, its plastic wrapping still intact, a strange relic of the morning. I’d bought it not because I needed it, but because the weight of a new object felt like an anchor. Something solid. I didn’t know what else to do with myself after the towers fell, after I’d called Reva at the gym and heard her voice on the line—distant, tinny, preoccupied. That voice haunted me, replaying in my head, a loop of “Can we talk later?” as if she had known this was coming and had somewhere better to be. I could have told her to stay on the line, begged her to come over, but I didn’t. Later, I’d sit on the floor, knees pulled to my chest, watching footage of a woman leaping from the North Tower. Her dress caught the wind like a parachute, her body poised, graceful, falling as though she’d chosen to fly instead of burn. The likeness to Reva—her height, her hair—was undeniable, but I didn’t cry. I pressed pause, rewound, played it again, squinting at the screen, wondering if courage could be beautiful or if beauty was just what we saw in things we didn’t understand. Reva was gone. Lost. And yet, in that leap, she was eternal.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: The last time I spoke to Reva, she was distant. Eager to get back to sweating on the elliptical, or stair-master, or whatever absurd machine she was convinced would keep away the horrors of arm flab. She’s distant now, too, but in a new way. That day, Trevor was on his honeymoon in Barbados, but Reva felt farther. She was gone, lost. I still feel a faint throb of theft when I think of them. On the morning of September 11th , I bought a TV/VCR and recorded the towers going down. When I find myself drifting, floating back to the state I had been in that previous year, I turn on the recording and watch. The footage isn’t soothing, it’s scalding—it wakes me up and keeps me conscious. In one clip, my favorite clip, a woman leaps from a window ledge in the North Tower. She looks enough like Reva that if I were feeling sentimental, I could pretend it’s her. The edge of her pencil skirt whipping up could be Reva’s knock-off designer, her shoes flying from her feet and floating up past her head could be Reva’s second hand Manolos, the glints of sunlight that could be Reva’s grandmother’s ring. But it doesn’t have to be. I don’t need her to be Reva. In dreams, when you feel like you’re falling, you jolt awake. I need her to wake me up.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Excerpt 2 is better because it sets up a tangible relationship between the author and the character Reva so that when the reader learns of her death it is more impactful and also provides a coherent narrative of how the author feels about Reva both before and after her death.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Reva seemed distant the last time we talked, though maybe I’m just imagining that now. She was breathing heavily into the phone when she picked up. She told me she’d call me back later, but she never did. Then she went missing after 9/11, and I knew she was dead. Not in any kind of mystical or spiritual way, but because I knew there was no other option. That same day, I bought a TV/VCR from Best Buy with cash because I wanted to record the news coverage. written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I suppose there's nothing quite like discovering your husband is having an affair when you're seven months pregnant. The timing is exquisite, really – your body has morphed into something between a beach ball and a whale, your ankles have disappeared into puffy clouds, and you're crying at paper towel commercials. And then there's Thelma Rice, with her perfect figure and that irritating habit of inscribing children's books with suggestive little notes, as if marking her territory like some literary-minded cat. I tried making jokes about it, naturally. That's what I do – turn tragedy into comedy, preferably before dessert. But somehow, quipping about being undatable while sporting a seven-month baby bump didn't land quite the way I'd hoped. The laughter that followed had that distinct pitch of pity, the kind that makes you wish you could crawl into a hole, except you can't because, well, pregnant. So here I am in my father's apartment in New York, surrounded by furniture that looks like it was rejected from a 1950s detective novel, crying into tissues and wondering how my life turned into this particularly unfunny sitcom. Sam, my toddler, doesn't understand why Mommy keeps staring out windows like she's auditioning for a Tennessee Williams play. The truth is, betrayal is a peculiar thing – it doesn't just break your heart, it retrospectively ruins perfectly good memories. Like how that book of children's songs, the one with Thelma's nauseating inscription, has now tainted every lullaby I've ever sung to Sam. The whole thing would be almost comedic if it weren't so tragically predictable – the younger woman, the secret notes, the pregnant wife. It's like someone took every cliché about infidelity and decided to stage it in my living room, with me as the unwitting star of this domestic drama. At least I can say this: nothing makes you reevaluate your life choices quite like finding your husband's mistress's handwriting in your child's bedtime stories.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: When I started living at my father's place in New York I couldn't stop crying. The weeping would be long and drawn out, dramatic affairs, and through my vision blurred with tears I would see my father's awful furniture, everything wooden and overly embellished, and the ugliness of the space I was in would only make me cry more. Often as I cried, I would think about how he told me about Thelma Rice. What made it all the more horrible was how utterly mundane it was. I was looking through Sam's little bookshelf for something to sing him to sleep. I was on autopilot, already thinking about what I would do after Sam fell asleep. I was not scrounging through my husband's letters, or stalking Thelma on the streets. I just pulled a book at random and flipped it open to the first page and there, in the most flowery, idiotic handwriting, a note: for the man with a mouth do a lot more than singing, love, Thelma. Disgusting, especially because it was a children's book, one that was on my son's bookshelf. Just thinking about her handwriting could make me cry for twenty minutes. To make myself feel better I would think about how ugly she was. Not very women's lib, I know, but she was my husband's mistress. And she was ugly, it was a fact. She had these bulging eyes and a veiny neck and nothing about her face was symmetrical. I would think about that and stop crying and then think about that note and the whole cycle would start all over again. In public, I put on a brave face. One night I went to dinner and at one point I said, no one wants to take out a lady who's seven months pregnant, she'll eat twice as much! It's not very funny when I write it down. When I said it, though, people laughed. Although, now I wonder if they were laughing because it was funny, or because they pitied me. I was certainly quite pitiable.
written_by_MFA001.Reason: Excerpt 1 is better because it reads like a good book and you can imagine the story in your mind. The second excerpt is worse because it reads more like the story happening all at once and is too confusing to follow along. Excerpt 1 flows wells and is fluent is telling a story.

To make myself feel better I would think about how ugly she was. Not very women's lib, I know, but she was my husband's mistress. And she was ugly, it was a fact. She had these bulging eyes and a veiny neck and nothing about her face was symmetrical. I would think about that and stop crying and then think about that note and the whole cycle would start all over again. In public, I put on a brave face. One night I went to dinner and at one point I said, no one wants to take out a lady who's seven months pregnant, she'll eat twice as much! It's not very funny when I write it down. written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I suppose there's nothing quite like discovering your husband is having an affair when you're seven months pregnant. And then there's Thelma Rice, with her perfect figure and that irritating habit of inscribing children's books with suggestive little notes, as if marking her territory like some literary-minded cat. I tried making jokes about it, naturally. That's what I do – turn tragedy into comedy, preferably before dessert. But somehow, quipping about being undatable while sporting a seven-month baby bump didn't land quite the way I'd hoped. The laughter that followed had that distinct pitch of pity, the kind that makes you wish you could crawl into a hole, except you can't because, well, pregnant. So here I am in my father's apartment in New York, surrounded by furniture that looks like it was rejected from a 1950s detective novel, crying into tissues and wondering how my life turned into this particularly unfunny sitcom. written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: It’s something you don’t expect from a second husband. Or, I don’t know, maybe you should suspect it more from a second husband. And that name. Thelma Rice. How can I not laugh when I think of the moment I found out? Let this be a reminder of how hungry I am for you. xoxo- Thelma. I remember the sound as I snapped the book shut. I remember Sam grabbing for it, wondering why story time was over before it had begun. I can see her when I close my eyes, hunched over that sweet and unassuming book, a hippo herself with that round, smug face, those manly teeth, that grayish skin. To be cheated on when you are seven months pregnant, by your second husband, is one thing. To be cheated on with a woman who resembles a cartoon hippo is entirely another. This, more than anything, is what makes me cry when I’m alone with just my father’s cuckoo clock and the rubber loveseat to keep me company.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Picture this: me, seven months pregnant, sprawled on the couch in my father's dreary New York apartment, tears streaming down my face. The backdrop? A symphony of beige, a decor so monotonous it could make a nun scream. The cause of this melodramatic scene? My second husband, Mark had just pulled a classic man move. He'd fallen in love with another woman. Now, I'd always been the type to handle heartbreak with a dash of humor. So, when I told my friends, "I'm not going to be able to date for a while because I'm seven months pregnant," I expected a chuckle. But the joke fell flat, and the silence was deafening. Maybe it was the delivery, the sheer absurdity of the situation. Whatever the reason, the only response I got was a smattering of pitying laughter. Back in my father's apartment, surrounded by furniture that seemed to mock my misery, I couldn't help but feel like a character in a bad sitcom. The beige walls, the lumpy couch, the faded floral wallpaper – it was all a recipe for despair. And then there was the discovery. The inscription in the book of children's songs, a gift from Thelma Rice to my husband. "To Mark, with love, from the other woman." It was like a punch to the gut, my husband's betrayal. Thelma Rice. The name echoed in my mind, a caricature of a woman with a voice like nails on a chalkboard and legs that went on for days. I pictured her, all blonde hair and fake smiles, and my anger burned even brighter. But amidst the tears and the anger, there was a flicker of determination. I wouldn't let this break me. I would pick myself up, dust myself off, and start over. I would find a way to be happy, even if it meant navigating the world of dating with a baby on my hip. After all, I was a woman, and women are resilient. We bend, we don't break. We fall, we get back up. We cry, we laugh. We love, we lose, we love again. And through it all, we find a way to keep going.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: I was seven months pregnant and couldn’t button my coat, which was how I ended up waddling into the room where my soon-to-be ex-husband Mark was laughing with his friends about something—or more likely, nothing—completely inconsequential. That’s when I said it. I said, “It’s funny, you know, Mark’s not available for affairs right now because he’s pregnant with me.” And they laughed. Oh, they laughed all right, but it wasn’t the right kind of laugh. It was that awkward, pitying chuckle that makes you realize your joke is less of a joke and more of a moment everyone wishes they weren’t part of. I felt like a stand-up comic bombing on open-mic night, only instead of hecklers, I had my own humiliation.That night, after crying for the hundredth time that week, I tried to find some solace in my father’s apartment, which was a masterpiece of misery. His brown corduroy couch sagged like it had given up on life, and every corner of the room was decorated in a way that screamed, “I haven’t been redecorated since Nixon resigned.” It was the kind of place that made sadness feel inevitable. And there I was, crying over Mark, who I now knew had been sneaking around with a woman named Thelma Rice—a name so cloyingly sweet it felt like it belonged on a box of cookies, not the antagonist of my life.The worst part? The discovery. A children’s songbook. A little gift from Thelma to Mark, inscribed with some nauseating drivel like, “For all the songs you’ll sing.” Songs he’d apparently been singing for her while our toddler, Sam, sang solo in his crib. I couldn’t believe the audacity, the gall, the absolute polyester pantsuit-ness of it all. And Thelma herself! I mean, have you seen Thelma? She looked like she spent her weekends alphabetizing her collection of decorative soaps. Yet there I was, a hormonal, bloated mess, crying into a pillow that smelled like mothballs. It was unbearable. And yet, somehow, it was also just another Tuesday.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: I'm seven months pregnant, and Thelma Rice is sleeping with my husband, so I'm sleeping with no one. Thelma Rice does not understand the struggle of dating inherent to being a 38-year-old pregnant woman, though maybe one day she will! It's a thought I comfort myself with, and it makes me laugh. I miss laughing. I don't think the joke would make anyone so much as giggle, not when said out loud and especially not when I look at it written on paper. It's just pathetic, I can hear the awkward chuckles now, the kind clusters of people make when trying to be sympathetic, or to prevent tears. I'm crying now, but I'm pregnant so it's to be expected. My life has turned quite ugly, filled with droll tragedy and my father's hideous furniture. It's good of him to let me stay in his New York apartment, but the place is so grey and miserable that it makes me grey and miserable. The lights in all the lamps flicker, and the few windows face a brick wall, so the apartment resembles a cave more than a home. It's fitting, I suppose. A nice cave, buried deep in the building, where I can retreat to lick my wounds. If my father's apartment had looked like a real home, I would have been reminded of what I lost. Ever since I found that crude inscription, in a book of children's songs of all places, I've had no home. Thelma Rice, with her endless entitlements, dragged Sam into this too, scrawling out her wantonness on the pages of a book suited for a small child, not a grown man. I can just see her now, her short and stubby fingers clutching at the pen as she tried to rhyme words together into her approximation of a clever lyric. I imagine her chewing her pen with her crooked teeth and smudging her lurid lipstick down her chin. It makes me feel...better, to think of her this way. Like I can see her truest self.

I like the phrases "brown corduroy couch sagged like it had given up on life" and "polyester pantsuit-ness of it all." Both are very descriptive and vivid when describing the story.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: I was seven months pregnant and couldn’t button my coat, which was how I ended up waddling into the room where my soon-to-be ex-husband Mark was laughing with his friends about something—or more likely, nothing—completely inconsequential. I felt like a stand-up comic bombing on open-mic night, only instead of hecklers, I had my own humiliation.That night, after crying for the hundredth time that week, I tried to find some solace in my father’s apartment, which was a masterpiece of misery. I couldn’t believe the audacity, the gall, the absolute polyester pantsuit-ness of it all. And Thelma herself! I mean, have you seen Thelma? written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The people of St. Paul did not know what to make of the article; no, they could not even begin to wrap their heads around it. The New York Times, unforgiving and direct as they were, used such terms as "arrogant," "ethically compromised," and "Machiavellian" to describe Walter. These descriptions did not resonate with the mild folks of St. Paul, and, with Walter and Patty so far away in that vague place called DC, they found themselves remarkably able to preserve the veneer of what they believed Walter, and Patty for that matter, to be. The local women remembered handsome Walter, gold-skinned and smiling, commuting to work by bike, that sheen of sweat making a mustache of diamonds over his handsomely curved upper lip. The men remembered Walter rolling out the evergreen-colored recycling bin on those Wednesday mornings, the way it teetered with the weight of everything he had so meticulously and carefully separated from the regular trash.It just wouldn't do; no, it didn't compute—this image of Walter snuggled up in bed with the coal industry. That couple had poured life into Ramsey Hill, buying that decrepit and dirt-cheap Victorian house with the Napoleonic turrets and the cream wraparound porch. If they squinted, they could all picture Patty outside, painting over the word "Fuck" that a hooligan had sprayed onto the house's flank one night: she with her unflinching athleticism, the kind acquired in college sports, pushing a stroller with that well-weathered batting arm, a bag of apples in the other. If she was not standing on a ladder, scraping out the gutters like a man, she was drinking zinfandel at that gorgeous kitchen island she'd done herself, the public radio on, too loudly for most of the other women's tastes. It was the "house on the hill"—that was what everybody called it—and the Berglund children were disheveled and beautiful. The couple would throw dinner parties and put signs up in their yards about the ocean and sometimes fight so loudly that the people down the hill had to shut their windows to protect them, in their kind Midwestern way, from the shame of having been heard.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Walter and Patty Berglund had become a story, but not in the way anyone back in Ramsey Hill would have predicted. The couple who had once embodied the stubborn optimism of urban pioneers now found themselves marred by scandal—a New York Times exposé of Walter's coal industry dealings had labeled him "ethically compromised" and "arrogant." These descriptions felt alien to the neighbors who remembered the Berglunds as the beating heart of their crumbling Victorian enclave, a pair who had practically willed their corner of St. Paul back to life. Walter, the mild-mannered environmentalist biking to his nonprofit job rain or shine, had seemed incapable of the kind of cynical maneuvering now attributed to him. Patty, with her unapologetic bluntness and visible exhaustion, had once been the maternal force of the block, a woman who weathered stroller wars and zoning battles with an athlete’s unrelenting drive. That they’d traded their struggling but righteous lives in Ramsey Hill for a high-powered existence in Washington, D.C., seemed almost like betrayal, though no one would say it out loud.Back then, the Berglunds had been a testament to the grind. Their Victorian was a disaster when they bought it—broken windows, a rotting porch, graffiti tagging its sides—and their marriage hadn’t seemed much better off for a while, given the tensions that leaked out at block parties and PTA meetings. Still, they’d worked, pouring themselves into the kind of relentless self-improvement Ramsey Hill had demanded. Walter in his gardening gloves, Patty with a paint-splattered bandana tied around her head, both knee-deep in home renovation projects, had been symbols of what the neighborhood aspired to: upward mobility dressed in scrappy altruism. But the cracks had been visible even then—Patty’s wineglass refilled too often during neighborhood dinners, Walter’s simmering annoyance when the compost bin went unturned. Now, from a distance, those years seemed almost quaint. The Berglunds had been good at being admired, even if they’d never quite learned how to admire themselves. The irony of Walter's public disgrace was not lost on anyone, least of all Patty, whose clipped “I told you so” had lost its sting after years of being only half-true.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: Excerpt 2 is easier to understand and you can picture the characters in your mind as you read it. The first excerpt is too abstract and although descriptive, it is hard to follow along. Excerpt 2 flows more naturally like a book or movie and you can imagine what the people are doing.

She wheeled her infant son’s stroller through the gritty neighborhood, weaving deftly between cracks in the sidewalk, never breaking her strong, assured pace. She marched through a regiment of cooking, cleaning, repairing, and caring for the baby with an endurance forged in years of grueling, all-day swim practices. Even her indulgences—public radio and zinfandel—were stringently measured, slotted into the schedule with militant rigidity. Walter and Patty gave every indication that they were here in Ramsey Hill to stay, and nobody thought otherwise. But as the Berglunds built up their house and the surrounding area, they were really building less of a home and more of a ladder.

During city council meetings, he gave passionate speeches about sorting plastics from paper. The Walter of Ramsey Hill believed in a better America, a green America, wild in its terrain, a patchwork of sustainable farms. Now the news, or at least the decent people at The New York Times and The Associated Press and The Washington Post, too, accused him of taking bribes from the coal industry. Walter and Petty first moved to Ramsey Hill back when it was still a neglected neighborhood; they thought of themselves as pioneers, do-gooders who could be the first to clean it up. With the little money they had, they’d bought a run-down Victorian house, and through the following years, they poured everything into that house’s restoration, fighting off plumbing failures, electrical outages, a neighbor with a penchant for yelling at his wife on the street, rotted wood, basement floods, and teen vandals — to address the latter, Patty had used a bat and a few stern, almost maternal, words. Patty, a former cheerleader for UMN, never fit into the neighborhood, visually speaking, though it hardly seemed to bother her. In the mornings, she jogged with her stroller, her blonde ponytail swinging behind her as she swerved to avoid the sidewalk feces, her face unflinching as the occasional truck driver whistled at her. In the afternoons, she painted the sidings of the house or installed kitchen tile between diaper changes and nursing sessions. In the evenings, she sat on the couch after preparing dinner, sipping a glass of zinfandel and listening to NPR, a radio station that would, in the unforeseeable future, refer to her as “the wife of disgraced politician, Walter Berglund.”

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I am Nanapush, and my people, the Anishinabe, have borne floods of suffering that rose like tidal waves over the generations. We’ve learned to endure the violent waters. First, there was the terrible spotted sickness that came from the south, killing us by the dozens and scarring the faces of the living. There was the long migration west, where we were marched to the Dakotas with an army at our backs, and the treaty we signed at gunpoint. Then came another exile—a slow dismemberment of the land that remained, bled dry by a series of laws and documents. My people were left alone for some time after that. But in 1914, consumption began to prowl the perimeter of the reservation. Its footfall was silent, though its presence was anything but invisible. When consumption snapped its jaws, it unraveled the community death by death, trapping families like the Pillagers inside, left to huddle in their close quarters and wait out the disease. I see now that the disease was waiting them out instead. The Pillagers succumbed to the sickness one by one—all of them but me. Although I am only fifty, I have risen through the ranks by default. I am considered an elder now. In truth, I am merely a survivor. It is under my watch that our traditional way of life has finally been extinguished. It was I who led the final buffalo hunt, trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last of the old birch trees. Loss is my constant companion. It visits me as it visited my ancestors, but I have found a small mercy within its grasp. I have preserved the last of the Pillager family, refusing the men from the government who come with more papers to sign, seeking more ways to strip the Anishinabe of their land and identity. As long as my name is Nanapush, I will not forfeit that final power.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: The spotted sickness came first, creeping up from the south like a shadow that darkens the earth before a storm. We didn't know then that it was just the beginning, just the first thread being pulled from the fabric of our world. I was young when we were pushed westward to Dakota land, our feet leaving tracks in soil that wasn't ours, our hands reaching out to sign papers we couldn't read. The government men smiled with teeth like tombstones while our people's names were written down, recorded, filed away in drawers that would never open again. Then came 1914, and with it the consumption—slow, patient, hungry as winter. It ate through our families like fire through dry grass, starting with the Pillagers who lived close as bark to wood. I watched them fall, one after another, until the silence in their cabin was louder than any drum. My own family went the same way, leaving me to carry their names like stones in my pocket, weighing me down, making me an elder at fifty though my hair had barely grayed. I led the last buffalo hunt, my heart heavy as I watched the dust rise from their hooves. I was there when the last bear fell, when the last beaver with a mature pelt swam into my trap, when the last ancient birch dropped its leaves for the final time. The old ways slipped through our fingers like water, impossible to hold. But I refused to let it all go. When I saved the last of the Pillagers, I held on tight, my fingers cramping around what remained. Those government papers came again and again, whispering promises of money, of progress, of change. But I knew better. I'd seen enough of their promises turn to dust in our mouths. This time, I kept my pen still, my name unwritten, my piece of earth ungiven.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt 1 is easier to read and imagine in your mind. The first excerpt is more straight-forward and makes more sense. The second excerpt is a bit abstract and a bit harder to follow along. Excerpt 1 is better because it flows more naturally and effectively tells a story well.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: First it was the spotted sickness that unfurled from the south. I was not there, but I remember. Then forced migration westward, to Dakota land, and the Anishinabe signed a treaty. These were made to be broken and to break us. After came more displacements, the government making exiles of us again. So many documents and so much displacement. I lie on my back and these papers press hard on my chest when I think of them. In 1914 it was consumption, creeping slowly through the reservation like woodsmoke. Taking us one by one, and unraveling us, and my family could not escape it either. The Pillagers were unraveled by this new sickness and so was our community, huddled so close together as we were. Unable to escape each other, shoulder, pressed to shoulder, and unable to escape the sickness. I was the only one of us who lived. Nanapush, the sole survivor. For this suffering I am already an elder, but I am only fifty years old. And for this terrible privilege I have been witness to the end of the traditions. I have led the last buffalo hunt, saw the last bear killed. Trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last old birch. Sometimes we understood we were doing these things for the final time. Other times, we didn't realize until after. The loss hurts in my teeth. It lives in my early wrinkles and sore body. But I have saved the Pillager family. When the government comes with more papers, more opportunities to strip us of our land and our identity, I have resisted. I did not sign. I will not sign—we will not be exiles again. Too much has already been taken. The Anishinabe persist, and I will continue to resist for the Pillagers who are lost, and for those of us who carry on.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: In the damp quiet of that reservation, I stood as the last thread holding together the vast, frayed tapestry of our people, the Anishinabe. Sickness had come, spotted and relentless, rising from the south to crawl across our bodies, marking us for the grave. We fled westward, believing Dakota land might swallow us whole and offer peace, only to be met with treaties that tangled words into chains we could never untether. The land we walked became paper; paper became exile. Yet it was not over. In 1914, another ghost, slow and smothering, stalked us—consumption, it was called. It seeped through the fragile walls of our homes, latching onto breath, pulling entire families under its cold, merciless blanket. I saw the Pillagers go, one by one, slipping into the quiet where I alone remained. Fifty years old, they called me an elder, though my face bore fewer lines than my spirit. Time had sped in its cruelty. I had seen the last buffalo fall beneath our arrows, the last bear stagger through our woods, the final beaver with a pelt worth holding. The birches I once leaned against as a child, their bark aglow with the sun, were nothing but broken stumps. Each loss carved another hollowness, and still, I stood. I saved what was left—the last of the Pillager family, the name that carried its own strength. When they brought papers, government seals pressed flat against the lives they meant to strip away, I took the pen in my hand but never let it touch the page. They could take everything—our animals, our trees, even the air that filled our lungs. But they would not take the land, not from me, not from what I carried. I stared back at them, unflinching, as if daring them to try harder, without fear, without shame.
written_by_MFA026.Reason: Excerpt two has a clear flow of ideas and that makes the message easily comprehended. Excerpt 1 mixes ideas between sickness and forced treaties and it's difficult to find the connection. Excerpt 2 gives a clear sequence of events and how they unfolded starting with the sickness, followed by malicious treaties and consumption which sounds like the last nail in the coffin for the community.

The land we walked became paper; paper became exile. Yet it was not over. In 1914, another ghost, slow and smothering, stalked us—consumption, it was called. It seeped through the fragile walls of our homes, latching onto breath, pulling entire families under its cold, merciless blanket. I saw the Pillagers go, one by one, slipping into the quiet where I alone remained. Fifty years old, they called me an elder, though my face bore fewer lines than my spirit. Time had sped in its cruelty. I had seen the last buffalo fall beneath our arrows, the last bear stagger through our woods, the final beaver with a pelt worth holding. The birches I once leaned against as a child, their bark aglow with the sun, were nothing but broken stumps. Each loss carved another hollowness, and still, I stood. I saved what was left—the last of the Pillager family, the name that carried its own strength. When they brought papers, government seals pressed flat against the lives they meant to strip away, I took the pen in my hand but never let it touch the page. They could take everything—our animals, our trees, even the air that filled our lungs. But they would not take the land, not from me, not from what I carried. I stared back at them, unflinching, as if daring them to try harder, without fear, without shame.

Unable to escape each other, shoulder, pressed to shoulder, and unable to escape the sickness. I was the only one of us who lived. Nanapush, the sole survivor. For this suffering I am already an elder, but I am only fifty years old. And for this terrible privilege I have been witness to the end of the traditions. written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Since John’s death, my memories (of him, but also of most things), once acute, have become soft and mudgy. For a while, I was able to maintain a handle on reality by way of an elaborate method of timekeeping. It was calming to look back at what John and I were doing one year ago, and keep track of the days that way. One year ago today, I would remind myself, we were in Mexico, preparing a dinner of heavily spiced chicken in our rented kitchen. One year ago today, we were at the Met, looking at the new rooftop exhibit, which John loved but I disliked for its uninspired crudeness. These memories were vivid, acute, and I was able to almost watch them, like one would a television show. And then, December 31, 2003 arrived. In that moment, one year ago no longer included him. John had morphed, officially, into a part of the past and not the present. I came to this burning realization while I was crossing Lexington Avenue. I had a bag of groceries in my hand. It was snowing, quite faintly. I realized I had spent the year trying to keep him alive, because I have always believed, been told, that it is our duty to keep the dead alive. But what about the living? I realized it, then, that the key to all of this was to keep them dead. There was no other way, in my view, to continue living myself.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: It is December 31, 2004, and I find myself at the intersection of memory and absence, crossing Lexington Avenue on a day John never knew. The light changes, the traffic hums, but the world feels displaced, as though operating on a parallel timeline I can no longer inhabit. I ask myself where we were this day a year ago, but the question folds into itself, unanswered. There was no "we" then. There is no "we" now. It is just me, standing on the edge of a moment I never thought would arrive, tethered to someone who no longer exists in the present tense.Time has turned traitorous, reshaping vivid recollections into something blurred, soft-edged, mudgy. I want the sharpness back—the sound of his voice calling my name, the exact tilt of his head when he laughed—but instead I am left with echoes that refuse to hold their shape. For months I kept time through him: what we ate, where we sat, how the hours unfolded a year ago. That tether, too, is breaking, and I know it must. To live is to keep the dead where they belong, not erased but sequestered, a layer beneath the surface of everything we do and feel. I loved him, love him still, but loving him has become the act of holding his absence, acknowledging the permanence of it, walking forward through the days he will never know. This is the life left, the one that does not wait.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: Excerpt 1 is easier to read because it is very descriptive and makes sense in what is happening. The second excerpt is too abstract and rambles like someone overthinking things. Excerpt 1 flows well and reads like book. There's more vivid images and ideas in the first excerpt as well.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Time moves in peculiar circles when you're carrying the dead. I found myself caught in this ritual of backward glancing, measuring each day against its twin from the year before, when John was still here, still breathing, still marking time with me. It became a kind of obsession, this constant calculation – where were we last March, what were we doing that April afternoon, did we have dinner at that place on Second Avenue in May? The memories started clean, sharp-edged, but they grew mudgy around the corners, like old photographs left too long in sunlight. Then came that morning on Lexington Avenue, unremarkable except for its mathematical significance: December 31, 2003, a date John never saw. The realization hit me with the force of a physical blow – I had crossed some invisible line into a time he never knew existed. We tell ourselves we keep the dead alive through memory, through these endless retrospective inventories, but perhaps what we're really doing is learning to keep them dead. It's a peculiar arithmetic, this subtraction of the living from the dead, this slow release of what was into what is. The truth about grief, I was learning, is that it operates on its own timeline, indifferent to our careful calculations, our desperate attempts to hold onto what slips away with each passing day, each remembered and then half-remembered moment.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Time erodes memory, smudging away the finer details of a scene until all that remains are stage directions. Grief forces us to look back, to fall into stories that lack the danger of surprise. It was possible for me to sit across from John’s empty seat at the table so long as I could fill that chair with all my memories of him sitting in it. 2003 folded into 2004, the dates layered on top of one another. I wanted to believe I was pulling John’s ghost along with me. On December 31, 2004, as I was crossing Lexington Avenue, I realized that I was chasing after his echo, instead. Every day of that first year was endurable, if only because the date was glossed over by what John and I had been doing the previous year. No longer could I use this crutch. December 31, 2003 was the first full day I was a widow. Those memories remains sharp, regardless of if I’d prefer them smudged. Agonies are often the loudest in hindsight, whereas comforts are soft and slippery. After a death, we cling to empty air. We turn back, and we turn back again to memories until our fingerprints have worn them fuzzy. This is all there is now. Memories and photographs and people who knew him. Death draws a fine line between then and now, and if one wishes to live, they must let their dead be dead.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Though they both were quite good. Excerpt 2 is better in the following areas, the flow of events felt a little more vivid and easy to follow up. Its fluency and more natural feel of writing made it easier to follow and keep concentration. Its choice of vocabulary as well was easy to comprehend.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: The air in the apartment is heavy, thick with the scent of lilies and the ghost of his presence.  Time, that relentless tide, keeps moving, yet I seem stranded, caught in the undertow of grief.  It's been a year and four months since John, my John, slipped through the veil, and the world insists on reminding me.The calendar, that cruel arbiter of time, mocks me with its relentless march forward.  Each day is a faded echo of the one before, a year removed.  I find myself trapped in a loop, rewinding the reel of memory, asking, "Where were we a year ago? What were we doing?"  It's a futile attempt to hold onto him, to keep him alive in the only way I know how.Yesterday, I crossed Lexington Avenue, the same way I've done a thousand times before.  But this time, it was different.  This time, I carried the weight of December 31, 2003, a date that exists in my world but not in his.  It was the day he ceased to be, the day the world shifted on its axis.And in that moment, I realized the terrible truth.  We who are left behind, we try to keep the dead alive in our memories, clinging to their fading essence like a lifeline.  But in doing so, we create a purgatory, a liminal space where they are neither here nor there.  To truly live, to move forward, we must keep them dead.  It's a harsh reality, a bitter pill to swallow.  But it's the only way to navigate the treacherous terrain of grief.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: When I think of John now, whether in grief or joy, time makes a mirage of our parting. Memories are distant, those vibrant, vivid images inevitably softened by the passing days and nights into muddy and distorted reflections. My practice of keeping time in relation to what John and I were doing last year is a game of questions. When he was alive, who did we see today? Where did we go together? Above all: What did he say to me then? Crossing Lexington Avenue in the wintry haze enveloping New York, a cold, damp curtain hung above the city, I come across the date—December 31, 2003—and realize John never saw this day last year. My exercise for keeping time has expired, and my husband lives in the distant past. I might transplant him here, invite him as memory into this moment to maintain our profound connection, the sort unsevered by death so long as he is kept within the perfect safety of memory. Yet it occurs to me—in this exercise of resurrection, I am only ensuring that I, too, never see December 31, 2003. That I, like John, live only in my recollections. Thus: we must keep them dead. To continue living, to draw oneself up from the smudged and mildewy twilight of the place where memory is real to us, there can be no resurrection; for the living to carry on, the dead must remain dead.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: Boy, it was raining like a madman. I mean really coming down. Cats and dogs, like they say. I was watching old Phoebe go around and around on this carousel, and all I could think was, "If only you knew how happy this makes me." She looked so good in that blue coat of hers, just riding that thing like she didn't have a care in the world. Me, I was soaked to the bone. My hunting hat was doing its best, but there's only so much a hat can do when the sky's practically falling down. But I didn't care. I was too busy feeling good to worry about a little rain.You know, it's funny. I'm stuck in this place, and they keep asking me these stupid questions. This one guy, this psychoanalyst or whatever he is, he wants to know if I'm going to apply myself at school. Can you beat that? Like it's the only thing that matters. And then there's old D.B. He's not as bad as the rest of them, but he still asks a lot of questions. He came to see me the other day with this English actress. A real glamour girl, if you know what I mean. Anyway, she went to the bathroom or something, and D.B. starts asking me what I think about all this stuff that's been going on. You know, the stuff I've been telling you about.I don't know why they care so much. It's my life, isn't it? I guess they think they're helping or something. But all they do is make me feel worse. Like I'm some kind of freak show or something. I just wish they'd leave me alone.The thing is, I don't even know what I think myself. It's all so messed up. I mean, I was just telling you about Stradlater and Ackley and Maurice, and now I'm starting to miss those guys. Can you believe that? I didn't even like them that much. But now that I'm not around them anymore, I keep thinking about all the stupid stuff we did together. It's like I'm lonelier now than I was when they were around.I guess that's what this whole thing is about. Loneliness. It's like this big, empty hole inside me that I can't seem to fill. I keep trying to find people to connect with, but it never seems to work out. It's like I'm always looking for something that's not there.Anyway, I'm getting tired of talking about myself. It's boring. Maybe I'll tell you more about old Phoebe sometime. She's a real character, that kid. But for now, I think I'll just sit here and watch the rain. It's kind of peaceful, in a way.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: The rain started a few minutes after Phoebe got on the carousel. It started out light, then almost immediately it began to pour. I mean it was really raining—my shoes started to get soaked, and my hair, but watching her atop the fake little ponies I only felt an overwhelming sense of joy. There was my sister, in her blue coat, laughing and riding on the carousel without a care in the world. I stood there in my soggy shoes for a while just watching her; my hunting hat protected me slightly from the rain, but mostly I didn’t even mind how wet I was getting. I was just so happy watching her there. Really I think that was one of the last times I can remember feeling happy without anything else getting in the way. Later, once I arrived in the facility, I remember the psychoanalyst there asked me some stupid question, something about my future—whether I would start to finally apply myself in school or something. I never knew how to answer dumb questions like that, so usually I’d stay quiet or say something snarky in reply so that they learned to stop asking. Sometimes D.B. would come and see me, which wasn’t so bad, except for the fact that he was always rattling on about his screenwriting career and asking me more stupid questions. “Isn’t there anything you’re passionate about? Anything at all?” I remember once, he came to visit me with this actress woman he had been seeing. She was really glamorous, and I remember she had said she was from England, or maybe I’m just thinking that because she had this snotty-sounding accent. She didn’t really ask me any questions; she mostly just sat there and would speak if D.B. spoke to her. Anyway, there was one time that the two of them came to visit me, and I remember that once the actress went to the bathroom, D.B. leaned in and asked me what I thought of everything that had been going on. “What do you mean?” I asked him, annoyed to have to field yet another question. “I guess I just mean—all of this,” he said, and he stuck his hand out to gesture all around us. I realized then how pointless it had been to share anything with D.B. in the first place, with him or even the one's I didn't like—Stradlater, Ackley, Maurice. I kept thinking that somehow, I’d figure out a way to help them see things the way I did, and then we’d finally understand each other and I wouldn’t have to explain anything anymore. But in the end, all it did was make me feel more alone.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Boy, it started raining like hell while I watched old Phoebe going around and around on that crazy carousel. I mean it really started coming down, but I didn't give a damn about getting wet. I really didn't. I just stood there with this goofy grin on my face - I probably looked like a complete madman - watching my kid sister in her blue coat having the time of her life. That killed me. It really did. My hunting hat was getting soaked but I didn't care about that either. It's funny, sometimes the things that make you the happiest are the things that get you all sopping wet and probably looking like a complete moron to everybody else. But that's the thing about happiness - it doesn't give a damn what you look like.Now I'm stuck in this crumby place, this rest home or whatever the hell you want to call it, and this hotshot psychoanalyst keeps asking me all these stupid questions about what I'm gonna do with my future. Like if I'm gonna "apply myself" when I go back to school. Jesus Christ, that kills me. These people and their goddam questions. Even old D.B. - he's not as bad as the rest of them, but he still can't help himself. He came to visit me yesterday with this English actress who was sort of beautiful in this fake, Hollywood way. As soon as she went to the bathroom - girls are always going to the bathroom when you're in the middle of something - D.B. starts in with the questions about everything I've been telling him. All about what happened and what I think about it now and all.The funny part is, the more I talk about all this stuff, the more I keep thinking about everybody. Even the people I didn't particularly like, for Chrissake. Like old Stradlater with his secret slob tendencies and Ackley with his pimples and Maurice. I keep thinking about them and missing them, in this crazy way. I don't even know why. I mean, they were all phonies in their own way, but I miss them anyway. That's the thing that drives me crazy in here - how you can hate somebody's guts one minute and then start missing them like hell the next. It's really ironical as hell. Sometimes I think maybe that psychoanalyst isn't so dumb after all, but I'd rather get kicked in the teeth than admit that to him. He'll probably ask me about my violent tendencies next time I see him. That's the trouble with psychoanalysts - they always want to know what everything means, even when things don't mean anything at all.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: While I was watching Phoebe circle round and round on the carousel, it started to rain real hard. It was the heaviest rain I’d seen in a long, long time. Maybe ever. It was coming down in buckets. Even barrels. My hunting hat helped protect my hair a little, but I was soaked all the way to my bones. I didn’t think I’d ever get dry. But even though I was cold and wet, I couldn’t stop feeling so happy that every raindrop was like a miniature sun. I watched Phoebe laughing and waving in her blue coat. She was smiling real big, and after a little while, I realized I was smiling too. The painted horses on the carousel went up and down, and I didn’t want them to ever stop. Then I ended up here, where nobody smiles like Phoebe and I’m not allowed outside by myself. It doesn’t rain very often around here, but when it does, I sit by the windows and remember what it felt like to stand in that crazy downpour. Then I smile just to myself, like a secret. Everybody here asks me the stupidest questions I’ve ever heard. Especially that one doctor. He asked me the other day about whether I plan on applying myself when I go back to school. “That’s none of your goddamn business,” I said to him. “You’re right,” he said. “It isn’t really my business. But it’s your business, isn’t it? Don’t you think your future deserves some consideration?” I told him he was the biggest phony I’d ever met in my life. It probably wasn’t true, but in the moment, it sure felt like it. This doctor keeps telling me I have lots of potential and that if I don’t get better, I’ll waste it. I think he should worry about wasting his own potential. What kind of doctor wants to be stuck in a place like this talking to people like me? Sometimes my brother D.B. comes to visit. He’s a screenwriter, and not as bad as the other people here, but he still asks lots of questions. Mostly stuff about medicine, which I don’t like talking about, and television, which I’m not even allowed to watch here. The last time he came, he brought along an English actress who wore lots of sparkles. She seemed nervous and kept telling me how brave I was. When she left to go to the bathroom, D.B. asked me what I thought about everything that happened. And I realized that talking about everything made me miss everyone it happened with. Even people I didn’t like—even Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice. And I don’t want to miss anyone anymore.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: I think that excerpt 1 is better written.  It creates an image in your mind much better than excerpt 2 about what's going on.  Neither story gets into what made that situation the way it is.  Why is this guy locked up in a psychiatric hospital or jail.  Doesn't really indicate which one, but I think excerpt 1 gives a better description of what's going on in the writers head.  I also felt that excerpt 2 had some choppy sentences.  Many of the sentences were a similar length, and this could affect the fluency.  They could have been combined into complex sentences that would make it a better fluency.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: It started raining like hell out of nowhere, the way it does when you don’t have a goddam umbrella. I was standing there, freezing my tail off, watching Phoebe ride the carousel. She was wearing this blue coat that flared out every time the horse went up, like it had its own personality or something. I swear, she was the only one who didn’t look phony on the whole goddam planet. I pulled my hunting hat down tight, the one I always wore backward, like some kind of idiot. It didn’t do much, but I didn’t give a damn. Watching her, I got this weird lump in my throat, like I wanted to bawl and laugh at the same time. It was the damnedest thing. I just stood there getting soaked and didn’t even care. The next part’s harder to talk about. It’s all tied up with that place I’m in now—the rest home or whatever the hell they call it. The shrink keeps asking me about my plans, like he’s expecting me to say I want to be a goddam astronaut or something. “Are you going to apply yourself?” he keeps asking, like that’s the magic question that’ll unlock the universe. I told him I didn’t know and asked if he had a cigarette. He didn’t think that was funny. Shrinks never do. D.B. came to visit me once. He brought this actress he’s dating—some glamorous British type who probably says “lovely” instead of “nice.” She went to the bathroom, and D.B. leaned over like he was about to share some deep, brotherly wisdom. He asked me what I thought about everything that happened, the whole damn mess. I didn’t know what to say. I mean, I hate talking about stuff like that. It just makes you miss people. Even the ones you don’t like all that much, like Stradlater and Ackley. Hell, even Maurice, that lousy pimp. It’s like, the more you tell the story, the more it feels like they’re right there with you, and then, poof, they’re gone again. I told D.B. it was fine, just fine, and then the actress came back, smelling like expensive soap or something.Anyway, that’s the thing about telling people stuff. You think it’ll make you feel better, but it just makes you feel worse, like you’re carrying around this big, stupid ache. But maybe that’s the point. Maybe you’re supposed to miss people. Even the ones you don’t want to. It’s goddam beautiful and sad all at the same time, and I don’t know if I’ll ever figure it out. Maybe nobody does. Maybe that’s the whole thing.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: It seemed to me that it had never rained that hard. I might as well have been out in the next great flood with all that rain, but I didn’t mind. Watching Phoebe in her new blue coat go round and round on that shiny carousel horse made me feel so damn warm, that I hardly even noticed the cold wet of it all. My hunting hat shielded me a bit, but that got soaked fast. In no time at all, I was drenched. Totally soaked, but totally happy, too. I could hear Phoebe laughing on the horse, and of course she wasn’t wet under the carousel’s awning. She seemed to me completely free. I guess I could have gotten upset, shivering as I was and my clothes so heavy with water that they were falling off of me. My shoes squished when I moved even a little, but I felt like a million bucks watching Phoebe. The happiness didn’t last, though, not through to right now. I’m stuck in this miserable “rest” home, where I can’t even rest. How am I meant to relax when these idiot psychoanalysts keep pelting me with idiot questions? One of them badgers me with nonsense like, “But how do you expect do have a future if you don’t care to maintain your present? You need to try in school. Do you intend to try in school?” My brother, D.B., the screenwriter, likes to visit and ask me mind-numbing questions, too, though he’s not nearly as bad at the psycho- babblers. He’s not so bad because he’s my brother, and I do love him, so I tolerate the million- and-one questions, but I still wish he’d cut back on the interrogations. He brought this glamorous actress, a Brit, to visit with him, and while she’s off powdering her nose or whatever girls do in the bathroom, D.B. asks me: “How are you feeling, champ, about everything that’s happened?” I tell him, slowly, the details of the last few days. It’s strange to say it out loud, rather than just in my head, where I can say whatever I want. But it’s nice, too, a relief, even. Telling D.B. about it makes him lean in close to listen, and I feel close to him, not just physically but emotionally. Like my brother is really with me. Talking about Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice, it feels like they’re with me, too. I don’t even like those guys, but talking about them makes me feel…surrounded. I don’t think I’m a happy person, but talking about when I was happy, with Phoebe, I feel like I could be.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: It started raining like hell out of nowhere, the way it does when you don’t have a goddam umbrella. I was standing there, freezing my tail off, watching Phoebe ride the carousel. She was wearing this blue coat that flared out every time the horse went up, like it had its own personality or something. I swear, she was the only one who didn’t look phony on the whole goddam planet. I pulled my hunting hat down tight, the one I always wore backward, like some kind of idiot. It didn’t do much, but I didn’t give a damn. Watching her, I got this weird lump in my throat, like I wanted to bawl and laugh at the same time. It was the damnedest thing. I just stood there getting soaked and didn’t even care. The next part’s harder to talk about. It’s all tied up with that place I’m in now—the rest home or whatever the hell they call it. The shrink keeps asking me about my plans, like he’s expecting me to say I want to be a goddam astronaut or something. “Are you going to apply yourself?” he keeps asking, like that’s the magic question that’ll unlock the universe. I told him I didn’t know and asked if he had a cigarette. He didn’t think that was funny. Shrinks never do. D.B. came to visit me once. He brought this actress he’s dating—some glamorous British type who probably says “lovely” instead of “nice.” She went to the bathroom, and D.B. leaned over like he was about to share some deep, brotherly wisdom. He asked me what I thought about everything that happened, the whole damn mess. I didn’t know what to say. I mean, I hate talking about stuff like that. It just makes you miss people. Even the ones you don’t like all that much, like Stradlater and Ackley. Hell, even Maurice, that lousy pimp. It’s like, the more you tell the story, the more it feels like they’re right there with you, and then, poof, they’re gone again. I told D.B. it was fine, just fine, and then the actress came back, smelling like expensive soap or something.Anyway, that’s the thing about telling people stuff. You think it’ll make you feel better, but it just makes you feel worse, like you’re carrying around this big, stupid ache. But maybe that’s the point. Maybe you’re supposed to miss people. Even the ones you don’t want to. It’s goddam beautiful and sad all at the same time, and I don’t know if I’ll ever figure it out. Maybe nobody does. Maybe that’s the whole thing.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: It seemed to me that it had never rained that hard. I might as well have been out in the next great flood with all that rain, but I didn’t mind. Watching Phoebe in her new blue coat go round and round on that shiny carousel horse made me feel so damn warm, that I hardly even noticed the cold wet of it all. My hunting hat shielded me a bit, but that got soaked fast. In no time at all, I was drenched. Totally soaked, but totally happy, too. I could hear Phoebe laughing on the horse, and of course she wasn’t wet under the carousel’s awning. She seemed to me completely free. I guess I could have gotten upset, shivering as I was and my clothes so heavy with water that they were falling off of me. My shoes squished when I moved even a little, but I felt like a million bucks watching Phoebe. The happiness didn’t last, though, not through to right now. I’m stuck in this miserable “rest” home, where I can’t even rest. How am I meant to relax when these idiot psychoanalysts keep pelting me with idiot questions? One of them badgers me with nonsense like, “But how do you expect do have a future if you don’t care to maintain your present? You need to try in school. Do you intend to try in school?” My brother, D.B., the screenwriter, likes to visit and ask me mind-numbing questions, too, though he’s not nearly as bad at the psycho- babblers. He’s not so bad because he’s my brother, and I do love him, so I tolerate the million- and-one questions, but I still wish he’d cut back on the interrogations. He brought this glamorous actress, a Brit, to visit with him, and while she’s off powdering her nose or whatever girls do in the bathroom, D.B. asks me: “How are you feeling, champ, about everything that’s happened?” I tell him, slowly, the details of the last few days. It’s strange to say it out loud, rather than just in my head, where I can say whatever I want. But it’s nice, too, a relief, even. Telling D.B. about it makes him lean in close to listen, and I feel close to him, not just physically but emotionally. Like my brother is really with me. Talking about Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice, it feels like they’re with me, too. I don’t even like those guys, but talking about them makes me feel…surrounded. I don’t think I’m a happy person, but talking about when I was happy, with Phoebe, I feel like I could be.

written_by_MFA021.Excerpt1: Of course, the man thought bitterly, of course the second you killed one damned autocrat a new one popped up, like an inconvenient erection, to take his place. It was Saturday. The man was sitting in a car in his dead uncle’s garage, pretending to drive. He couldn’t actually drive because he wasn’t on the run. The on the run part was over. Now he was simply in hiding. It was Saturday, and he’d killed the old premier on Tuesday, and the new premier had come to power on Thursday, and already his administration had implemented a series of performance improvement plans for striking agricultural workers that relied heavily on murder, or, as state media called it, “right-sizing the population through proactively attritionary removal policies.” The man looked down at the car. It was red. Blood red. An egregious cliché. But of course blood was red. He, of all people, should know that: his nightmares were full of it. The man stared at the steering wheel. There were two choices, right or left. Right meant he kept his head down. It wouldn’t be all bad. Right might mean a job, a house, a wife, at least once it was safe to assume a new identity. Right meant fear but not danger. His stomach turned. Left meant killing the new guy. Left meant assassination wasn’t just something he had done; “assassin” would be something he was. It would mean going public. Producing soundbites. Practicing a firm, inspirational set of his jaw for the inevitable Wanted poster. The man leaped up, determined.
written_by_MFA021.Excerpt2: The man in the red car, a car he'd stashed in his dead uncle's garage, a car he sat in now, thinking, This is it.  It was a Saturday.  He was grappling.  With his conscience.  The premier had to go.  This premier, worse than the last.  And the last one, well, he'd taken care of that.  Hadn't he?  The man in the red car, the car in the dead uncle's garage, the man who'd done it before, the man grappling, the man with the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats.  He'd thought they'd be a good thing, the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats.  A just price.  For taking out the bad guy.  But now he was thinking, Maybe not.  Maybe the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats, maybe they weren't a just price.  Maybe they were just panic attacks, nightmares, cold sweats.  The man in the red car, the car in the garage, the dead uncle, the dead premier, the grappling, the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats, the thinking, the thinking, the thinking.  Go or stay.  This was it.  Or it wasn't.  Do it again and step into the light.  He could lead a movement.  Take credit.  Tell the world, You want justice? I'm justice.  Or go back to being the guy he'd been before.  The guy no one suspected.  The guy who did what he had to do and then went back to work on Monday.  Like nothing had happened.  The thought of it, the thought of going back to being that guy, that's what made him leap out of the car.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: The red car was old, a wheezing relic. He sat inside it in the dark, in his dead uncle’s garage, and felt his heart doing that flutter thing again, like it might bail out of his chest. Panic attack. His gaze found the steering wheel’s crumbling rubber grip, then his hand, sweaty and pale against it, as if asking: What have you done? What are you about to do? Murder wasn’t a thing you could just stop doing like sugar or carbs. It left its hooks in you, lodged under the ribs, twisting whenever you tried to breathe easy. The old premier’s face kept appearing in dreams—wide-eyed, slack-jawed, like a failed ventriloquist dummy. No strings to pull. Just the weight of a man who’d screamed, but only silently. And for what? A better world? Please. The world had gone on, more evil, more absurd. The current premier was a caricature of cruelty, all shiny teeth and too-tight suits, gliding through bulletproof banquets while people starved. This was justice, wasn’t it? To step into the role, a public avenger, claim the credit, lead the charge? But another part of him—a sad little whisper—said, Just stop. Be obscure. Be no one. That thought sickened him. No. Obscurity was the real death. He flung the door open, the cold air a slap. Time to go.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: That Saturday morning the light was orange through the window in his uncle's garage, bouncing off against the car, making the red paint seem redder. His uncle's ghost had made an appearance in the man's dream last night, making woosh-whee-whooo sounds. There were also smears of blood and the sound of the last scream of the man he had killed. The former premier. A Nouveu Fascist, the worst kind you could be, other than a Neo-Nouveu Fascist, which was much worse. The dreams had started after the pull of the gun (the newest Bang Alert model, funny, because it was a silent gun) that caused the last scream of the Nouveu Fascist. And now, on his lap, the faded picture of the Neo-Nouveu Fascist, who could be the next target of the Bang Alert. Could be? Would be. Would be his next target. And afterwards, the masses would flock around him chanting revolution, the city burning and a new one emerging. Yes, would be. written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: One Saturday morning, he found himself sitting in the red Arviana sportscar he’d stashed in his dead uncle’s garage. He remembered assassinating the former premier as if it were yesterday, although of course a long time had passed. For him, the intervening years had been: nightmares in the evenings, panic attacks in the mornings. Long days spent toiling in obscurity. Each year a little bit worse than the last. Meanwhile, for the new, even more evil premier? Every year he’d steadily consolidated his base. Eliminated his opponents. Misled the public. Until finally, his troubling rise to power was complete. What was a good man supposed to do? Shut the door on his uncle’s garage and continue a life of repulsive passivity – while reliving, each night, the misdeeds of his past? Or – commit to the violent path which he’d already chosen and which the present situation demanded? Kill the new premier. But this time, no more secrets, no more obscure toil. He’d claim credit right away, before he had a chance to overthink it, and declare himself the leader of a new movement of justice. He could hear, almost, his future supporters’ cheers, as he’d often heard – over and over – the thump of his car’s rear tires as they’d reversed over the former premier. He leapt from the sportscar and let the cheers carry him out into the street.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: He sat in Uncle Pete's cherry-red Civic (deceased), which smelled like those little pine trees times infinity, contemplating what the HR folks call Career Enhancement via Strategic Premier Elimination. The last one had been easier—younger him, dumber him, him before the Sleep-EZ pills and the nightly Personal Terror Management Sessions. Now he knew things. Like how a dying premier's eyes go all WhatThe? and BetYouFeelBadNow. Like how the headlines say Justice Served! while your brain screams MurderGuy! MurderGuy! at 3 A.M. But this new premier? Total sicko. Made the last one look like a Kindness Enhancement Specialist. The way those thick-necked guards stood around him at press conferences, all We'reNotThinkingAboutGunsUnderOurJackets. The way he signed those Special Citizen Reduction Orders with that gold pen, smirking. A guy could become somebody, taking him out. Could go on TV, start a movement: Area Man Admits to Double-Premier Elimination, Seeks Followers. Better than sitting here hyperventilating in Uncle Pete's garage, waiting for the next Premier-Initiated Civic Improvement Program to accidentally-on-purpose disappear more "undesirable elements." The old him, Pre-Premier-Removal him, would've just gone home, watched GameShows™. But that guy? That guy was dead as Uncle Pete. He grabbed the door handle, feeling that old familiar Here-We-Go-Again tingle. Time to make history. Again.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I went to see my father and found him in a much worse state than I had left him. He was disoriented and dazed, mumbling to himself about taxes and missionaries knocking on the door. He couldn't remember much about what he was working on. My mother gently reminded him that he was writing about the Bible and anti-Semitism. "Oh yes," he said, "that's right," and nodded as if to confirm this to himself. While the three of us ate supper, he turned to me and told me that he was quite proud of me. "You are a good kid," he said. "Always have been." "Is that so?" I asked. He nodded again. "I just have nothing to say to you," he said, and I told him I understood. After my mother and I washed the dishes together, she showed me a photograph from forty years ago. In it, my father had a full head of dark curls. His eyes were alert and his smile untroubled. I was perched in his lap like a small pet, staring up at him as if I had just noticed he was there. All five of my fingers could fit around his thumb. Everything that would follow in the years to come might never happen. "This was such a nice day," said my mother, stroking the photograph. "You probably don't remember, do you?" I had forgotten what her smile looked like, so I told her I remembered it perfectly.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: He sat in the chair by the window, where he always sat, though I wasn’t sure if he recognized the chair. He had been writing about the Bible, about anti-Semitism, about something urgent, something that had mattered. He looked at me and said he was proud of me, but then added, almost apologetically, that he had nothing to say to me. I nodded back. We sat, the three of us, not saying anything. He looked out the window, or at the window. My mother left the room and came back holding a photograph. “This was him,” she said. “Forty years ago.” I looked at it. She held it up next to his face, as if she could prove something that way. He did not look at the picture. He closed his eyes. My mother sighed. Later, she would tuck the photo back into the album, where it belonged. He would remain in his chair, where he belonged. I would leave, where I belonged. It was not that we did not love each other, only that love had become a kind of stillness, a sitting together, a waiting for words that had already been forgotten.
