My mother gently reminded him that he was writing about the Bible and anti-Semitism. "Oh yes," he said, "that's right," and nodded as if to confirm this to himself. While the three of us ate supper, he turned to me and told me that he was quite proud of me. "You are a good kid," he said. "Always have been." "Is that so?" I asked. He nodded again. "I just have nothing to say to you," he said, and I told him I understood. After my mother and I washed the dishes together, she showed me a photograph from forty years ago. In it, my father had a full head of dark curls. His eyes were alert and his smile untroubled. I was perched in his lap like a small pet, staring up at him as if I had just noticed he was there. All five of my fingers could fit around his thumb. Everything that would follow in the years to come might never happen. "This was such a nice day," said my mother, stroking the photograph. "You probably don't remember, do you?" I had forgotten what her smile looked like, so I told her I remembered it perfectly.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: He sat in the chair by the window, where he always sat, though I wasn’t sure if he recognized the chair. He had been writing about the Bible, about anti-Semitism, about something urgent, something that had mattered. My mother told him this. “Your work,” she said. “You’ve been writing about the Bible.” He nodded, as if this was something he could accept, though not something he quite believed. He looked at me and said he was proud of me, but then added, almost apologetically, that he had nothing to say to me. I nodded back. We sat, the three of us, not saying anything. He looked out the window, or at the window. My mother left the room and came back holding a photograph. “This was him,” she said. “Forty years ago.” I looked at it. She held it up next to his face, as if she could prove something that way. He did not look at the picture. He closed his eyes. My mother sighed. Later, she would tuck the photo back into the album, where it belonged. He would remain in his chair, where he belonged. I would leave, where I belonged. It was not that we did not love each other, only that love had become a kind of stillness, a sitting together, a waiting for words that had already been forgotten.

written_by_MFA027.Excerpt1: I barely recognized my father when I entered the kitchen, which was probably because he completely failed to recognize me. All my life I had felt only he knew my name. I was a stranger to everyone else, even to my mother, whose voice had repulsed me ever since I was a girl. I probably should not have said this, but I was relieved when I realized I was not the only fact of his life he forgot. "What was I when I was?" he asked my mother in the kitchen. She ran to the bookcase. "You wrote this all yourself," she told him, extra nasally. "It was a Bible on the Bible. A seminal take-down of anti-Semitism." I could tell he was not listening. Then suddenly he turned to me. Suddenly I was me again. When he said my name I returned to my skin. "What are you?" he asked me, and when I told him, his eyes filled with something I recognized. "If I had any words left I'd spend them on voicing just how proud I..." he stuttered before a long pause. "I have nothing to say," he whispered. Night fell again. When he went to sleep in the kitchen I was not sure he would wake up, but my mother decided tonight was a fine time to dig up their 40-year-old wedding pictures. "He is a gorgeous man," she said, then yawned the word "was."
written_by_MFA027.Excerpt2: I visit my father and immediately notice new changes. The way he holds his coffee cup with both hands now, like a child. The way his eyes move around the room without settling. When I ask about his work, he stares at the wall behind me. My mother quickly fills the silence: "Tell her about your writing on the Bible, dear. The anti-Semitism research." He nods, but I can see he's already forgotten the prompt. "I'm proud of you," he says to me suddenly, then adds, "though I have nothing to say." I wonder if this is what therapy feels like - this careful observation of painful things while maintaining a scholarly distance. Later, my mother pulls me aside to show me a photograph. "Look," she says, "this was forty years ago." In it, my father stands straight-backed beside a podium, papers spread before him like fallen leaves. I notice how his collar sits perfectly against his neck, how his hands rest purposefully on the wooden edge. My mother's fingers tremble slightly as she returns the photo to its drawer. I think: This is how we measure time now - not in years or months, but in the growing distance between who he was and who he is becoming.
written_by_MFA027.Reason: Excerpt 2 follows a clear emotional progression where there is recognition of change and the some reflection before it ends with the photogarph scene which is symolic off how time passes."This is how we measure time now - not in years or months, but in the growing distance between who he was and who he is becoming.".This excerpt shows how there is indeed some kind of change.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: My father, a stranger in his own house, sits hunched in his armchair, a shadow of the man I knew.  His eyes, once bright and full of life, are now clouded with confusion.  He struggles to remember what he's working on, a question met with a sigh and a shake of his head.  My mother, her face etched with worry, reminds him gently, "Your writing, dear, on the Bible and anti-Semitism."  A flicker of recognition crosses his face, a brief spark in the fading embers of his mind.He looks at me, a ghost of a smile touching his lips.  "My daughter," he says, his voice a fragile whisper, "so proud of you."  But the light fades quickly, replaced by a vacant stare.  "Nothing to say," he murmurs, lost in the labyrinth of his own thoughts.  The silence that follows is heavy, filled with unspoken words and a growing sense of loss.Later, my mother shows me a photograph from forty years ago.  My father, young and vibrant, stands with his arm around her, both of them radiating joy.  My mother's voice cracks as she speaks, her words laced with a quiet despair.  "It's like he's already gone," she says, her eyes filled with tears.  I look at the photograph again, the image of my father frozen in time, a stark contrast to the frail figure sitting in the other room.  The weight of his absence, even in his presence, settles over me, a heavy cloak of sorrow that I cannot shake off.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: I had gone there and didn’t know what to do after I’d gone there. At my father’s house, I entered his study where he sat at his desk staring at his hands. Next to his hands, his work––book stacks on biblical theology and anti-Semitism. I stood behind him. I stared at his hands. This was a turning point of sorts of ours, his hands, our staring at them. So many hours of ours went to this, had come to this. I thought: when did we get here? And: what do I do now, now that we’ve gone here? My mother came in and laid her own hand on his shoulder. She said, “Gerry” which was my father’s name, “Gerry, remember, you were working on your essay on biblical theology and anti-Semitism.” She made a sweeping motion with her hands before him. When he finally saw me, he said, “My daughter…” and told me how proud he was of me and all that I’d been doing. Then he said he had nothing else to say to me. He went back to his hands. Later that evening, my mother and I sat in the dining room together, where she showed me an old photograph of my father. “What happened to him?” my mother said, and I couldn’t tell her. I couldn’t even come close to saying.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: Excerpt 1 paints a picture and makes you feel like you are actually in the scene with this family, experiencing what they are experiencing. Excerpt 2 is just kind of telling you thinks that are happening- not describing and immersing you in the world. Excerpt 2 is also hard to follow sometimes, specifically this section: "I stood behind him. I stared at his hands. This was a turning point of sorts of ours, his hands, our staring at them. So many hours of ours went to this, had come to this. I thought: when did we get here? And: what do I do now, now that we’ve gone here?". Excerpt 1 has beautiful descriptions and flows nicely.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: In the heart of Charles de Gaulle Airport, where the Parisian winter raged outside, a vision of timeless beauty emerged amidst the sterile expanse of the terminal.  A striking woman, her skin kissed by the sun like ancient amber, her eyes pools of liquid obsidian, moved with the grace of a lioness through the bustling crowd.  A flowing, emerald-green kaftan draped her form, its edges embroidered with intricate symbols that whispered of forgotten civilizations.  A necklace of hammered gold, adorned with a single, luminous pearl, rested against her throat, a relic of a time when emperors and empresses ruled the world.For a fleeting moment, she was an apparition from a forgotten era, a goddess who had wandered into this modern temple of travel.  Her presence was a stark contrast to the gray, snow-covered landscape outside and the hurried, harried travelers who scurried around her.  She was an oasis of exoticism and tranquility in a desert of steel and glass.As I stood behind an elderly Dutch woman in line, her eleven suitcases causing a commotion due to their excessive weight, my gaze drifted back to the enigmatic woman.  She was gone, vanished into the crowd, leaving behind only a lingering scent of jasmine and a sense of profound wonder."Only anything other than that is impossible," the ticket clerk chuckled, his eyes twinkling, when I inquired about the possibility of love at first sight.  His words echoed in my mind, a reminder that in the realm of human experience, the extraordinary often lies hidden in the ordinary, waiting to be discovered.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I stood in line with my luggage at the Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris when my eyes landed on the most striking woman in the building, perhaps the most striking woman I’d ever seen; her pearly skin, antiquated dress and golden eyes gave her the aura of a masquerading goddess who’d absconded from her oil painting. The cardigan draped around her neck popped with magenta zags and her gold necklace turned the bleachy overhead lights to warm shine. With the grace of a lioness, she stepped out of sight and I lost her. I waited for my chance to pursue her down the terminal hall, but an elderly Dutch woman haggled with the clerk in front of me, producing short vehement barks about the weight of her eleven suitcases. There was time to plan. I looked around for an avenue for conversation with the beauty ahead, assuming I might never catch her, and found myself gazing at the snow falling like ash outside, silent out there, a perfect contrast to the balmy and chatty world inside the terminal. I edged around the Dutchwoman and her astonishing pile of luggage, which could easily fill a cargo barge, hoping for another glimpse of the leoline woman. There she went, distant now, turning left at the junction down the hall, heading in the same direction I soon would--there was still a chance. “Is love at first sight possible?” I asked the clerk when my turn came. He smiled. “Anything else is impossible,” he replied.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: excerpt  one was too confusing and distracting from the beginning I had to read and reread several times to organize the words in my head. The words felt as if they were physically placed one by one as compared to excerpt two which has a smoother flow. Much more engaging.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: I saw her emerge from the December mist of Charles de Gaulle like an apparition from the ancient kingdoms of Mali, her skin the color of honey-glazed chestnuts that reminded me of those afternoons in Cartagena when the sun would melt gold into the sea. She moved through Terminal 2F with the deliberate grace of a lioness, her caftan catching whispers of air that seemed to carry the scent of frankincense and myrrh, though later I would learn it was nothing more than the perfume of duty-free shops mixing with the aroma of croissants from Paul's bakery. Her eyes, set like amber stones in an Ethiopian crown, caught the fluorescent lights in such a way that made me believe she had lived a thousand years, perhaps more, and had witnessed the rise and fall of civilizations that existed only in forgotten dreams. The snow outside fell with the determination of white butterflies against the glass walls, while inside, the terminal maintained its eternal springtime, as if nature herself had conceded to this woman's presence. I might have followed her forever through the labyrinth of gates and shops, but fate, with its peculiar sense of humor, placed me behind an elderly Dutch woman who carried eleven suitcases and argued with mathematical precision about each gram of their weight, her voice rising and falling like a baroque opera. When I finally reached the ticket counter, my head still swimming with visions of the mysterious woman, I asked the clerk, a man with a mustache that seemed to have been drawn by a child's uncertain hand, if he believed in love at first sight. "Monsieur," he replied, adjusting his tie with the gravity of a philosopher, "in this airport, the only impossible thing is to find a reasonable price for a cup of coffee."
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: In Paris I spotted her walking gracefully in short suede heels, a timeless click to her step on the shiny floors of the Charles de Gaulle Airport. She was magnificent, her limbs like tributaries each meeting at the river made by her dark and wavy hair. Her eyes, though I could not see them, were certainly slant and blue. Fortuitously she sat some feet away from where I stood in line at the counter, crossing her ankles neatly beneath her in the French way, and at last I could admire a charoite skirt and matching cinched blazer that met the milky skin at her thighs and neck. The whole of her became a river to me then, or perhaps instead a lioness paused to drink at cool water; soon, I knew, she would be gone, and the springtime warmth and vibrancy brought by her into this terminal would fade to match the great blank whiteness of snowy winter beyond our shared space. Infatuated as I was by this lion-headed goddess, it took me some time to process the bickering before me, an elderly woman with a thick Dutch accent and some eleven suitcases haggling with the ticket clerk over their weight and associated cost. Returning my attention to the woman cloaked in purple and, for the time being, likewise cloaked in the wholeness of my affection, I missed the ticket clerk calling me forward after the Dutch woman had been sorted. I smiled a wide and generous smile. “Do you believe love at first sight is impossible,” I asked him, and tilted my head gently so that he might see the object of my sighted love.The clerk, evidently harried, was still inspired to smile at the glimpse of an exceptional woman. “In Paris,” he told me, “Anything other than such a love is impossible.”
written_by_MFA026.Reason: I felt that both excerpt s were coherent.  Probably equally so.  The fluency in both was similar as well, however I did feel that some of the sentences in excerpt 2 were a little wordy and diminished the quality of the description at times.  They could have been broken up into two sentences, or they were not necessary at all. I think this affected the effectiveness of he excerpt for me, which made excerpt 1 a better choice for me to clearly understand what was being said.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: The moment I saw her, I was convinced that time had halted to let her pass—a striking woman who seemed neither of this world nor any other. Her skin was the sun-dappled bronze of desert sands at twilight, her eyes the unfathomable green of jade worn smooth by centuries of whispers. She moved with the languid elegance of a lioness in repose, her steps unhurried yet commanding, as if she carried an invisible crown. Her long scarf of woven gold and crimson thread draped over her shoulder like a relic stolen from Byzantium, glimmering faintly under the harsh fluorescent lights of Charles de Gaulle. The terminal swirled with the metallic clink of luggage carts, the nasal calls of final boarding, and the mingling scents of espresso and frost melting off winter coats. Outside, snow veiled Paris, but inside, the air buzzed with the restless vitality of spring—a contradiction that matched her presence. Behind an elderly Dutch woman stubbornly arguing with the ticket clerk over the weight of eleven battered suitcases, I stood transfixed, calculating how the infinite could fit into the brief arc of her passing. When my turn came, I mumbled a question to the clerk about love at first sight. She glanced up, her eyes carrying the faint smirk of someone long weary of life's questions. "Impossible, monsieur," she replied with practiced precision. "Only everything else is." I laughed, but it was hollow, for the woman who had remade time itself was already gone.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: Walking into Charles de Gaulle Airport, I saw a woman, exotic and striking in her beauty. Astonished, I stood frozen in the terminal as I gazed at her timeless features. Her skin was dark and glowed with youth, her eyes were clear as a glacial lake. She wore a garment of gold and red fabric that looked as though it came from a culture that was entirely unfamiliar to me, and I stood for a long time admiring it, as though in a trance. Her look suggested an aura of antiquity, and she moved in grace like a lioness, striding confidently across the bright, balmy terminal that contrasted with the snowy world beyond its walls. In a moment, she was gone, her presence as fleeting as it was alluring. I took my place in line, and for a moment I found myself distracted by an elderly Dutch woman who took it upon herself to argue with the ticket clerk about the weight of eleven suitcases, “I’ve weighed them at home,” she said, “they can’t possibly be more than 10 kilograms—” and by the time I reached the front of the line I found myself in a pensive and dreamy mood. Who was that woman of such incredible mystery and poise, whose eyes shone so brightly? Smiling, I asked the ticket clerk if he believed in love at first sight. He laughed and replied that of course he did, how could he not. "Anything short of this , would be impossible", the clerk said.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: Excerpt 2 is better written and more understandable. Excerpt 1 feels cumbersome to understand. It feels like an attempt to show intelligence and not an attempt to communicate. Sun-dappled, centuries of whispers and spring-a contradiction are all terms that make excerpt 1 difficult to read. The writing of course is understandable but difficult to.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: "It's amazing, how the same things that happen between a man and a woman can be so different simply because of their race." She paused, swirling the wine in her glass, the crystal catching the light. "Before I came here, I never really thought of myself as Black." The table, a mix of faces, both familiar and new, leaned in, intrigued. "But here, suddenly, I'm not just Ifemelu, I'm a Black woman dating a white man." She let out a small, humorless laugh. "It's like this whole other layer gets added, this… awareness, this constant hum in the background that you can't quite ignore." "But things are so much better now, no?" The Frenchwoman, her accent a delicate lilt, tilted her head. "You couldn't even… you know…" she trailed off, gesturing vaguely. "Marry each other?" She finished for her, feeling the familiar sting. "Yes, we've 'progressed.' Now we can be together, but we still have to tiptoe around all the unspoken things." She took another sip, the wine warming her throat, loosening her tongue. "Like, I can't get too angry, can't disagree too strongly, because then I'm not just Ifemelu, I'm the angry Black woman." "Oh, but that's…" the poet, his brow furrowed, shifted uncomfortably. "I mean, surely, it's not…" "Food's getting cold, don't you think?" Blaine, ever the diplomat, interjected smoothly. But she was on a roll, the words tumbling out, fueled by the wine and years of unspoken frustrations. "And it's not just him, it's everyone. This constant… need to remind me how far we've come. As if I should be grateful." She looked around the table, their faces a mixture of fascination and discomfort. "You know, 'Remember when you couldn't even have a drink at the same bar?' As if that somehow makes everything okay now." "But…" the poet started, but she cut him off. "It's like this weird performance, you know? Always being aware of how I'm perceived, what I represent." She met Blaine's eyes across the table, his expression unreadable. "And sometimes, I want to… scream, to break free from this invisible script that everyone seems to have for me." A heavy silence settled over the table. She knew she was oversharing, knew she'd regret this in the morning. But tonight, the wine had given her a voice, a raw, unfiltered voice. "Like with Curt, for example…" she began, feeling a new wave of memories, a new wave of honesty, washing over her.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Ifemelu looks at her Frenchwoman host and her American husband, both grinning with rows of straight teeth, and puts down her wine glass. The wine loosens her tongue and she cannot help it when she says, "America is obsessed with race. I never realized how much until I moved here and now I can't get away from it." She speaks quickly, the words coming easily to her despite the many eyes now firmly fixed on her. With her captive audience, she could almost be a college professor, the kind that reminds her of cult leaders. The watching usually makes her skin crawl, but now it feels like the eyes are attached to ears that are earnestly listening. written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: The wine had softened the edges of her caution, and Ifemelu found herself speaking with the kind of raw honesty that would later keep her awake at night. "You want to know about being black in America?" she said, watching the poet across the table touch her water glass nervously. "I'll tell you something nobody says at these nice dinner parties. In Nigeria, I was just me. Then I came to America and became black, and suddenly everything changed. Even love changed." She paused, feeling Blaine's eyes on her, his expression unreadable in that way that meant he was already preparing for the aftermath of her words. "You talk about progress, about how interracial marriage is legal now, as if I should be grateful for permission to love. But let me tell you what it's really like. It's lying awake at night, next to someone you love, wondering if you should mention the casual racism at his family dinner. It's smiling when his friends make those little jokes, those little slips, because you don't want to be that angry Black woman who can't take a joke. It's watching him discover racism like it's a new thing, while you've been carrying it on your back since the day you landed in this country." The Frenchwoman's husband shifted in his chair, his liberal discomfort a familiar sight, but Ifemelu pressed on, the truth spilling out like wine on white tablecloth. "And the intimacy, oh, the intimacy is the worst part. Because in bed, in the dark, you wonder – does he see my skin? Does he see past it? And which would be worse?" She laughed, a sound with edges sharp enough to cut. "Then there's the performance of it all, ndi oma. The nice progressive couple at the farmer's market, at gallery openings, at dinner parties like this one, where everyone pretends we're all the same underneath, where I must be just Black enough to be interesting but not enough to make anyone uncomfortable." The other guests leaned forward, titillated by her frankness, as though she were telling them gossip instead of truth. She could feel tomorrow's regret already forming, but the wine urged her forward, made her bold and reckless. "Should I tell you about Curt?" she asked, watching the poet's bangles jingle with anxiety. "Now that's a story about race in America."
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: "It means something different, to be Black here. Something wide and heavy, and I wasn't expecting that, when I moved. You can meet someone, and they can seem perfect for you. But if they're white - when you go outside, that's all anyone cares about. Their whiteness, your Blackness. And you have to dodge the dirty looks people give you on the street. And if you want to talk about that, with your partner - suddenly you're the bad guy. You can't bring up how racism makes you feel because all of a sudden they're defensive and angry, they think you're calling them a racist. And they can't understand, really, what it feels like to be looked at the way people sometimes look at me. Like I'm nothing, or less than nothing." As Ifemelu spoke, Blaine's lips were pressing into a thin, straight line. He looked studiously at his fork, refusing to meet her eyes. A part of her brain cautioned her to stop talking, but the wine had made her tongue heavy and her jaw loose. "People are always saying to me - fifty years ago, you would have been locked up if you tried to date a white man, look at how far this country has come! That's all people ever want to talk about, how much progress has been made. Everyone expects me to be so grateful and happy to be here, but all I can think about is how awful it feels sometimes, to live here and always be thinking about how other people are seeing me." Ifemelu paused. Her own words were echoing in her ears, and she felt the stinging truth of them. The poet seized upon this break and pointed down at his plate. "How did you make these Brussels sprouts?" he said, and the French host seemed not to hear him at all; her eyes were trained on Ifemelu. "But why so pessimistic?" she asked, almost breathlessly, leaning in like Ifemelu was delivering scandalous gossip. "Maybe the people in your past were just wrong for you in some way. Maybe they're skewing your perception." Ifemelu drained the rest of her glass and tightened her fingers around the stem. "The people in my past didn't skew my perception - they showed me the truth," Ifemelu said bitterly. "Let me tell you about this one man I used to date - his name was Curt."

"You want to know about being black in America?" she said, watching the poet across the table touch her water glass nervously. "I'll tell you something nobody says at these nice dinner parties. In Nigeria, I was just me. Then I came to America and became black, and suddenly everything changed. Even love changed." She paused, feeling Blaine's eyes on her, his expression unreadable in that way that meant he was already preparing for the aftermath of her words. "You talk about progress, about how interracial marriage is legal now, as if I should be grateful for permission to love. But let me tell you what it's really like. It's lying awake at night, next to someone you love, wondering if you should mention the casual racism at his family dinner. It's smiling when his friends make those little jokes, those little slips, because you don't want to be that angry Black woman who can't take a joke. It's watching him discover racism like it's a new thing, while you've been carrying it on your back since the day you landed in this country." The Frenchwoman's husband shifted in his chair, his liberal discomfort a familiar sight, but Ifemelu pressed on, the truth spilling out like wine on white tablecloth. "And the intimacy, oh, the intimacy is the worst part. Because in bed, in the dark, you wonder – does he see my skin? Does he see past it? And which would be worse?" She laughed, a sound with edges sharp enough to cut. "Then there's the performance of it all, ndi oma. The nice progressive couple at the farmer's market, at gallery openings, at dinner parties like this one, where everyone pretends we're all the same underneath, where I must be just Black enough to be interesting but not enough to make anyone uncomfortable." The other guests leaned forward, titillated by her frankness, as though she were telling them gossip instead of truth. She could feel tomorrow's regret already forming, but the wine urged her forward, made her bold and reckless. "Should I tell you about Curt?" she asked, watching the poet's bangles jingle with anxiety. "Now that's a story about race in America."
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: "It means something different, to be Black here. Something wide and heavy, and I wasn't expecting that, when I moved. You can meet someone, and they can seem perfect for you. But if they're white - when you go outside, that's all anyone cares about. Their whiteness, your Blackness. And you have to dodge the dirty looks people give you on the street. And if you want to talk about that, with your partner - suddenly you're the bad guy. You can't bring up how racism makes you feel because all of a sudden they're defensive and angry, they think you're calling them a racist. And they can't understand, really, what it feels like to be looked at the way people sometimes look at me. Like I'm nothing, or less than nothing." As Ifemelu spoke, Blaine's lips were pressing into a thin, straight line. He looked studiously at his fork, refusing to meet her eyes. A part of her brain cautioned her to stop talking, but the wine had made her tongue heavy and her jaw loose. "People are always saying to me - fifty years ago, you would have been locked up if you tried to date a white man, look at how far this country has come! That's all people ever want to talk about, how much progress has been made. Everyone expects me to be so grateful and happy to be here, but all I can think about is how awful it feels sometimes, to live here and always be thinking about how other people are seeing me." Ifemelu paused. Her own words were echoing in her ears, and she felt the stinging truth of them. The poet seized upon this break and pointed down at his plate. "How did you make these Brussels sprouts?" he said, and the French host seemed not to hear him at all; her eyes were trained on Ifemelu. "But why so pessimistic?" she asked, almost breathlessly, leaning in like Ifemelu was delivering scandalous gossip. "Maybe the people in your past were just wrong for you in some way. Maybe they're skewing your perception." Ifemelu drained the rest of her glass and tightened her fingers around the stem. "The people in my past didn't skew my perception - they showed me the truth," Ifemelu said bitterly. "Let me tell you about this one man I used to date - his name was Curt."

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: Ifemelu took another sip of her chardonnay. She knew she should let the subject drop, but the wine was giving her a slight buzz that made her feel emboldened, and she suddenly felt they all needed to hear what she had to say. "Racism is nowhere near over in America," she said, "despite what we may tell our white friends and lovers because we don't want to make them feel uncomfortable." She gestured with her wine glass, pointing at her hosts, then at herself. "The truth is, I've never been more aware that I'm Black than I have been since coming to America. In Nigeria, I hardly thought of my race. But here, I'm constantly reminded of it, and not just by racists and rednecks like you might think, but by white liberals, academics, even other Black people, to tell you the truth. And to make matters worse, I can't say anything about it, or I'll be seen as making a fuss since we've apparently come so far. They'll point out that I have a white boyfriend and no one gives me any trouble for it, when interracial marriage used to be illegal. They call that progress when that's the bare minimum. Frankly, it's patronizing." Ifemelu looked pointedly at the poet, who had kept her head down and was picking at her salad. The poet avoided her eye contact and instead turned to the hostess, as if she sensed an opportunity to change the subject. "This salad is so delicious," she said, holding up a forkful of greens. The hostess thanked her, but she was still watching Ifemelu with anticipation and maybe some detached amusement, since this wasn't her home country, and Ifemelu had said nothing about France. Her American husband, meanwhile, seemed excited to have his cadre of polite and well-educated liberals challenged by this unfamiliar woman, his friend's new girlfriend. Ifemelu reached for the wine glass again and looked up at Blaine to see if she'd gone too far, but his gaze was inscrutable, though fixed on her. Well, if what he loved about me is my mind, he can't be mad if I speak it, she thought. And if she said something too scandalous, she could always write them an apology note later. And before she could stop herself, she was telling them all the deeply personal stuff about her struggles while dating Curt.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2:
You know," Ifemelu said, pausing just long enough to sip from her wine glass, the red liquid pooling against her lips before she swallowed, "America is a country where you don't realize you're Black until you’re already inside it, moving through it, breathing it. And then, suddenly, you are." She looked at the poet, the one with the too-smooth bald head and the vaguely British accent that made him sound more thoughtful than he really was. He shifted in his seat. She had said something that made him uncomfortable, which meant she had said something true. "It’s funny," she continued, ignoring the way Blaine was watching her, his face unreadable, "how love is supposed to make you forget these things. As if race is a scarf you can slip off when you’re with someone who loves you. But it’s always there, waiting, pressing against your throat."  

The Frenchwoman, her teeth unnaturally white, gave a performative sigh. "But we have made such progress, no? Fifty years ago, interracial love was illegal!"  

Ifemelu laughed, a dry, humorless sound. "And what am I supposed to do with that? Be grateful? Tell myself I am lucky that I can now hold my white boyfriend’s hand in public without being arrested? That’s like telling me I should celebrate because women can now vote. It's not a gift. It's not progress. It's just removing something that should never have been there to begin with."  

The poet, desperate now, reached for his fork, stabbing aimlessly at the roasted carrots on his plate. "This is delicious," he muttered, and Ifemelu almost felt sorry for him, because what else was he supposed to say?  

"Race in America is like the weather," she said. "You can pretend it's not there, pretend that the sun is shining, but at some point, it will rain. And when it does, some of us will have umbrellas, and some of us will just get wet."  

A silence settled, the kind that stretched and pulled, thick with the weight of something unspoken. Ifemelu glanced at Blaine, saw the way his jaw was set, and knew there would be a conversation later. Maybe an argument. Maybe a quiet, careful "I think you were too harsh." But for now, she felt the soft, warm buzz of the wine, the thrill of having said something raw, something true. And when she said, almost offhandedly, "Curt used to say he didn’t see color," she knew she was not finished yet.
written_by_MFA005.Reason: P2 was my preferred excerpt. It felt more immediate from the first sentence - as readers we feel more closely connected to Ifemelu as we read that the wine pooled against her lips rather than she just sips it, somehow - we identify with her much strongly from the first, the writing feels more personal as we see the other guests very much through her eyes. The analogies felt more effective also - e.g. the weather reference

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: Holme kept to the road that wound long into a landscape of ash and cinder, charred trees skeletal in their moorings of roots twisting up through a hellscape of the dead. He walked on. Further on he came to a swamp that fell nightmarish on his eyes in all its nakedness of trees and dark figures dimly hominoid seemingly skulking in the mire. With a wary toe he tested the swampwater and reeled backwards at its unsure footing of bog and moss, crags of rock wet against the backdrop of windcurrents clashing the sodden vegetation and his feeling of desolation. He would not go this way. Retracing his steps back to the road and setting out upon it again he soon saw a man up ahead. The man tapped and swept a walking stick before him, feeling his way through that forever darkness only the blind knew the language of. The man smiled at Holme as he passed. Where the blind man was going Holme had already been, and Holme wondered then if anyone had informed the man of the grimness of what lay ahead at the end of the road. Walking on he lingered on what was not lost on him, the blind man’s incapability of seeing the burnt-out trees or even the road before him, not ever knowing where he’s going, but still following the road. No, he thought. He didn’t know where he was going.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: The road stretched out before Holme like a wound in the earth, ash drifting across its surface in spectral waves that moved without wind. The charred and twisted trees rose up from the swampland like ancient mariners frozen in their death throes, their blackened limbs reaching toward a colorless sky that held neither sun nor promise. He tested the mire with one boot and watched the earth shudder and contract like something alive yet unborn, the surface dimpling and rising again in slow persistent waves that spoke of depths best left unplumbed. Through the dead forest came a sound like bones rattling, though there was nothing there but naked branches clicking together in a wind that seemed to carry voices. Then came the blind man, tapping his way along the road's edge with a stick worn smooth as glass, his face lifted in permanent expectation, smiling as if he knew some secret that the seeing world had lost. Holme watched him pass, this prophet of the wastes, and thought how the man's blindness might be a mercy in such a place as this. For what use were eyes in a world become nothing but ash and shadow, where even the trees had forgotten their own names and stood like sentinels at the gates of some darker realm that lay just beyond the next bend in the road, waiting with infinite patience for travelers who would never return.

It feels like a great story teller has weaved together just the right words to help truly grasp what exactly is happening. Excerpt 1 just feels like each sentence was given a very heavy period after each thought.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: He walked down the empty road. There was nothing there but charred remnants of trees now quivering in a sullen breeze. The land, like Holme, was ash-strewn and barren. It was all black and gray and there was nothing else. Further along he passed into a swamp made up of naked trees and other dimly hominoid forms that moved too slowly and caught their breath at each others' fingerlike edges. Holme tested the swampy mire. It spat at him then sucked his foot deeper as the wind picked up through the clashing trees, through their cavernous notchhole mouths. He took a step back. Retracing his steps Holme came across a blind man on the once-empty road, tapping his way along with a surprising calm. His step was sure. The blind man acknowledged him with a smile, though Holme was standing still and had offered no greeting. The man’s shirt was stained rust red. Has anyone told him? The irony was dark and clean. Empty too as was everything else. He was tapping his cane on to nowhere. Holme let pass this sign of life on a futile journey. Was it better to know? No, a gift to be unseeing. There is nothing to see. I have been ruined by all the nothing. Holme turned away from the blind man and pulled his jacket close to him. Behind, where Holme was heading, the sky had already blackened.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: The road lay before him, a trail of ash and dust, a ribbon unfurling through the skeletal remains of a forest.  Charred trees clawed at the sky, their branches like the limbs of the damned, twisted and broken.  The air, thick with the taste of ash, lay heavy on his tongue, a grim reminder of the world's passing.He ventured on, the road leading him into a swamp, a place where reality seemed to fray at the edges.  The trees, stripped bare, stood like specters against the gray sky.  Strange forms, vaguely human, lay half-buried in the mire, their faces obscured by the mud.  He prodded the soggy ground with his boot, and it shuddered beneath his weight, a living thing, a beast of the earth.  The wind whispered through the reeds, a mournful sound, and the trees swayed and creaked, their branches clashing like bones.He turned back, the path ahead too treacherous, too unreal.  And there, on the road, he saw a blind man, tapping his way along with a cane, a strange serenity on his face.  The man smiled, a smile that held no malice, no despair, just a quiet acceptance of his fate.  Did he know where he was going? Had anyone told him that the road led nowhere, that the world had ended?He watched the blind man disappear into the distance, a figure of futility in a futile world.  The road stretched on, a path to oblivion, and the wind howled, a lament for the living and the dead.

The inclusion of the blind man in the second excerpt felt more like a minor observation whereas it felt like it was the substance of excerpt 1. The final sentence in excerpt 2 was more effective way of describing the futility and desperation of the situation.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: Holme walked on. He walked until the vast indistinct openness through which the road passed gave way to swampland and the road itself grew muddy and damp, enshadowed by dense clusters of naked trees through which Holme thought he glimpsed flickering forms of dimly hominoid creatures making strange lurching movements in the distance. A cold wind howled through the vegetation and the mud grew deeper until he reached a point where setting his boot in the mire Holme felt it sucking on his leg as if into a deep bubbling pit. No way forward. He retraced his steps. A while along the way he’d come he encountered a hunched old man tapping his way down the road with a stick. The man raised his face and Holme saw two voids where his eyes should be. Yet though he could not see Holme the blind man sensed him and smiled in greeting. Holme wondered if the man sensed also the desolation around him or if someone had described it or directed him to the grim swamp to which he now headed. He thought of warning the blind man but did not. For in truth he thought there’s no better fate on the other end.

The blind man’s face was tilted skyward, the hollow sockets veiled in shadow, and yet a smile touched his lips as if he knew some secret. Holme felt the weight of the question press against his ribs: who had told him where this road would lead? Or had the knowing been the blind man’s alone, a truth borne in darkness?

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: There are times when to long for something is almost as satisfying as to finally receive it, or when the essence of that which is desired is evoked so clearly that to receive it is no longer necessary. As when one yearns to pluck a berry from the vine and savor its ripeness, so that the sweetness seems to precede the taste of the juice itself. Sylvie had said earlier that in springtime we could pick berries here. I searched for Sylvie's hand beside mine, but I found that she had slipped away silently and left me alone in the clearing. Yet in some way, I felt I could sense her closeness and thought she might be watching me from the woods, so I showed no change in my expression and pretended to be ignorant of my solitude. Around me, the sun cast long shadows through the partings of the tree branches, from which the browned leaves had already begun to fall into the clearing. A thin layer of frost was formed on the mud around where I sat. I imagined forming out of this cold clay earth a statue of a woman whom I would adorn with rare flowers. She would be a calm presence standing among the trees, not the cold, hard pillar of salt into which Lot's wife was transformed as punishment for her desire, for turning back with regret to look at all she had lost. A figure free of yearning, around whom the wild children of the forest would gather to marvel at her beauty and warmth. They would take solace in the vivacious beauty of such a figure and cling to her almost as a mother, even as her frozen hands could not caress them as one would their own children. Again I looked for Sylvie and thought of how I was, in searching for someone who had left me, not unlike the poor woman who had been turned to salt. Unlike the taste of those imagined berries, I was not sure if my longing for connection could ever be quite enough to evoke the presence of the thing itself.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: The taste of a berry is sweetest when it has been tasted a thousand times in anticipation, the bloom of a flower most lovely when it has been craved through a winter.Sylvie had disappeared without a word, and I was alone.She might have been hiding in the woods, watching me, and I pretended I did not know it, and I called her name, and she did not answer.I looked up at the slope of the mountain, where it was white with dogwood, and thought I would make a statue of a woman, tall and quiet, and set her there among the trees.She would be like Lot's wife, but not in that she was barren and regretted what she had left behind.She would be beautiful and hands would be full of lilies and wild roses, and the children would come and lean against her knees, and look up at her face, and think she was their mother, though her hands were too cold to touch them.They were wild, and orphans, and not my children, and I was not her.I have spent my life watching, not to see beyond the world, merely to see, great mystery that is plainly before my eyes.I think concept of transcendence is based on a misreading of creation. With all respect to heaven, scene of the miracle is here, among us.The eternal is idea much less preposterous than time, and this very fact should seize our attention.In certain contexts, improbable is called miraculous.What is eternal must always be complete, if my understanding is correct.So it is possible to imagine that time was created in order that there might be narrative – event, sequence and causation, ignorance and error, retribution, atonement.A word, a phrase, a story falls on rich or stony ground and flourishes as it can, possibility in a sleeve of limitation.Certainly, time is occasion for our strangely mixed nature, in every moment differently compounded, so that often we surprise ourselves, and always scarcely know ourselves, and exist in relation to experience, if we attend to it and if its plainness does not disguise it from us, as if we were visited by revelation.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I closed my eyes and thought about the nature of longing, how it shapes itself around absence like water flowing into an empty vessel, becoming more precise in its form the more complete the void becomes. Sylvie had left in that way of hers, without sound or ceremony, as if she had simply dissolved into the thick afternoon air, and I found myself studying the treeline where the shadows gathered, imagining her watching me pretend not to notice the solitude she had left behind. There is something about craving that makes the thing craved more vivid than itself could ever be—like the memory of a wild berry's tartness being sweeter than the actual taste, or how the thought of rain can feel more quenching than the drops themselves when they finally fall. I began to imagine crafting a statue, not of cold marble but of living stone that would draw up minerals from the earth like a tree draws sap, and I would place her among the pines where the light filters down in dusty columns. Unlike Lot's wife, who turned to salt in her backward glance of regret, this woman would be adorned with rare blooms that only grow in the deepest parts of the forest, and her face would hold all the forgiveness that Lot's wife could never find. The wild children—for there are always wild children in these woods, moving like shadows between the trees—would gather around her feet, marveling at the strange flowers that crown her head, at the way her stone hands, though forever still, seem to reach for them with infinite tenderness. They would sense in her something of mothers they barely remember, of homes they might have had in some other life, and they would leave small offerings at her feet: interesting pebbles, abandoned birds' nests, fragments of colored glass that catch the light like trapped pieces of sky. And I thought perhaps this is what Sylvie and I were both seeking: not the thing itself, but the holy shape of its absence, which holds more truth than presence ever could.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I’ve realized that craving and fulfillment are not connected in the way I once thought. A craving is so intense and visceral that it cannot be truly satiated by consuming the thing you want. For example, berries are always sweeter before I eat them. I wonder if that’s how Eve felt in the garden after she tasted the forbidden fruit—disappointed, hungry, running her tongue over her teeth in search of satisfaction. I’ve been thinking about Sylvie, and how she disappeared silently into the forest and left me alone. I suspected she might be hiding somewhere, watching from a perch atop a spruce tree or huddled inside a hollow log. She liked to tease me. I didn’t want to give her the satisfaction of calling out for her, making her think I was afraid of being alone. I didn’t want her to feel like she’d rescued me by returning. I meandered around the little clearing and looked at the great towering tree trunks and their long shadows and the patches of grass poking up from the dark earth. In the center of it all, I imagined a statue. She was carved from some kind of pale, luminescent stone, something that seemed to give off its own light from within. Rare flowers were twined in her hair—orchid doves, lenten roses, midnight clematis. Blossoming vines wound up her body, not trapping her, but protecting her. My statue was a radiant mother, utterly unlike the barren, remorseful wife of Lot. She was vibrant and forgiving, always surrounded by children who marveled at her quiet beauty. The children, wild vagabonds of the forest, would be drawn to her through some mysterious summons, and they would huddle before her and bask in her gentle solace. Though her frozen hands would never touch them, she would look upon them with a kindness they had never known, and their happy tears would feed the vines and flowers that had made her their home. When the children were with her, they were not orphans, but children who had been made to be loved by a mother.

written_by_MFA009.Excerpt1: Sometimes I wonder about the difference between craving something and fulfillment. Sometimes I want something so much I feel like I’m going to break open. written_by_MFA004.Excerpt1: The morning air reunited Clarissa Dalloway with Bourton, her younger face and younger days, her eighteen-year-old solemnity. She had a bright evening ahead, an ambition to entertain Rumplemayer's men. She was in wonder among the flowers, having traversed the market in lieu of her servant, Lucy. The young girl deserved a break, an evening to mind her own affairs. What else was a girl but this? But back to Bourton, where the air had kissed Clarissa's cheeks like the finest gentleman, where Peter Walsh had teased her over breakfast, asserting that cauliflowers were surely superior to men. He was on a sojourn in India, which he'd detailed in rambling letters. His letters were stiffened by truisms, cloyingly personal, a bore to spend one's evening with. What Clarissa recalled most were his teeth, their hue of yellow, not unhygienic but telling of inferior genetics. He had a laugh like a doctor's, inappropriate. He'd tell you about your muggy insides, then chuckle because there was nothing wrong with his. But alas, the flowers. Lavender or Rose? This called to mind Peter again and his oddly feminine smells. That he smelled unlike a man endeared Clarissa to him. Scent was a signature, a tell of how one moved through the world. To share a scent with a woman, one must also share her sensibilities, her gentleness, her sense of utter safety. If Peter were to return early, to meet Clarissa in the market right then, she'd recognize his teeth first, then his scent. She'd think how familiar the dull yellow of his mouth was. Admittedly, his remaining details might strike her as unfamiliar.
written_by_MFA004.Excerpt2: Clarissa Dalloway, a woman of exquisite sensibility, stepped out into the vibrant London morning. She had decided to buy the flowers herself, a small act of consideration for Lucy, her servant, who was already bustling about with the preparations for the evening's gathering. The crisp air carried a hint of the past, and Clarissa's thoughts drifted back to Bourton, her childhood home. She remembered the mornings there, the dew still clinging to the roses, the world awakening with a freshness that was both exhilarating and solemn.At eighteen, the world had seemed to stretch before her, a tapestry woven with infinite possibilities. Now, years later, the edges of that tapestry had frayed. But some threads remained bright, indelible marks on the fabric of her memory. Peter Walsh, with his sardonic wit and his penchant for the dramatic, was one such thread. "I prefer men to cauliflowers," he had declared one morning at breakfast, his eyes twinkling with amusement.Clarissa smiled at the memory. Peter was returning from India soon, his letters filled with tales of his adventures and misadventures. He was a man of contradictions, capable of great passion and profound melancholy. Clarissa had always found him both exasperating and endearing. His return would stir the waters of her well-ordered life, she knew, but it was a disruption she welcomed. For Peter, with all his flaws and foibles, reminded her of a time when life was less predictable, less constrained by the conventions of society. He was a relic of her youth, a symbol of a time when her heart was still open to the world, before the disappointments and disillusionments of adulthood had begun to close in.

The crisp air carried a hint of the past, and Clarissa's thoughts drifted back to Bourton, her childhood home. She remembered the mornings there, the dew still clinging to the roses, the world awakening with a freshness that was both exhilarating and solemn.At eighteen, the world had seemed to stretch before her, a tapestry woven with infinite possibilities. Now, years later, the edges of that tapestry had frayed. But some threads remained bright, indelible marks on the fabric of her memory. Peter Walsh, with his sardonic wit and his penchant for the dramatic, was one such thread. "I prefer men to cauliflowers," he had declared one morning at breakfast, his eyes twinkling with amusement.Clarissa smiled at the memory. Peter was returning from India soon, his letters filled with tales of his adventures and misadventures. He was a man of contradictions, capable of great passion and profound melancholy. Clarissa had always found him both exasperating and endearing. His return would stir the waters of her well-ordered life, she knew, but it was a disruption she welcomed. For Peter, with all his flaws and foibles, reminded her of a time when life was less predictable, less constrained by the conventions of society. He was a relic of her youth, a symbol of a time when her heart was still open to the world, before the disappointments and disillusionments of adulthood had begun to close in.
written_by_MFA004.Excerpt2: The morning air reunited Clarissa Dalloway with Bourton, her younger face and younger days, her eighteen-year-old solemnity. She had a bright evening ahead, an ambition to entertain Rumplemayer's men. She was in wonder among the flowers, having traversed the market in lieu of her servant, Lucy. The young girl deserved a break, an evening to mind her own affairs. What else was a girl but this? But back to Bourton, where the air had kissed Clarissa's cheeks like the finest gentleman, where Peter Walsh had teased her over breakfast, asserting that cauliflowers were surely superior to men. He was on a sojourn in India, which he'd detailed in rambling letters. His letters were stiffened by truisms, cloyingly personal, a bore to spend one's evening with. What Clarissa recalled most were his teeth, their hue of yellow, not unhygienic but telling of inferior genetics. He had a laugh like a doctor's, inappropriate. He'd tell you about your muggy insides, then chuckle because there was nothing wrong with his. But alas, the flowers. Lavender or Rose? This called to mind Peter again and his oddly feminine smells. That he smelled unlike a man endeared Clarissa to him. Scent was a signature, a tell of how one moved through the world. To share a scent with a woman, one must also share her sensibilities, her gentleness, her sense of utter safety. If Peter were to return early, to meet Clarissa in the market right then, she'd recognize his teeth first, then his scent. She'd think how familiar the dull yellow of his mouth was. Admittedly, his remaining details might strike her as unfamiliar.

Also in excerpt 1 I got a much better feel for what Peter represents to Clarissa whereas in excerpt 2 I felt like the focus was oddly on Peter's mouth and teeth...which may have some symbolism but it is hard to tell out of context.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Mrs. Dalloway, stepping out into the June morning, thought how she would fetch the flowers herself, for Lucy had quite enough to manage with those men from Rumpelmayer's coming. The fresh air caught her face (how young she felt, how perpetually astonished!) and sent her mind spinning back to Bourton, to those mornings when she was eighteen, when she would burst out onto the terrace and feel the world pause, crystalize, become both solemn and effervescent in that early hour. Peter Walsh (he was coming back from India, his letters said) had laughed at her that morning at breakfast, saying she preferred men to cauliflowers — how like him to say such a thing, to pierce through to some truth while making it all seem ridiculous! His letters, scattered now across her desk at home like fallen leaves, still carried that sharp wit, that capacity to wound and heal in the same breath. And how strange it was, she thought, pausing at the corner of Bond Street, that while whole years dissolved into nothing, that single moment remained: Peter's fork suspended, his eyes twinkling with mischief, the morning light streaming across the breakfast table at Bourton. The way he would tilt his head when amused (she could see it now, with perfect clarity) while all else blurred and shifted like patterns in water. For that was what memory did, was it not? It preserved these fragments, these bright shards of experience, while whole seasons fell away into darkness, into that great pool of forgotten things that lay beneath the surface of one's daily life.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: She had decided to buy the flowers herself, to spare Lucy the trouble — Lucy, who was rushing about with preparations for the party, and Rumpelmayer’s men were about also; Yes, thought Mrs Dalloway, I will buy them myself. It was all coming together as many parties had done before, with great bustle, and would come together in the end as all parties do, as did those parties from her youth when she was not the host. And the fresh morning air returns her to younger days at Bourton, stepping out into other early mornings — how exhilarating it was then, and how solemn also, to be eighteen and just beginning. The chill this air carries, and the slow warmth rising into one’s cheeks, and ears, and hands. What had Peter said to me: something about cauliflowers, about preferring men to cauliflowers. A conversation over breakfast with Peter Walsh, always teasing then; still teasing now, albeit separated by so many years and kilometres. Clarissa thinks of his letters, the glint in his eye she can still feel in those pages — his promise, too, steady as his voice, to return from India, to return and to see her. Cauliflowers! Such a thing to remember as clearly as if their breakfast was shared only yesterday, when in fact yesterday Clarissa had been deciding about the flowers, deciding to buy them from the yellow and blue shop she now rapidly approaches, with the vibrant window displays; the freshest flowers, she knew, those with the richest and most enduring smell, must come from this shop, and now she would buy them herself.
written_by_MFA026.Reason: I prefer Excerpt 1. It stirs feelings of nostalgia and pondering the passage of one's life, the moments that stand out. It hints at there being something more between this Peter and the narrator. Perhaps an unspoken fondness, hidden by childish teasing as suggested in mentioning the letters in which Peter possesses "that capacity to wound and heal in the same breath."

written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: Clarissa stepped into the brisk morning air, her gaze lifting to the soft haze of London streets, a breath catching in her chest, carrying with it the scent of fresh blooms and the faint rumble of Rumpelmayer’s men unloading their crates. She would buy the flowers herself, sparing Lucy the trouble, and in the act, indulging that faint, persistent thrill of slipping out unencumbered, her steps crisp, her thoughts unfurling. Bourton, as if summoned by the cool touch of the breeze, rose vivid before her. The mornings there had carried a peculiar gravity, the air saturated with the promise of youth, of life, at eighteen—the world trembling on the cusp of discovery. She could feel it still, the dewy grass against her shoes, the sharp burst of laughter carried on the wind, and Peter Walsh, always Peter, his voice teasing yet tethered to something deeper. “I prefer men to cauliflowers,” he had said once, over breakfast, as if the absurdity of the phrase could mask the intensity beneath it. And now, after all these years, Peter was returning. From India, of all places, with letters she could scarcely recall opening properly, their pages crammed with the tangents of a restless mind. She had always thought of him as a man on the edge of some revelation, never quite within reach. His words lingered, some sharp, some softened with time, like the murmur of a distant wave retreating. Yet it was the texture of him she remembered most—the way his presence filled the room, the peculiar weight of his silences. The day unfolded before her, rich and strange, and as the sunlight broke through the fog, she felt herself poised, a solitary figure on the cusp of past and present, out in the world, yet curiously, utterly alone.
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: She was in danger of a mood; if I am to remain still, Clarissa thought, it will overtake me, it will make the world unwelcome with me, turn it dim and desiccated, and poor Lucy will bear the brunt, or Rumpelmayer’s men, who were laying the table. “I’ll do it,” Clarissa said, and she said it again, as if worried that the words had not escaped the confines of her thought, “I’ll get the flowers, Lucy.” She left the house. Outside, it was almost Bourton—the air was sharp, like a country wind, she thought; at eighteen, in Bourton, it had felt more like a gale; yes, at eighteen years old, simply placing one foot in front of the other had lent Clarissa purpose—a stroll around the garden was as grand as an expedition to India. Yes, at Bourton, the thought of sending Lucy would not have arisen; Clarissa would purchase the flowers and admire them freely. But in London, a strong wind carried the brine of the Thames; it stank; it irritated her lungs, her heart; the odor of the flowers would, too. And there came Peter Walsh, sailing in on an airy, unnamed ship, saying, “What match is a cauliflower for a man?” (Around his voice, Clarissa recognized the faint crunch and tinkling of a decade-old breakfast.) Peter will return from India like that—on which date and at which time his ship would dock in England should have been unimportant to Clarissa, and yet she wondered; she called up his last letters, filed away in a familiar groove, and read them again, and with each word, London decayed, fell away like petals, and in its place, she erected another cathedral. Inside it, relics, some potent to the touch, some no more than shriveled digits, long-empty boxes.
written_by_MFA032.Reason: Excerpt 2 is a little better than excerpt 1. Excerpt 2 is descriptive and it flows well. It provides deep insight into the characters thoughts, feelings and, actions, achieving its purpose with interconnected ideas. It is coherent and powerful. The excerpt provides vivid imagery and makes it easy for the reader to visualise and feel emotion.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: The elevator hummed its ascent , its metallic echo chamber filled with the rustling of starched white coats and the hushed murmurs of worried voices.  Doctors and nurses, their footsteps brisk and purposeful, pressed against me, their faces etched with lines of clinical concern.  A woman, her hand clutching a crumpled tissue, sobbed softly in the corner, her body trembling with a grief I could not touch.  The tinny voice of the intercom announced, "Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine," its monotone a stark contrast to the silent anxieties swirling within the elevator's steel box.I stood amidst this symphony of human emotion, my heart a steady drumbeat against my ribs, my purpose clear.  I was going to see her, the woman who had entrusted me with her memories, her fears, her hopes, woven into the very fabric of the bag I had crafted for her.  I would smile, offer gentle words, tell her how the bag, her bag, was a masterpiece, a testament to her strength, her resilience.  I would ask her to try it on, to feel the weight of it, the way it settled against her, a perfect fit. And then, as her eyes lit up with a flicker of trust, a spark of recognition, I would watch her heart, that fragile vessel of memory, beat against her chest, a tiny bird trapped within a cage of ribs.  I would slice the shears through her skin and cut her heart out. I'd hold her heart in my hands, its warmth a perverse comfort, its rhythm a dark symphony. And then, I'd claim the bag, mine alone, its rightful place by my side, its true purpose fulfilled.The elevator lurched to a halt.The shears lay nestled in my pocket, their sharp blades whispering promises of possession, of a bond that would be mine alone.It was the the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: I approach the hospital elevator. It is almost full up with nurses, doctors, and their patients. I slip myself between the heat of their bodies, which are all dressed in blue gowns or white coats. I press the button six. A voice comes on over a speaker hidden somewhere up above. “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine,” the voice says. It repeats the words as the elevator whirs into motion and begins to rise. I wonder where in the building Dr. Y could be. I look down at the bag in my hands, admiring my fine craftsmanship–the softness of the leather, the straight, simple lines of my stitches. I have made it for the woman exactly to her specifications. It is undeniable. “Look,” I will say. “Look what I have made for you. See how beautiful it is?” I will offer it to her to try on. She will be grateful, of course, and in awe of the beauty of my hard work. She will try it on, adjusting the straps to her liking. She will arrange it this way and that: cross-body, or dangling from her fingers, or slung carelessly off the shoulder. “Do you trust me again?” I will ask. In the face of the beauty of the bag, she will have no choice but to say yes, to be nothing but thankful. And then, after she has given me her trust, I will take out my sheers and use them to cut out her heart. The heart and the bag will be mine alone to claim. My grip tightens on the sheers that I keep tucked behind the bag. The blades are long and sharp. They are a silver so bright that it flashes in the glare of the overhead elevator lighting when I sneak a look down at them. The elevator dings; we have arrived at the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA006.Reason: Response 2 seems to be very vivid and makes a lot of sense, in the sense that you can easily and freely follow the story with the hope that you will get the full understanding. The choice of words used are very simple, and they make a lot of meaningful statements.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: The elevator doors opened. It was crowded, so I pushed my way inside. Doctors and nurses stood shoulder to shoulder in one corner. I joined the patients and visitors that grouped in another. The doors closed, and the elevator began its ascent. The tightly packed bodies offset the hospital's sterile smell. I had been told that I would find Rin on the sixth floor. I clutched the bag I brought for her, made heavy by the shears within. I wondered if she'd notice the care I put into making her bag the same way I noticed the care with which she used to tend her shrubs. Before her accident, she'd rise early to trim them, and I could see her from the window of my workshop. Watching her felt almost voyeuristic at first. The precision with which she used her shears excited me, reminiscent of the delicate way I stitched my handbags. We rarely spoke, but perhaps watching her in this way made me envy her. I had seen her work, but she had never seen mine. I planned to present her with the bag, one of the best I'd constructed, as a gesture of good will in hope of regaining her trust. I would politely request she accept the bag, and see if she admired it the way I admired her shrubs. Then I would remove the shears. I imagined that revealing them to her, while she was in such a helpless state from her injuries, would cause alarm. After all, I could easily plunge them into her, trim around her chest like one of her shrubs, and cut away her heart. She'd be helpless to stop me, and I could claim the bag I made for her alone. written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: The elevator opened onto the third floor, and I flattened myself against the side as a patient and his doctor exited. “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine,” said the intercom. On the fourth floor, two nurses entered the crowded elevator. As I was forced into the corner, I heard “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine” bleat over the intercom again. I had two more floors left before I’d reach hers. Whether Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine appeared or not, I had a plan, infallible and precise. I would see her, lying prone on her hospital bed, and hold up the bag. “I have to apologize for everything,” I’d say. “I made this bag for you. I crafted it myself.”“How lovely,” she’d respond, her voice lax from the painkillers. “How many pockets does it have?”“Six,” I’d say. “What material did you use to stitch it together?” “Cowhide. It feels like a baby’s cheek. Feel it,” I’d say. “Please, feel it.”When she reached out to touch her finger on the belly of the bag, I’d lean over and, taking my shears out, throw away the hospital linens covering her body. Then, as her hand caressed the bag’s soft skin, I’d cut into her chest. I’d trim the strings of the heart first, the extraneous vessels and tissue that fastened it to her insides. Once it was freed, I’d toss the shears aside. Then I’d grasp it with my bare hand. In my palm, her heart would fit like a baseball. After it was done, I’d leave, my bag in hand, alone. “Dr Y. from Respiratory Medicine,” repeated the intercom. As another nurse shuffled past me, I clutched the bag to my chest. Its delicate construction couldn’t dull the shears hidden inside. Their blades were so sharp that, when the elevator moved upward once more, they pricked me. The elevator dinged for the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: I clutched the bag closer to my chest as the elevator ascended, surrounded by the sterile scents of antiseptic and floor cleaner. A young doctor in a white coat pressed against the back wall, studying a clipboard, while two nurses whispered near the buttons, their voices barely audible above the mechanical hum. The speakers crackled: "Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, please report to Ward 3." I watched the numbers illuminate one by one: three, four, five. The bag I had made was perfect—every stitch aligned with precision, the leather supple and warm like living skin. I had spent weeks crafting it, imagining her face when she would first hold it, how her fingers would trace the seams I had sewn with such care. Now it felt heavy in my hands, weighted with purpose, like the shears tucked carefully in my coat pocket. They were old and reliable, the kind my grandmother used for trimming roses, their blades still sharp enough to slice through fabric—or flesh—without resistance. "I've come to show you the modifications I made," I would say, smiling. "See how the clasp catches the light?" She would lean in close, trusting, the way she did before. Her heart would be exposed then, vulnerable beneath her hospital gown. I imagined it beating steadily, unaware of my intentions, like a bird resting in its nest. The elevator chimed for the sixth floor, and I stepped out into the fluorescent-lit corridor. A faint tremor ran through my hands—anticipation, perhaps, or fear. But I knew what I had to do. The bag deserved to be mine alone, freed from her unworthy grasp. I had created it, after all, breathed life into every fold and corner. As I walked toward her room, my footsteps echoing in the empty hallway, I felt a strange calm settle over me. The shears knocked gently against my ribs with each step, a quiet reminder of what was to come.
written_by_MFA007.Reason: Excerpt one has an unnatural flow. It keeps repeating the name: 'Dr Y from Respiratory Medicine' which interrupts your train of thought and makes the story harder to follow. I don't like the conversation held with himself in the middle of the excerpt as it just seems self-indulgent and unrealistic. The ending is too graphic which makes it seem weird. I much prefer excerpt 2 as it doesn't try to do too much. It tells the story in a natural, fluid way. Presenting one idea and then the next. It introduces the bag and that it might contain something important in a gentle way - at the start it says: 'I clutched the bag closer to my chest,' 'now it felt heavy in my hands, weighted with purpose'. I like this descriptive writing. It seems believable and you want to find out more. The description of her perceived thoughts on the bag are relevant and realistic. I like the use of metaphors to describe her heart. The ended is not too graphic but tells you enough so that the plot is effective.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: I stood in solitude in the grass field near the beach. Ten feet away, the grass gave way to sand, which then gave way to the ocean. The wind blew, scattering rubbish and abandoned belongings. An umbrella tumbled along the shoreline, and a plastic bag drifted past me. A wide variety of objects – presumably lost at sea or lost by patrons of the beach – washed up on the shore. I imagined that anything I’d lost throughout my life could be returned to me by those waves. Then I pictured Tommy approaching from the horizon, the hair on his legs wet and flat against his skin. I saw him wave at me, and was overcome by the pain of his absence. Tears welled in my eyes. I knew that he was not really there, Tommy had long since passed. Nevertheless, I found myself longing for him to come join me in the grass. I shut my eyes and stood still for a long moment. I dried my tears and became composed. I returned to my car, without looking back. Tommy was gone, I reminded myself. Life must go on.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: The field stretched barren before me, littered with scraps of rubbish that danced and swirled in the wind’s restless grip. Torn plastic bags snagged on brittle weeds, while papers tumbled past, their jagged edges fluttering like messages lost to time. I stood there, unmoving, as the chill seeped into my skin, anchoring me to the emptiness. It was then, amidst this desolation, that I let myself imagine. I pictured this field as a shore where all I’d lost had been washed ashore: friendships eroded by time, promises broken, dreams that had long slipped beyond my reach. And then, through the haze of this thought, I saw him. Tommy. He was walking toward me from the far horizon, his arm lifted in that familiar wave—assured, kind, so unmistakably him. For one brief, aching moment, it felt real, so vivid that I almost called out. But I caught myself, the breath halting in my throat as I reined the vision in, folding it away like something fragile. Tears welled, then fell, unbidden, but I held my composure. After a moment, I turned back to the car, its cold metal unyielding beneath my touch. Life waited, indifferent, as it always had.

The writer used a very simple choice of words in making the statement complete, hence having a great balance in all forms. It is therefore the best out of the two.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: Standing in that vast field, with discarded papers and empty bottles tumbling past in the wind, I found myself giving in—just briefly—to an old habit of fantasy. Perhaps it wasn't entirely sensible, but I allowed myself to imagine this desolate spot as a kind of gathering place, where all the things one has lost might eventually wash up. The thought came to me quite naturally, watching a plastic bag rise and fall in the gusting wind, that this could be where everything drifts to: old photographs, missed opportunities, unspoken words—all the things one somehow let slip away. And then, as though my mind had been waiting for just such a moment, I saw him—or rather, allowed myself to see him—Tommy, emerging from the hazy horizon, his hand raised in that familiar wave of his. But of course, one can't afford to let such fancies go too far. Even as I felt the tears sliding down my cheeks, I maintained a certain composure, the way one must. After all, what sense was there in pursuing these rather foolish thoughts? So I stood there a moment longer, letting the wind dry my face, before turning back to my car. There were things to be done, and one simply had to get on with them.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before. But now the world has filled it up with itself. Children’s playthings that were surely once my own, kites wrapped around a wayward branch, brought here as if they’d always been. Because maybe they always had. It gets so I can see Tommy now, coming up over the hillside, waving at me the way he used to––as if I was all he wanted and could want out of this life. There was a morning much like this one, only as far back as a month ago. I’d seen him as himself then, with that same wave, that same wanting. But now he wasn’t anywhere, and it makes me ashamed to say I feel less of that darkness now than I did then, the day after we lost him. Tommy isn’t anywhere on the hillside. I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it. I allow my feet to carry me back to the car, to head back into town for the night, with the hope that no one there knows my name.
