written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Marianne and Connell sit in silence, the weight of their unspoken feelings hanging heavy in the air. Their relationship, once a source of solace and shared dreams, has reached a crossroads. Marianne, ever the observer, has noticed a shift in Connell's behavior. He seems distant, preoccupied, and his eyes hold a flicker of uncertainty that she can't quite decipher. She wonders if she's no longer enough for him. Connell, on the other hand, is grappling with his own internal turmoil. He's aware of the changes within him, the growing sense of responsibility and the desire for a more conventional life. He knows that Marianne is the one person who truly understands him, but he also fears that their relationship is too intense, too consuming. As they sit there, the silence stretches on. Marianne breaks the silence, her voice barely a whisper. What's happening to us? she asks, her eyes searching for answers in Connell's face. He hesitates, unsure of how to articulate his own feelings. I don't know, he finally admits, his voice laced with regret. I think... I think we're growing apart. Marianne nods, her heart sinking. She knows he's right. They've both changed, evolved into different people, and their paths are diverging. Despite the pain, there's a sense of acceptance between them. They understand that this is a natural part of life, that relationships ebb and flow, that sometimes people grow apart. They hold onto the memories of their shared past, the laughter, the intimacy, the love that once bound them together. As they part ways, Marianne and Connell exchange one last lingering glance. There's no bitterness, no resentment, only a deep understanding of what they've lost and what they've gained. They walk away, their hearts heavy but their spirits unbroken. They know that they will always carry a piece of each other within them, a reminder of the love that once bloomed between them.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: Remember how different we were when we first met, Connell said. Marianne paused, face warmed by his shoulder. She thought that perhaps they were at the sort of height one jumps from and survives jumping from, that she would, despite the loneliness, be able to carry on from this: two plants sharing a large pot, space and light made for them both as their stems grew in opposite directions. Often she felt this way with her friends. Sometimes young friendships to her seemed featherweight and passing, and even in the depths of real connection, these relationships felt unimportant and survivable. Survivable, she meant, if they ended. But with Connell, she would not really survive losing him forever. Marianne could not imagine for them any real or permanent parting, nothing as serious as death. This moment between them was unlike that unfathomable permanence and unlike how she felt with friends, and bearable for it. She told him this.You've been the person who shaped my life, really, Connell said, who I am today. She shrugged against him and felt sick to imagine them parted but could see in that possibility an uncertain future that took nothing from their certain past. You were the first person to really see me, she said, and then laughed at herself, insecure. In this way, pieces of their early dynamic still clung to her: a certain unsteadiness that sometimes made her mean but never cruel. A feeling, perhaps, that despite all they had meant to each other, there was some part of her still unworthy and always seeking more of him. But Connell smoothed her hair and sighed, his inhaling chest elevating hers, and said sadly, We were made to make each other into adults, I think. For a moment they, attached to each other, shared breath in an afternoon marked by parting but not only by sadness.
written_by_MFA026.Reason: Para 2 is less straightforward to understand than excerpt  1, and less direct in its expression, but seems to me more realistic as a depiction of the complexities of human emotion. Para 2 focuses on the perspective of one character, rather than trying give a bird's-eye view of both characters, and this enables a more insightful and deep depiction of Marianne's emotions. Para 2 has more imagery e.g. "two plants sharing a large pot", rather than (as in excerpt  1) simply stating things outright.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: It was Saint Patrick’s Day, though there was no room for festivity in the hospital room where my mother lay suspended between this life and the next. Outside, the sunlight refracted sharply off the icy snow, casting a dazzling brilliance that mocked the stillness inside. Beside her, a bowl of green Jell-O sat untouched, its lurid color out of place in the solemnity of the moment. My mother’s eyes, blue and unyielding, remained open, vivid against the pallor of her skin and the muted sterility of the room. She was there but not there—unresponsive, yet undeniably present. I watched her, saw her dying like a fire slowly extinguishing into smoke, the embers of her vitality winking out one by one. Her eyes, once fierce with bitterness, shifted to bewilderment, and finally, to a quiet, unspoken heroism. They were the eyes of someone who clung to life even as it slipped from her grasp, a desperate yearning embedded in that piercing blue. The blue of her eyes became my lodestar, a symbol of her fight, her grace, her inevitability. And as I held her hand, I knew that when she closed those eyes for the last time, they would remain etched in me forever, as luminous as the snow outside.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: My mother died on St. Patrick’s Day. There was snow outside, and sunlight glanced off the ice and back into her hospital room. A cup of green Jell-O lingered untouched on its tray. My mother was unresponsive, but not quite asleep. Her eyes were open and vivid. There was an alertness in them still, but what she was looking at, I could not say. The bright blue of her irises was like a frozen lake, contrasting the dull wash of beige and gray shrouding the room. The sky lived inside my mother. It lived inside her then, too, even as we bided time together at the very end, knowing there was only one thing left for her to do. Her fading life was a fire flickering down to smoke—it would only last as long as there was something to burn. There was bitterness too in her eyes, then bewilderment, then a stoic, quiet heroism. A commitment to her own dignity. A promise to endure this final test, no matter how unfairly it had been imposed on her. Her eyes were so blue, my mother’s eyes, a fierce blue, a frozen lake, a sheen of ice that refused to melt, even as the sun broke it apart.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: I just lost a friend, and what Excerpt one describes is what I saw in her. The strength of the last sentence, that those eyes would stay etched forever, overpowers the description in two of a sun breaking ice. Both excerpt s are clear and fluent, but Excerpt one carries the emotions of such a moment.

written_by_MFA009.Excerpt1: It was Saint Patrick's Day when I watched my mother die, though there was nothing lucky about that bitter-bright morning. The sun bounced off snow banks outside her window, creating a cruel sparkle that seemed to mock the dimming light within. A cup of green Jell-O sat untouched on her bedside table – some nurse's attempt at festivity that now seemed obscene in its cheerfulness. My mother's eyes were the color of forgotten summers, a blue so startling against her pallid skin that it made my chest ache. They remained open, fixed on something I couldn't see, something beyond the sterile hospital walls and my desperate presence beside her. I watched death move through her like smoke through a burning house, slow and inevitable, claiming each room until nothing remained but ash. Those eyes – I saw everything in them. First came the bitterness, sharp as broken glass, then confusion that softened her face into something childlike, and finally, a quiet courage that broke my heart and rebuilt it in the same moment. The blue of her irises burned like pilot lights, struggling to stay lit even as the rest of her failed. Even now, I can close my eyes and see that color, that last fierce flag of life she waved, refusing to surrender until the very end. How wild it was, to watch someone both fight and accept their fate in the same endless moment.
written_by_MFA009.Excerpt2: It is one thing to know something and another other thing to live it. I knew that my mother would eventually leave. All of us eventually leave. I knew that it would be hard. It was Saint Patrick’s day. I’d brought her a green cup of Jell-O, which of course she didn’t eat. When she died, I had stepped into the bathroom. I was in the shower, running water through my hair. What a ridiculous place to be when someone dies. It wasn’t that I thought there would be some movie-scene ending. That she would wait to go until I was holding her hand, looking into her eyes. That death itself would wait until I could walk her to its door and burn with her until her fire turned to smoke and her sparkling blue eyes flipped through the stages of departure. From anger to confusion to something like heroism, the whispering heroism we all embody when we face our last moment. A heroism shining in the blue of her eyes, a deep, flickering blue which proclaimed how much she wanted to stay, here, with the rest of us, even as she left. I knew, after all, that death didn’t wait for anyone. And yet, no matter how much I thought I knew, when she went, what did I find myself shouting in my head? What other than “wait”?
written_by_MFA009.Reason: The first sentence of excerpt 2, " it was one thing to know something and...." made the writing very engaging very coherent. Excerpt one is very engaging too but is quite straight forward and has some interesting phrases such as "...claiming each room until nothing remained..." But I prefer excerpt 2 to excerpt 1.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: The winter light was dimming, Saint Patrick’s Day fading into a muted gray.  I sat beside her bed, the green Jell-O untouched on the bedside table, a festive offering she couldn’t partake in.  Outside, the snow was falling, the last of winter’s icy grip, the sunlight reflecting off the white expanse in a dazzling display.  But in this room, there was a different kind of dimming, a slow, inevitable burning down to smoke.She wasn’t asleep, not quite, but somewhere between here and there, her breath shallow, her body still.  Yet, her eyes, those strikingly blue eyes, remained open, vivid against the pale skin, the stark white sheets.  It was in those eyes that I saw it all unfold – the bitterness that had clung to her like a shroud, the bewilderment at the body’s betrayal, and then, finally, a quiet heroism.  The blue, so vibrant, so alive, was a defiance, a refusal to let go, even as the current pulled her away.I watched her, my mother, her spirit flickering like a candle flame in the gathering darkness.  And in those blue depths, I saw the echo of the life she had lived, the love she had given, the strength she had shown.  It was a story written in the language of the heart, a story that would live on, even as the last embers of her life faded away.

written_by_MFA031.Excerpt1: After our fourth week on the plantation, what had begun as horrifying became mundane. The muscle memory of sweeping Kevin’s constant stream of coffee mugs from the computer desk blended with the new habits of setting the table just well enough to avoid Margaret’s scrutiny. What was trivial to her was a mystery — sleeping with the master was fine, but leaving out a dish could mean being “fired”. I never realized how dailiness, even under the most brutal form of slavery ever conceived, could lull you into false security. On a Friday afternoon, Kevin snuck by to make small talk. “I never thought I would see you folding napkins at a dining table.” What the hell was wrong with him? I seethed back, “Do you think I’m doing this for any other reason than my survival?” He replied, “Well, of course not. But I don’t exactly like going into town making social calls every which way as the master’s errand boy either.” Before I could interject to explain the mortal difference between indentured servitude and slavery, he went on to say, “We should escape, take advantage of this insanity, and see things people in our time dream of. I’ve always wondered what the real Wild West was like.” In the fields outside, I heard someone moan in pain. “The real West? This is the real West, Kevin. The fieldhand slaves outside generate the profits that the master reaps from the government. The government will use his raw goods to wipe out entire bloodlines of Lakota, Sioux, and countless other tribes. And in 200 years, white men will let their imaginations run wild in the lands their great-great-grandfathers slaughtered empty.
written_by_MFA031.Excerpt2: Kevin sat by the window, staring out at the land he claimed was filled with opportunity. “Imagine it,” he said, his voice tinged with awe, “traveling west, seeing the land untouched and untamed.” His excitement was palpable, like a boy imagining adventures in a storybook, but I couldn’t bring myself to share it. “Untamed for who?” I asked, keeping my tone measured. He looked at me then, his brow furrowed in confusion. “Do you think the people already there see it as empty? Do you think they want explorers or settlers taking their homes, their lives?” He didn’t answer immediately, only turned back to the window. The days had been dragging on, each one blurring into the next. Kevin filled his time with idle musings and trivial social obligations, frustrated by the lack of stimulation. I filled mine with a monotony that, while easier than I feared, left me feeling complicit in something vile. Margaret's constant watchful eyes didn’t help; she wasn’t a threat like the physical punishments or the lashings some endured, but her presence unsettled me nonetheless. It wasn’t anything as simple as jealousy—it was something more insidious, a lingering discomfort I couldn’t name. When I finally spoke again, my words were bitter and sharp. “You’re fascinated by their myths, but they’re built on blood. While you dream of cowboys and frontiers, others are living nightmares of chains and whips.” He didn’t look at me, didn’t respond, and for a moment, I hated the silence between us almost as much as the world we were trapped in. It wasn’t just Margaret, wasn’t just Kevin. It was the slow, gnawing realization that we were adapting. That we were becoming something we swore we’d never be.
written_by_MFA031.Reason: Excerpt 2 feels more coherent as ideas are presented well and flow well together through the use of various literary devices. Fluency is there with the use of a range of descriptive language, metaphors and similes which brings the text to life for the reader. Overall, an effective piece with excellent sentence starters.

I’ve always wondered what the real Wild West was like.” In the fields outside, I heard someone moan in pain. “The real West? This is the real West, Kevin. written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: My husband’s plan, while shame-inducing, worked. The master of the house believed I was Kevin’s slave, not his wife. I felt awkward around the house’s slaves. written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I lay on the hard floor in the slave quarters, worrying about Margaret. I knew she was mean and vindictive, and looking for places to put her anger. She could get me whipped, or kicked out. Not for something as normal as sleeping with one's master - there were already slaves who were forced to do that. No, my transgressions would be more subtle - and so I would have to be on closer guard. I made a note to speak to Kevin about this. In the weeks we had been at the house, I'd notice how we'd both adjusted to our new life. I did the work of a slave with the same attitude I had done my chores as a child. Endless drudgery. Bowed heads when the white folks passed. And then dinner out back and a dreamless sleep on the floor. Meanwhile Kevin spent his days in the library; asking Tom questions about how to get out West. "Maybe we could escape, to California," Kevin had said, a few nights ago. "California's a thousand miles away," I said, shaking my head. "Even if we could forge convincing freedom papers, we'd probably die of dengue fever along the way." I didn't add the other thing I was thinking - that it wouldn't be any better out West, where Native Americans were being slaughtered. I couldn't stand to see Kevin get that mystified look on his face. The longer we remained in the house, the more aware I became of our differences.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I sat in the corner of the room, watching Kevin's face light up as he talked about exploring the West, and felt the familiar twist of unease in my stomach. The shame wasn't sharp anymore – that's what frightened me most. We had learned to live here, learned to accept the unacceptable with a casualness that made my skin crawl when I let myself think about it. The work wasn't what haunted me; it was the easy way we slipped into this life, like wearing someone else's clothes until they started to feel like your own. Margaret's presence loomed over us, not because she might seduce our master – that would have been too simple, too normal – but because she represented everything we were becoming: adaptable, compliant, surviving. Kevin didn't see it that way. His eyes held that historian's gleam, that detached fascination with a time he saw as a story to be witnessed. "Think of seeing the Old West firsthand," he said, and I had to bite back bitter laughter. I wanted to shake him, make him understand that while black bodies were being broken in these Southern fields, native peoples were being slaughtered in his romantic frontier. There was no safe place to stand and observe, no neutral ground from which to watch history unfold. We were in it, drowning in it, and our very ability to adapt was becoming our curse.
